title: Public Schools in the US
one_liner: Public K-12 education in the U.S. remains a tax-funded, non-profit utility-like sector with rising per-pupil costs, persistent workforce friction, and increasing state-local control over how federal dollars are used.
overview: The sector is financially and operationally large, with NCES reporting 99,073 operating public elementary and secondary schools and 19,183 operating districts in SY2024-25, serving 49,269,882 students (pre-K through grade 13 where available). The U.S. Census Bureau’s FY2024 release shows current spending per pupil at a record $17,619 and total elementary-secondary revenue of $994.9 billion, while major federal guidance in 2026 increased state-local flexibility through Ed-Flex and related transferability/AFUA mechanisms. NCES hiring data for the 2024-25 start showed that staffing stress remains elevated, but improved versus 2023-24, with fewer schools reporting broad hiring failure. Overall, growth in demand is moderate; cost and workforce composition are the main margin pressures.

baseline_2022.growth: 1.11% CAGR projected to 2027 in IBIS baseline (with 1.48% CAGR in FY2002-21 context)

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is mainly from government education funding streams: federal grants and formula funds, state appropriations, and local sources (notably property-tax-based support and other local school funding). Local governments are the dominant financing base because operations, payroll, and student supports are embedded in district budgets.

cost_structure.current_vs_capital: Current spending: $842.3 billion (85.6%); Capital outlay: $113.1 billion (11.4%)
cost_structure.labor_intensity: Instructional salaries were $291.8 billion (29.7% of total expenditures), underscoring payroll as the largest single cost category.

major_players: Local educational agencies and school districts
State and local taxing authorities (especially property-tax-sensitive systems)
Largest district operators: New York City schools, New York City area systems, New York State/Los Angeles Unified School District cohort context
current_dynamics: FY2024 finance data show top-line spending strength and a rising per-pupil trend while federal support is a shrinking share of total funding. NCES hiring indicators show persistent but easing vacancy pressure, with shortages concentrated in specialized positions. Policy is moving toward fewer federal operating constraints and more flexible use of federal dollars at the state and district level.
whats_growing: FY2024 current spending per pupil rose to $17,619 (+6.6% over FY2023).
Record FY2024 public school total revenue climbed to $994.9 billion.
Use of federal flexibility tools expanded, with 18 states using Ed-Flex by May 2026.
Community collaboration models shifted toward targeted operational supports and flexible staffing approaches in some systems.
whats_shrinking: Federal share of FY2024 public school revenue fell 4.4% to $115.1 billion.
Schools reporting difficulty filling non-teaching vacancies declined from 80% (2023-24) to 69% (2024-25) in NCES School Pulse data.
Use of school-wide community/wraparound model participation declined from 60% to 48% from 2023-24 to 2024-25.
recent_developments: Oct 17, 2024: NCES School Pulse reported 74% of schools had difficulty filling at least one certified teaching vacancy and six teaching vacancies on average at the 2024-25 start.
Mar 20, 2025: President Trump signed EO 14242, framing a policy shift toward school choice and state/local operational flexibility.
May 19, 2026: U.S. ED approved additional Ed-Flex waivers and reported 18 states using Ed-Flex, plus guidance on transferability and AFUA for greater discretion.
May 7, 2026: Census press release reported FY2024 current spending per pupil at $17,619 (up 6.6% from FY2023).
May 7, 2026: Census also reported FY2024 revenue of $994.9B and expenditure of $983.7B, with federal education revenue at $115.1B.
outlook: Short-term outlook is modestly positive on fiscal throughput but constrained by inflation-linked labor and health/safety service costs; per-pupil spending growth is likely to continue unless state and federal funding formulas tighten further. Enrollment is relatively stable in aggregate, so productivity, staffing quality, and fund-use flexibility will be the principal levers of performance in 2025-26.
themes: State-local flexibility as a defining policy trend
Rising per-pupil costs despite shrinking federal share
Persistent staffing gaps concentrated in special education/ESL and support roles
Technology-supported monitoring and school climate/wraparound service optimization
one_sentence: The industry runs on school-district operations financed mainly by state and local budgets, with FY2024 spending at a record in per-student terms and continued policy shifts toward greater state and local flexibility.

title: Public Storage & Warehousing in the US
one_liner: US warehousing in 2025-26 is being driven by continued e-commerce, omnichannel fulfillment, and integrated logistics demand, while labor intensity and rising operating costs keep margin expansion difficult.
overview: This industry serves as the midstream layer between manufacturers/retailers and end-market delivery, with facilities that hold, process, and dispatch goods for other companies. In 2025-26, growth is anchored by sustained online sales volume and resilience in last-mile-dependent categories, even as operators absorb tighter labor-market pressure and fluctuating freight costs. Long-term contracts and vertical specialization remain the main stabilizers, while integrated 3PL models are still taking share from single-function providers.

key_stats.market_size_source: Gross Domestic Product: Warehousing and Storage (NAICS 493) in ALFRED/FRED
key_stats.growth: n/a

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes primarily from contracted storage/warehousing space and handling fees under multi-year service agreements, with material add-on revenue from pick-pack, fulfillment, kitting, value-added processing, and transportation arrangement services. Top-line resilience is tied to contract renewal cycles and customer shift toward bundled supply-chain solutions rather than standalone in-house warehousing.
cost_structure: Labor is the dominant cost driver; BLS shows all-employee average hourly earnings at $26.85 in Jun 2026 (preliminary), while a leading logistics filing reported salaries, wages, and employee benefits around 42% of 2025 revenue and major operating expenses concentrated in transportation, warehouse labor, and facility/tech operations. Automation and systems spend are increasing as firms pursue throughput gains despite wage growth and productivity constraints.
current_dynamics: E-commerce remains a core pull: U.S. Census reported Q4 2025 e-commerce sales of $316.1B, up 5.3% from Q4 2024 (16.6% share). Major logistics providers are expanding data-center-related warehousing (including 7M sq ft announced by DHL), while leading real-estate operators report record lease activity but still guide mixed rent progression.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 demand for e-commerce fulfillment remains elevated with 2025 total e-commerce sales of $1.233T, supporting more short-cycle outbound operations.
Healthcare and data-center logistics demand is translating into new high-security, high-value warehousing capacity expansions.
Integrated 3PL models (storage + fulfillment + transportation + planning) continue to gain share, as noted by major operators’ disclosures.
whats_shrinking: Industry-level value-added productivity remains modest; BLS shows labor productivity and output-per-hour improved only marginally in 2024, reflecting cost pressures on margin.
Facility rent and energy headwinds remain uneven across metros, and operators report narrower pricing power outside high-demand nodes.
recent_developments: 2026-03-10: U.S. Census reported Q4 2025 e-commerce sales of $316.1B, +5.3% y/y, 16.6% of retail sales.
2026-03-19: DHL announced adding 10 dedicated North America data center logistics sites totaling more than 7M sq ft to launch in 2026.
2026-01-21: Prologis 4Q25 results cited 228M sq ft leases signed in 2025 and 95.3% owned-and-managed average occupancy.
2026-01-21: Prologis 4Q25 guidance included strong 2026/27-2028 Core FFO outlook and moderate rent-growth expectations.
2026-04-16: Prologis 1Q26 reported 64M sq ft of leases commenced and $1.783B development starts.
2026-01-07: DHL announced a dedicated 1M sq ft logistics center of excellence in Annville, PA for life sciences and healthcare.
outlook: Near-term, the sector should remain growth-positive in 2026 as omnichannel demand, healthcare, and hyperscale-adjacent distribution keep facilities utilization above recessionary lows, but margin upside likely depends on productivity gains from automation and selective service/pricing repricing in lower-barrier segments. The medium-term is likely to be one of slower but durable expansion through integration-led operators and continued concentration around carriers and logistics real-estate platforms.
themes: Integrated logistics consolidation
E-commerce fulfillment velocity
Labor efficiency vs wage pressure
Data-center and hyperscaler service infrastructure
Healthcare logistics specialization
Digital automation in warehouse operations
one_sentence: Third- and fourth-party operators are gaining share in high-touch fulfillment and healthcare/data-center storage niches, but margin growth is being constrained by wages, automation spend, and competitive pricing.

title: Public Transportation in the US
one_liner: US public transit is in a post-pandemic recovery phase, with riders, funding, and clean-fleet investment rising but still below full pre-2020 peaks.
overview: U.S. public transportation recovered strongly after pandemic lows, with unlinked passenger trips rising in 2024 and 2025 and operating activity supported by strong federal, state, and local support. NTD and APTA data show broad service rebound, especially on bus and demand-response products, while rail-heavy markets recover unevenly by city size. Funding intensity remains high, with the industry still dependent on subsidy-heavy operating models and increasingly tied to modernizing fleets, electrification, and service reliability investments.

key_stats.market_size: $96.3 billion total public transportation expenditures in 2024 (operations + capital), with approximately 3,000 reporting agencies, 3,000+ vehicles and about 380,000 public-transit workers enabled in daily service conditions
key_stats.growth: Ridership rose 9.8% from 2023 to 2024 (to 7.6 billion trips per NTD), APTA reported 7.7 billion trips in 2024 (+491 million vs 2023), and 2025 reached 8.07 billion trips (+5.3% from 2024 reported in APTA 2026 factbook)
key_stats.current_funding: FY 2026 FTA apportionments total $20.6 billion; about $14.6 billion in formula funding to states/UZAs/transit agencies

baseline_2022.market_size: US public transportation baseline in the 2022 IBIS snapshot was reported near $83.286 billion in annual revenue (2021 currency)
baseline_2022.growth: 2002-2021 CAGR: +2.42%; IBIS outlook at that time showed -1.06% projected annualized 2021-2027 revenue trend

how_it_makes_money.fares_and_user_revenue: Passenger fare and agency revenue was $16.9 billion in 2024 (23% share in operating funding mix)
how_it_makes_money.government_support: 2024 operating funding was dominated by local/agency sources at $24.4 billion (34%), state support at $18.3 billion (25%), and federal operating support at $12.4 billion (17%)
how_it_makes_money.capital_subsidies: 2024 capital funds were $11.5 billion federal (39%), with state at $5.6 billion (19%) and local/directly generated at $12.4 billion (42%)

cost_structure.opex_by_function: 39% vehicle operations ($25.9b), 20% general administration ($13.1b), 15% purchased transportation ($10.3b), 15% vehicle maintenance ($9.7b), 11% non-vehicle maintenance ($7.6b)
cost_structure.opex_by_object: Salaries and wages (33%), fringe benefits (26%), purchased transportation (15%), services/materials/supplies and utilities make up the remainder
cost_structure.labor_intensity: Labor-heavy model: 58% of operating expenses are salaries/wages and fringe combined

major_players: Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority
Bay Area and San Francisco operators
current_dynamics: Demand recovery is increasingly multi-purpose (work, shopping, health, and recreation), while fuel prices, staffing stability, and service reliability continue to influence mode choice. Agencies report improved bus accessibility and station/service technology deployment, while zero-emission bus uptake and electrification remain major transition vectors. Congestion pricing and office attendance recovery in anchor metro areas are creating localized ridership gains, but transit systems are still highly sensitive to appropriations timing and local matching rules.
whats_growing: Public transit rider volume is rebounding, with 2025 at 8.07 billion trips in the APTA 2026 factbook
Zero-emission bus deployment is scaling (hybrid/electric share moved from 7.0% in 2010 to 20.8% by 2025 in APTA reporting)
Demand for non-peak service variants (including demand-response use cases) remains supportive of ridership recovery in smaller and mixed-use labor markets
Federal and state transportation support remains elevated versus the pandemic trough with FY 2026 apportionment support
whats_shrinking: Commuter and rail mode recovery remains slower in some major cities versus bus-led rebound
Demand-response remains the highest-cost service bucket per rider, limiting broad profitability
Farebox-led recovery remains incomplete, with fares contributing less than a quarter of operating funding
recent_developments: 2024-2024: NTD 2024 report logged 7.6 billion trips, a 9.8% increase from 2023 (with 3,000 reporting agencies and 502 urbanized areas)
2025-05: APTA reported U.S. ridership at 7.7 billion trips in 2024 and 85% of pre-pandemic levels in first 2025 window
2025-09: APTA said 2025 Q2 ridership was 7.3% higher than Q2 2024 and had exceeded 2 billion trips in the quarter
2026-03: FTA published FY 2026 current apportionments totaling $20.6B, including $14.6B in formula transit support
2026-07: FTA announced $610M FY26 bus-program funding opportunity ($21M bus/facilities, ~$589M Low/No Emission)
outlook: Demand should continue to expand into 2026 as office and non-office travel stabilizes, especially in service-economy and mixed-use corridors. Near-term industry risk is still tied to federal-state-local funding alignment and payroll/service-cost inflation, but policy momentum from IIJA-era appropriations and clean-transit procurement supports capital and service upgrades.
themes: Ridership recovery is durable but still uneven by mode and metro size
Public funding mix remains critical to operating stability
Electrification and clean fleet modernization are accelerating
Bus-led recovery and accessibility investments are leading recovery in mobility
Congestion management and intermodal integration are strengthening transit competitiveness
one_sentence: The industry is expanding service demand and capital activity as public funding and lower congestion alternatives drive a gradual ridership rebound.

title: Pump & Compressor Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US pump and compressor makers are seeing low-single-digit equipment-demand growth in 2026, but margin expansion is constrained by price pressure, component costs, and consolidation.
overview: The latest publicly available segment metrics still show a smaller base than older IBISWorld totals due to narrower definitions. US industrial pump revenue is estimated at USD 5.28 billion in 2025 and USD 5.44 billion in 2026 (4.3% long-run CAGR from 2026–2033), while US air compressor demand is estimated at USD 3.69 billion in 2026. Industry activity is reinforced by sustained oil-and-gas, water/wastewater, chemicals, and industrial manufacturing demand, with increasing attention on smart pump and predictive-maintenance systems. At the same time, both domestic and imported component cost pressure is visible in manufacturing and import price indexes, and major players are increasing scale through M&A and digital-product integration.

growth.method: year-over-year proxy from Grand View US pump dataset

air_compressor_proxy.note: Used as adjacent segment context for broader pump/compressor thesis

key_stats.baseline_growth_proxy: 4.3% CAGR from 2026 to 2033 in US industrial pumps

baseline_2022.notes: Exports represented ~30.3% of 2022 industry revenue; imported goods represented ~40.4% of domestic demand in baseline file

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is primarily from sale of new pumps, compressors, and process components to industrial and utility customers, with increasing recurring revenue from spare parts, rebuilds, service contracts, upgrades, controls, and digital condition-monitoring/automation upgrades; software/data-driven optimization is increasingly bundled to justify higher equipment and service pricing.

margin_pressure: Price competition in commoditized equipment segments
Import substitution and international supplier efficiency
Higher inbound input costs, reflected in manufacturer and import price indexes
cost_structure.resilience_note: Aftermarket and service work has remained the stronger margin buffer in a competitive manufacturing environment.

current_dynamics: US crude oil production is being maintained at 13.5 million barrels per day in both 2025 and 2026 in EIA’s latest STEO update, supporting petrochemical, gas-compression, and pumping demand signals.
US industrial pumps are estimated at USD 5,280.3 million in 2025 and USD 5,437.4 million in 2026, indicating low-single-digit near-term growth.
Pump and compressor PPI and import price indexes remain elevated, indicating ongoing supplier and pricing pressure on original equipment and replacement parts.
Deal activity remains active: Honeywell completed a US$2.16 billion Sundyne integration, and ITT announced a US$4.775 billion SPX FLOW purchase.
Customer demand is increasingly favoring energy-efficient and digitally connected pumping systems that offer predictive maintenance and operational visibility.
whats_growing: US industrial pump revenue increase from USD 5,280.3m (2025) to USD 5,437.4m (2026), driven by ongoing infrastructure and industrial maintenance cycles.
Aftermarket/service share and retrofits tied to uptime, energy savings, and emissions goals are gaining share relative to pure greenfield replacements.
AI-enabled diagnostics, smart-pump controls, and remote monitoring are becoming standard in new equipment bids.
Water and wastewater renewal projects and process-plant reliability programs continue to support replacement demand.
Consolidation among major players is expanding service depth and portfolio breadth around fluid handling and compressor systems.
whats_shrinking: High-competition segments (standardized pump types) remain price-sensitive, limiting margin expansion.
Mid-cycle capex uncertainty in cyclical upstream/downstream sectors can defer discretionary upgrades.
Import-competitive pressure remains from lower-cost alternatives in select commodity pump and compressor categories.
The shift toward smaller niche local manufacturers is constrained by scale requirements for software integration, service footprints, and compliance capability.
Legacy standalone hardware-focused models without analytics/service layers are losing competitiveness relative to bundled solutions.
recent_developments: 2025-06-09: Honeywell completed its acquisition of Sundyne for US$2.16 billion, adding industrial pump and gas-compressor capabilities.
2025-10-07: EIA’s October STEO update revised U.S. crude production outlook to 13.5 million b/d for both 2025 and 2026.
2025-12-05: ITT announced a US$4.775 billion acquisition agreement for SPX FLOW with expected close by Q1 2026.
2026-05-22: Grand View Research listed US industrial pump estimates at USD 5,437.4 million for 2026 and a 4.3% CAGR through 2033.
2026-07-15: FRED showed Pump and Compressor Manufacturing PPI at 239.948 (Jun 2026, Dec 2003=100).
2026-07-17: FRED showed Import Price Index (pump/compressor manufacturing) at 121.0 in Jun 2026 (Dec 2013=100).
outlook: Base-line is modest but constructive: low-single-digit near-term growth on equipment demand, with higher-value capture concentrated in smart, service-linked, and energy-saving solutions. Supply-chain cost volatility and ongoing competition suggest margin upside is more likely from retrofit/service mix than pure volume expansion. A 2026–2028 outcome likely remains positive but uneven across subsegments.
themes: Energy process support demand
Industrial automation and IoT-enabled pumping
Aftermarket and uptime economics
M&A-driven product + service bundling
Cost pressure from materials and import inputs
Infrastructure and water/wastewater modernization
one_sentence: The U.S. market is moving toward higher-value service-heavy and automation-linked offerings as near-term pump demand remains tied to resilient industrial and utility activity.

title: Quick Printing in the US
one_liner: Quick Printing in the US remains a low-margin, increasingly niche retail-print segment as demand shifts toward digital channels and higher-value production jobs.
overview: Quick Printing in the US has transitioned from a volume-driven walk-in market into a short-run, customization and service-led segment. Demand pressure now comes from household and small-business digital self-service, high in-store substitution, and ad spend moving to measurable online channels, while surviving players add adjacent business services to maintain revenue.
how_it_makes_money: Walk-in and online quick-print demand for short-run documents, marketing collateral, signage, and custom stationery.
Higher-margin services around pre-press, finishing, binding, and custom promotional formats.
Bundled service sales (printing + managed workflow + shipping/fulfillment + digital document services).
BOPIS/same-day convenience for SMB document and marketing jobs.
cost_structure: High fixed labor and facility burden relative to transaction volume, consistent with declining throughput and modest margin dilution.
Material intensity in paper, inks, finishing consumables, and equipment utilization remains a major cost lever.
Industry data show print sector output pressure with rising unit labor costs and productivity stress in supporting manufacturing support segments.
Input costs remain volatile, while wage pressure remains relevant despite sector-wide demand softness.
current_dynamics: US consumer internet use is near-universal (96% of adults in 2025), enabling direct-to-home and self-service alternatives to walk-up copy/print tasks, while digital advertising accelerated to near-record levels and continues to pull marketing budgets away from traditional print channels; print-ad and commercial print-and-delivery demand is still under pressure in major local media groups.
whats_growing: Digital and programmatic ad growth, with US internet advertising at $294.6B in 2025 and +13.9% YoY.
Custom, higher-touch jobs (promotional graphics, branded materials, variable finishes).
Print-shop offerings that combine document services with shipping, packaging, and small-business workflow support.
AI-enabled ad targeting and design tools that shift SMB marketing spend toward measurable channels while still requiring print execution for events and campaigns.
whats_shrinking: Plain, commodity print jobs and routine document copying as SMBs perform more internally.
Traditional print ad-linked demand, including newspaper/consumer magazine ad segments.
Low-complexity one-off volumes that can be handled by office printers and online templates.
Industry enterprise base and local print-only footprint relative to broader business-services competitors.
recent_developments: 2025-06-18: Pew reported 96% of U.S. adults used the internet in its 2025 survey cycle, reinforcing substitution risk to in-store print tasks.
2025-07-01: U.S. Census Business Formation Statistics showed July 2025 business applications at 470,571 (seasonally adjusted), +2.6% vs June.
2025-09-30: Gannett’s 2025 Q3 filing noted Print advertising revenues decreased, with local print spend under pressure.
2025-12-30: AF&PA reported printing-writing capacity fell 13.9% in 2025 to 7.7 million tons.
2026-01-28: IAB forecast 2026 US ad spend growth at 9.5%, with digital expected to outpace other channels.
2026-05-01: The UPS Store media kit (updated May 2026) reported 5,503 U.S. locations and broader print/document-service positioning.
outlook: The industry is unlikely to reaccelerate in topline terms and should continue to contract at a slower pace than in the early 2020s, with profitable pockets concentrated in customization, same-day fulfillment, and mixed-service local hubs. Winners will be operators that reduce low-margin copy dependence, expand managed services, and secure recurring SMB workflows.
themes: Consolidation toward managed print + shipping bundles
Shift from commodity jobs to customization and brand touchpoints
Digital acquisition of jobs, physical fulfillment of outputs
Labor and scale compression in walk-in-first business models
Input volatility and high fixed-cost discipline in local print operations
one_sentence: The industry’s baseline remains declining, but operators that combine quick print, fulfillment, design support, and shipping services are best positioned for resilience.

title: RTD Coffee Production in the US
one_liner: U.S. ready-to-drink (RTD) coffee production is in a productivity-led expansion phase, with cold/iced formats, convenience-ready packaging, and retail innovation offset by tougher competition inside the broader RTD beverage aisle.
overview: IBIS World’s baseline framing (last updated 2021) described a fast-growing US RTD coffee production market with 2021 revenue of $4,024.0M and a move toward stronger competition from both imports and new entrants. 2025–26 commercial signals are still consistent with growth: the category has become more mainstream through grocery and convenience channels, while product development is shifting toward protein, lower sugar, and wellness positioning. At the same time, unit and dollar shares in beverage portfolios show only modest or flat movement, indicating a maturing category structure despite absolute market growth.

market_size.2022: $4.25B (derived from IBISWorld 2021 estimate and 5.53% 2022-2026 projected CAGR)

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers primarily generate revenue by selling shelf-stable bottled/canned RTD coffees in grocery, convenience, mass merchant, and foodservice channels.  Strong brand-led operators also monetize through partnership models: packaging and manufacturing is often supplemented by licensing, royalties, and co-manufacturing agreements, especially for global brands distributed through third-party beverage systems. In-store coffeehouse-linked franchises continue to funnel demand toward at-home packaged variants, creating a two-sided system between cafe innovation and national retail distribution.

cost_structure.raw_materials: Green coffee, milk/cream alternatives, sweeteners, flavorings, and syrup bases are the dominant COGS line items.
cost_structure.packaging: Cans, PET bottles, cartons, closures, labels, and cartons are major controllable costs with durability and shelf-life implications.
cost_structure.processing: Blending, blending consistency controls, filtration, pasteurization/aseptic handling, and quality/safety testing add significant variable and fixed costs.
cost_structure.supply_chain: Freight, cold-chain where required, and warehouse-to-retail distribution support are key cost drivers.
cost_structure.marketing: Shelf-space, category management, promotional pricing, and launch campaigns are increasingly important for new functional variants.

major_players: PepsiCo, Inc. (RTD coffee JV distribution under NACP)
current_dynamics: Demand is moving up-market: NCA reporting for Fall 2025 indicates RTD coffee participation in daily consumer behavior remains elevated versus 2021.
Category strategy is moving from flavor novelty toward utility: protein, zero-sugar, and fiber-focused RTD launches are recurring (especially in 2025–26).
Distribution is increasingly off-trade and grocery-led, where SKU depth and refresh velocity can create margin-sensitive competition.
Partnership-led scaling remains critical, with global brands pushing US distribution through licensed or JV-led routes.
whats_growing: Cold/iced and blended coffee consumption, especially cold brew and functional energy-style RTD coffee profiles.
RTD coffee variants positioned as high-protein, lower-sugar, or wellness-led (example: Starbucks protein and zero-sugar launches in 2025–26).
Plant-based or dairy-light recipes used to widen daytime-use occasions.
Distribution reach in grocery/convenience and online channels through packaged launches and SKU expansion.
whats_shrinking: RTD coffee’s standalone dollar share is pressured inside broader non-alcoholic ready-to-drink categories (Nielsen snapshot showed modest/negative short-term movement in 2025 data points).
Single-format RTD coffee products with weaker differentiation face faster margin compression versus premiumized cold brew/functional alternatives.
Lower-margin volume growth is harder to sustain when bean costs and packaging costs rise faster than price realization.
recent_developments: 2025-09-29: NCA Fall 2025 NCDT reported 19% of past-day coffee drinkers had ready-to-drink coffee (up from 9% in 2021), alongside strong cold/iced and blended consumption.
2025-09-29: Starbucks announced new in-store protein lattes/cold foams and said a ready-to-drink version would launch in U.S. grocery and convenience stores in 2026.
2025-11-15: Nielsen xAOC data summarized in a public filing showed RTD coffee at 2.0% of non-alcoholic ready-to-drink beverage dollar share and -0.2% year-over-year change.
2026-02-26: Starbucks launched RTD Coffee & Protein beverages (22g protein, lower sugar, launched in grocery/convenience and online).
2026-03-23 (announced rollout timing): Starbucks expanded RTD portfolio with Frappuccino Lite and Doubleshot Energy Zero Sugar variants, reinforcing the low-sugar/functional trend.
2026-07-22: Grand View updated its U.S. RTD coffee database values, showing continued mid-single-digit growth through 2033 under its base forecast.
outlook: Near-term outlook (through 2026-2028) is for continued but uneven growth: the category should expand in value as innovation and distribution continue, while competitive intensity likely keeps unit growth choppy and makes execution on formulation differentiation and channel mix critical.  Companies with strong retail relationships, portfolio breadth, and cost discipline should win as consumers prioritize convenience plus functional value.
themes: Cold/iced-first consumption
protein and low-sugar differentiation
partnership and JV distribution architectures
off-trade channel dominance
commodity volatility management
one_sentence: US RTD coffee producers in 2025–26 are gaining from strong convenience demand and premium wellness variants, but category share is pressured by competition and high input costs.

title: RTD Mixed Spirit Production
one_liner: Convenience-led cocktail-format spirits products are replacing a portion of full-bottle spend as U.S. ready-to-drink alcohol demand shifts to premium, format-flexible offerings.
overview: Industry modeling in the baseline indicates U.S. RTD mixed spirit manufacturing revenue rose to US$5.556 billion (2021) and was projected to reach about US$6.1 billion by 2026, while the category is becoming more cocktail-oriented and premiumized. Recent trade, sales, and scanner data from 2025–2026 show spirits-based RTDs growing faster than many other spirit segments, with small-format and premium cocktail variants helping offset category-level weakness in conventional spirits categories.

key_stats.market_size: US$6.1 billion (IBISWorld projection to 2026; spirits-ready-to-drink category context also shown as US$3.8 billion in 2025 for spirits RTD segment)
key_stats.growth: +1.9% CAGR (IBISWorld 2021-2026, US RTD mixed spirits projection); +16.4% YoY spirits-based RTDs to 2025 in DISCUS reporting

2025_2026_reference.total_RTD_dollars: US$12.6-13.6B range in NIQ 2025–2026 off-premise trend view, with RTDs accounting for 12.4% of total alcohol dollar sales by 2025
2025_2026_reference.spirits_RTD_dollars: US$3.8B (premixed cocktails incl. spirits RTDs) in 2025

baseline_2022.market_size: US$5.66 billion (estimated from IBISWorld 2021 anchor and 2021-2026 growth path)
baseline_2022.growth: +1.9% CAGR (IBISWorld-style projection basis from 2021 to 2026)

how_it_makes_money: Revenues are generated mainly by packaging and selling ready-to-drink spirit-based products (single-serve cans/bottles and small family packs) through supermarkets, liquor stores, convenience stores, and other alcohol distribution channels.
cost_structure: Material-heavy cost stack: spirit alcohol, sugar, sweeteners, flavors, and premium glass or aluminum packaging, plus labeling and compliance; costs are sensitive to commodity costs and packaging capacity while marketing and innovation spend remain elevated to refresh launches.
major_players: Pernod Ricard / Gallo ownership (High Noon; El Jimador-related RTD ecosystem)
Emerging RTD players and national distributors expanding mixology-like canned formats
current_dynamics: Growth is shifting toward spirits-based cocktails and tequila/vodka-forward flavor systems, while broad-category hard-seltzer style growth has softened. RIpe-ready formats (single and shareable sizes), smaller pack sizes, and premium-plus positioning are lifting per-occasion value despite tighter on-premise and broad spirits demand. Product novelty is maturing into incremental differentiation through ABV profile, flavor specificity, and format innovation rather than raw line-count expansion.
whats_growing: Spirits-based RTDs in the U.S. grew strongly and became a bright-spot despite total spirits value decline.
Higher-ABV cocktail-style and tequila/vodka expressions are gaining share.
Convenience, convenience-store, and small-pack demand continues to expand.
Premiumization pressure is increasing at both SKU and format level.
whats_shrinking: Hard seltzer and some flavored malt-based categories are losing relative momentum.
Broader total spirits off-premise channels show softness versus RTD pockets of growth.
Category seasonality and promotional fatigue are increasing for over-saturated flavor variants.
recent_developments: 2026-02-05: DISCUS said U.S. spirits supplier sales fell 2.2% to $36.4B, while spirits RTDs reached about $3.8B and rose 16.4% YoY.
2026-02-05: DISCUS also reported spirits RTDs gained ~11 percentage points in spirits category share in 2025; malt-based seltzers fell 14 points.
2026-01-03: NIQ reported total U.S. RTD dollars at $13.6B and 12.4% of total alcohol dollars in 2025.
2026-01-23: NIQ-linked reporting said spirits-based RTDs were near 80M cases in 2025, with High Noon at 24M and Surfside at 10.5M cases.
2026-06-04: Brown-Forman said its RTD portfolio rose 11% and New Mix rose 41% in FY2026 while Jack Daniel’s RTD declined 3% in the U.S. context.
outlook: Industry growth is expected to remain positive into 2026+ as consumers continue to trade toward convenience and ready-made cocktail experiences, but category performance is increasingly tied to successful differentiation and pricing discipline. Base spirits demand remains competitive, so manufacturers with strong portfolio mix, distribution access, and efficient aluminum/container costs should outperform.
themes: Cocktail/long-drink and premiumization trajectory in RTDs is replacing pure novelty-led expansion.
Small format and convenience distribution are becoming primary entry points for trial.
Regulatory access and tax/state policy changes can materially alter distribution and margin.
Trade friction and cross-border distribution uncertainty remain a key downside risk.
Ingredient and packaging inflation remains a structural margin pressure point.
one_sentence: The industry is transitioning from hard-seltzer-led growth to higher-value spirits-based RTDs, with 2025–2026 demand resilient even as broader spirits sales soften.

title: RTD Tea Production
one_liner: US ready-to-drink tea has shifted from pure volume growth to premium functional, lower-sugar formats, with category expansion increasingly driven by innovation and distribution reach rather than broad base-product gains.
overview: IBIS's latest available baseline shows US RTD tea at around USD 6.689 billion in 2021 with gradual growth, while 2025–26 research now points to a broader market now in the mid-teen billions. Recent data suggests US RTD tea is increasingly pulled by consumers moving away from high-sugar options, toward zero-sugar, botanical, and cognitive/wellness-positioned formats. Distribution remains highly concentrated in grocery and convenience channels, where shelf visibility and promotions continue to shape profitability.

baseline_2022.growth: ~+1.2% year-over-year (derived from IBIS 2021 base and 1.3% five-year trend)

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell finished RTD tea through packaged-goods retail and convenience channels, with value tied to branded flavor innovation, format and packaging choice, shopper pull in impulse settings, and promotional density. Premiumization (functional variants, zero-sugar lines, glass or premium-style packaging, stronger flavor/novelty SKUs) supports higher margins and trade support, while commodity-style SKUs remain discount-sensitive.
cost_structure: Major costs are tea/raw ingredient sourcing (import exposure), sweetener/fragrance and functional add-ins, packaging (PET/cans/aseptic systems), manufacturing and QA, distribution to high-turn channels, and category marketing/trade promotions. Regulatory-compliant labeling, digital shelf content, and retailer service requirements add incremental category-level overhead.
major_players: PepsiCo (Lipton, Pure Leaf, Brisk via Lipton Tea JV with Unilever)
The Coca-Cola Company (Gold Peak, Fuze Tea, Peace Tea brands)
Keurig Dr Pepper (RTD tea presence in North America)
ITO EN / Oi Ocha (premium unsweetened and low-sugar growth in niche)
current_dynamics: US NARTD scans in 2025 still show RTD tea as a meaningful but pressure-tested category: one SEC-filed market breakdown cited RTD tea near 4.0% unit share with -0.1% unit-year growth in the latest 52-week window, while the broader category remains exposed to sports, energy, and coffee tea substitutes. Large players are responding through zero-sugar and functional launches plus heavier trade support in convenience and grocery channels.
whats_growing: Zero-sugar and lower-sugar RTD tea SKUs with wellness/functional cues
Functional and cognitive-support claims (for example caffeine-focused and calming/focus-oriented variants)
Premiumization through flavor innovation and higher-quality positioning in convenience channels
whats_shrinking: Undifferentiated sweetened mass SKUs with weak flavor- or health-based differentiation
Pure-share growth in traditional sugary formulations under increasing consumer scrutiny
Pricing power at lower tiers due to cross-category promotional intensity and share rotation
recent_developments: 2025-03-17: PepsiCo announced agreement to acquire poppi for US$1.95 billion, signaling stronger positioning in prebiotic/functional beverage adjacency.
2025-05-19: PepsiCo completed the poppi acquisition.
2025-11-15: SEC-cited Nielsen data for 52-week U.S. non-alcoholic RTD category showed RTD tea around 4.0% unit share with -0.1% year-over-year unit change.
2026-04-28: PepsiCo launched Pure Leaf Mental Focus, a 0g sugar/0 calorie sparkling real brewed RTD tea format.
2026-07-28: Coca-Cola Q2 2026 update reported category tea growth of +6% in its global NARTD segment.
outlook: Through 2026, US RTD tea is expected to keep growing at a moderate-to-healthy pace, but likely more via premium mix shift than broad commodity expansion. Winners will be companies that combine lower-sugar/functional credibility, channel execution, and packaging efficiency; losers are likely to be heavily promotional, low-differentiation players.
themes: Wellness and sugar-reduction pressure shaping SKU strategy
Convenience-channel gravity remains dominant
Premiumization and functional features outperform commoditized SKUs
Aggressive distributor/retailer negotiation increases margin drag
Brand power and shelf-space ownership are major moats
one_sentence: The US RTD tea manufacturing category in 2025–2026 is steady-growth but hyper-competitive, with leading brands using health, flavor, and convenience innovation to defend share while managing pricing pressure.

title: RV & Camper Van Rental
one_liner: Domestic, value-conscious road travel is replacing traditional long-haul trip patterns, and peer-to-peer marketplaces are reshaping how RV and camper van rentals are sold in the U.S.
overview: In 2025 the U.S. RV & camper van rental market is estimated at $833.4 million, with growth described as positive but not exuberant compared with prior years. RV ownership is broad and still expanding demographically: RVIA reports 8.1 million U.S. households owning an RV in 2025, 16.9 million households expressing strong intent to buy an RV within five years, and a median RV owner age of 49.

key_stats.market_size: $833.4m (2025, U.S., IBISWorld)
key_stats.growth: CAGR 1.5% over 2019-2024 (IBISWorld); consumer travel behavior in 2026 shows cost pressure with 21% of travelers planning fewer trips year-over-year and a rising preference for shorter trips (15% -> 23%)

baseline_2022.growth: 2.1% projected growth in 2022; ~58% expansion across the prior decade

how_it_makes_money: Customers pay trip-based rental prices for Class A/B/C and towable RV types.
Platforms and operators add distribution and convenience revenue through pickup/drop-off delivery, one-way routing, bundled park packages, and advisory services.
Peer-to-peer operators monetize via marketplace fees while charging commission or service charges on booking transactions.
Insurance/Protection products are sold as mandatory or optional add-ons and often included in the booking flow.

cost_structure.traditional_rental_costs: Fleet acquisition/depreciation, financing, storage, cleaning, maintenance, insurance, roadside/compliance support, and labor are the largest cost drivers for operators.
cost_structure.platform_costs: Peer-to-peer and marketplace models pass a meaningful share to platform take rates; 2026 Outdoorsy host fees are 20%–25% of the booking subtotal (minimum $15/night for drivable, $10/night for towables), with 6.5% host fee when a new guest books from a host quote.
cost_structure.economics_note: RV rental economics remain sensitive to utilization because utilization and seasonal capacity are uneven across markets and vehicle classes.

current_dynamics: RV demand in 2026 is still strongest in domestic leisure travel, with RVs viewed as a flexible lower-cost alternative for many trips.
Demand is increasingly service-led: one-way planning, convenience packaging, and trusted destination repeatability outperform pure inventory expansion.
Both 2025 and 2026 RVshare trend data indicate strong cost sensitivity: a majority of travelers seek savings and shorter, off-season planning patterns.
Ownership propensity is still rising via younger cohorts and families; RV age demographics are getting younger and RV use intensity is increasing (median days used up 50% from the 2021 study).
whats_growing: Rental intent remains high with 71% of surveyed 2026 travelers likely to choose RVs for national park trips and 71% saying they would take more RV vacations if one-way options are available.
One-way mobility is accelerating: RVshare reports 71% of travelers more likely to take RV trips if one-way is easy, with 89% of Millennials responding positively.
Pet-friendly requirements are scaling (71% of pet owners want to travel with pets, 54% want more pet-friendly accommodations).
Digital planning is becoming standard: 26% of 2026 travelers plan to use AI tools for trip planning.
RV ownership pipeline remains strong: 16.9 million households in the RVia 2025 profile expect to buy in the next five years.
whats_shrinking: Interest in international trips weakened from 28% to 25% in the 2026 RVshare framing, signaling a stronger domestic travel tilt.
Longer trips are down (20% baseline context; 2026 data indicate trend toward shorter trips).
Trip volume intensity is not rising across all cohorts: 21% plan fewer trips than the prior year, versus 10% in 2024.
Crowded, mega-destination behavior is softening as travelers re-route to quieter alternatives and value-first itineraries.
recent_developments: 2025-12-10: RVshare released its 2026 Travel Trend Report, reporting 87% of travelers actively seeking trip-cost savings and 1,000-person traveler survey weighting in late Nov 2025.
2026-01-28: RVshare launched one-way rentals and park-based getaways, citing that 71% of travelers would be more inclined to take RV trips with one-way options and 89% of Millennials.
2026-03-18 to 2026-06-18: RVshare announced a gas rebate program worth up to $1M, with $50 for trips up to 5 days and $70 for 6+ day trips.
2026-03-09: RVIA 2025 Annual Report highlighted workforce growth, including 7,500 certified RV technicians and nearly 1,000 dealerships with at least one certified technician.
2026: RVIA 2025 Owner Demographic Profile shows 8.1 million U.S. RV-owning households and 16.9 million households planning to buy an RV within five years.
outlook: The 2025-2026 picture points to slower top-line expansion than the post-2020 peak, with competition intensifying between traditional fleet operators and marketplace-based supply. Winners likely build recurring value through delivery, one-way flexibility, reliable park-facing productization, and AI-assisted trip planning while controlling utilization and variable costs.
themes: Domestic and off-highway flexibility
Cost-sensitive trip design
One-way mobility and convenience
Pet-friendly outdoor travel
Platform-led distribution and service differentiation
one_sentence: The U.S. RV and camper van rental industry in 2025-2026 remains active but less growth-fast than the pandemic surge, with demand concentrated in flexible, shorter, and cost-conscious travel options supported by digital platforms, delivery logistics, and one-way itinerary tools.

title: Racing & Individual Sports in the US
one_liner: US racing and individual sports in 2025–26 are increasingly driven by streaming rights and sports-betting ecosystems, while horse-racing monetization remains the weakest link.
overview: The US Racing & Individual Sports industry combines horse racing, motorsports, individual events such as golf/tennis, and combat sports with highly different economics. The IBIS baseline shows a 2022 revenue base of $13.31 billion and low single-digit profitability, indicating a mature category with uneven segment health. In 2025–26, media rights deals and digital distribution are improving discoverability for UFC, PGA, and motorsports, while legal sports-betting expansion is lifting consumer touchpoints across sporting content. The principal structural weakness remains horse-racing: net wagering revenue growth is lagging participation gains elsewhere, making profitability sensitive to state policy and cross-channel economics.

market_size.basis: IBISWorld forward projection from 2022 base (industry report snapshot)

how_it_makes_money: The industry earns primarily from event attendance, venue concessions, and hospitality, media and streaming rights, sponsorship and advertising, licensing/merchandise, and wagering-linked revenue (especially horse-racing wagering and related channels).
cost_structure: Variable costs are dominated by purses, rider/horse or athlete-related participation economics, talent and promoter costs, and event operations; fixed costs include track/venue operations, staffing, veterinary or medical support where applicable, broadcast production, and compliance. The horse segment remains payout- and facility-intensive: payouts, purses, and operations are less flexible than digital distribution upside.
major_players: TKO Group Holdings (UFC, Zuffa Boxing, WWE, PBR)
current_dynamics: In 2025–26, consumer monetization is moving toward media-platform concentration and direct-to-consumer rights packages, with mixed outcomes: motorsports and elite individual events have secured major platform deals, while horse racing remains exposed to handle quality and structure changes. Adjacent legal sports wagering is the strongest external demand pull for sports content, and industry operators are increasingly integrating fan engagement with betting touchpoints.
whats_growing: 2025 U.S. sports-betting handle expected to exceed $165 billion, about 11% above 2024 levels.
UFC gained a seven-year U.S. rights framework in 2026 with a $1.1 billion AAV arrangement, signaling higher downstream media monetization.
PGA TOUR viewership recovered in 2025, with weekend broadcast average up 22% year-over-year.
US tennis participation increased 1.6 million to 27.3 million players in 2025.
whats_shrinking: NASCAR Cup ratings weakened in 2025 after rights migration, with audience metrics showing a 15% year-over-year dip in year one of the new deal.
US horse-racing faces structural strain as high-quality human-led wagering has weakened and total racing handle quality pressure has been highlighted in 2025.
Some legacy media windows for motorsport declined as more content shifts to streaming-only or DTC-heavy distribution.
PGA of America tournament program revenues dipped in 2024-25 versus the prior fiscal year.
recent_developments: 2025-08-11: Paramount secured exclusive U.S. UFC distribution in a seven-year agreement, AAV $1.1 billion.
2025-09-02: PGA Tour averaged 2.275M Saturday/Sunday TV viewers in 2025, up 22% from 2024.
2025-11-06: NASCAR reported a 15% drop in Cup Series ratings in year one of rights terms (2.5M viewers).
2025-02-18: USTA reported U.S. tennis participation at 27.3 million in 2025.
2025-06-21: Thoroughbred industry coverage cited total U.S. horse-racing handle around $11.8 billion in 2025.
2026-02-06: US sports-betting handle was projected to exceed $165 billion in 2025, up about 11% from 2024.
outlook: If streaming distribution and rights valuation continue to improve, league-level and star-event segments should support moderate top-line growth through 2028. The downside scenario remains horse-racing margin compression if wagering migration continues away from on-track human bettors and if subsidies remain unstable. Overall, this is a bifurcated market where long-term winners are platform-enabled sports properties with durable sponsor and media hooks, while heavily regulated wagering-dependent formats carry execution risk.
themes: Streaming-led rights consolidation for premium live sports
Cross-border sports-betting expansion into engagement and monetization
Horse-racing subsidy dependence and payout pressure
Safety and welfare scrutiny in equine segments alongside commercialization
one_sentence: The sector is seeing a split trajectory in 2025–26: stronger media and sponsorship momentum in major motorsport, golf, combat sports, and tennis, but persistent pressure on horse-racing economics from shifting wagering behavior.

title: Radar & Satellite Operations in the US
one_liner: Radar and satellite operators in the US are expanding TT&C, tracking, and shared ground-segment services as mega-constellations and defense demand lift traffic despite weaker satellite-TV spillover and tighter orbital/launch constraints.
overview: The industry remains a specialized services layer for commercial and defense satellite users: TT&C, telemetry, earth-station support, ground network integration, and radar-based space-monitoring operations. In the 2025–2026 period, the biggest directional change is policy-fueled capacity growth from mega-constellation scaling and satellite services reforms, while launch-port throughput and orbital traffic management are becoming binding constraints. Government demand remains a major stabilizer through satellite communications and missile-warning support.

key_stats.market_size: $29,421.9M (U.S. satellite communication market, 2026 estimate)
key_stats.growth: CAGR 10.9% (U.S. satcom, 2026–2033; published Jan 20, 2026)

baseline_2022.growth: 2022 annualized industry growth 1.9%; five-year-to-2022 growth was 5.3% with next five-year forecast 1.7%

how_it_makes_money: Mission and network operation services for satellite operators (TT&C, tracking, telemetry, earth-station management).
Ground segment and gateway operations for broadband, enterprise, maritime, aviation, IoT, and public-safety satellite traffic.
Government-linked service contracts and defense-oriented satellite communications infrastructure support.
cost_structure: High fixed costs in network stations, mission control software, spectrum monitoring, and certified operations teams.
Variable costs tied to launch cadence, satellite handover support, maintenance windows, and telecom integration work.
Economies from shared infrastructure and software automation are increasing as operators migrate to shared ground-station models.
current_dynamics: 2025–2026 regulatory acceleration is reducing approval friction for earth-station and satellite-network filings, which favors faster service deployment and third-party gateway entrants.
SpaceX’s Starlink regulatory expansion and constellation growth are increasing demand for U.S. TT&C and radar-supported traffic management.
US defense budget priorities in FY2027 materially increase satellite communications and mission-space architecture spending, directly supporting ground and control-side services.
whats_growing: Defense-backed satellite communications, especially SATCOM reliability and launch-to-orbit support, is strengthening through FY2027 budget cycles.
Ground-station-as-a-service, shared infrastructure, and cross-operator utilization models are becoming more commercially viable.
Mega-constellation traffic growth (including direct-to-device and mobile-satellite services) is increasing operations demand per constellation.
Ground-control modernization demand is rising for lower-orbit shells and mixed-traffic constellations.
whats_shrinking: Direct consumer satellite TV demand is structurally weak versus broadband/mobile alternatives in the broader value chain.
ARPU pressure remains evident in connectivity offerings, including consumer price elasticity in mega-constellation services.
U.S. launch throughput and pad/airspace coordination capacity are increasingly a short-term cap on how fast operators can scale operations.
Mature terrestrial competition is reducing incremental growth in traditional broadcast-linked satellite channels.
recent_developments: 2025-08-07: FCC adopted a Part 25 streamlining order (FCC-25-48) to speed satellite and earth-station filing steps for innovative operations.
2025-06-11: CRS reporting on FCC performance planning cited nearly 1,000 earth-station applications processed since January 2025 under temporary simplified review.
2025-12-31: Iridium reported 2,537,000 billable subscribers and total revenue of $871.7M for 2025.
2026-01-09: FCC authorized an additional 7,500 Starlink Gen2 satellites, bringing total approved Gen2 Starlink authorization to 15,000.
2026-04-21: U.S. Air and Space Forces request proposed $71.1B for Space Force and included $6.7B satellite communications plus $6.8B missile warning/tracking spending.
2026-05-18: CSF report noted over 180 U.S. launches in 2025 and flagged launch-capacity strain under rising demand.
outlook: From 2025 to 2026 the industry appears in a re-rating phase: lower-volume, TV-linked demand is offset by stronger defense and resilience demand, while orbital and launch bottlenecks create short-term execution risk. Expect modest overall industry expansion through 2027, with stronger growth concentrated in mission-critical and defense-linked channels and slower growth in legacy broadcast-linked satellite service models.
themes: Regulatory simplification for spectrum/earth-station filings
Defense funding-driven demand stability
Mega-constellation operational scaling
Satellite internet/mobile integration and direct-to-device services
Launch cadence and orbital safety/radar capacity as a structural constraint
one_sentence: This US segment is moving from slow mid-cycle growth toward defense-anchored and connectivity-backed expansion, with regulatory streamlining and rapid constellation upgrades driving near-term demand for radar/ground operations.

title: Radio Broadcasting in the US
one_liner: US radio retains broad audience reach, but growth increasingly comes from digital monetization.
overview: The US radio business remains structurally large but structurally pressured. Baseline industry filings in 2022 showed a mature market in slow decline, and 2025–2026 data indicate the same pattern: core OTA/radio advertising is under pressure while digital extensions and podcast-linked inventory are the main engine of incremental revenue. The practical industry split has become broadcast-plus-digital packages, with stronger demand for measurable, targetable campaigns.

market_size.2025_commercial_radio_ad_revenue: $9.4B (approx., per RAB industry digital share of 24.4% at $2.3B digital)

how_it_makes_money: Operators sell commercial spot ads, sponsorships, and event-linked inventory in local and regional markets, plus network and podcast advertising; satellite operators combine subscriber fees with advertising; digital add-ons include programmatic radio inventory, branded content, streaming, and podcast ad distribution.
cost_structure: Top expense buckets are talent and station operating payroll, content and music-rights/licensing costs, sales commissions and ad inventory operations, digital and data/tech costs (including AI tools and third-party ad platforms), and in some models subscriber acquisition/vehicle-install economics (notably for satellite).
current_dynamics: The industry is bifurcating: legacy broadcast radio remains dominant in reach, but advertisers increasingly require campaign-level accountability and cross-channel measurement, pushing operators toward digital, podcast, and addressable-radio bundles.
whats_growing: 2025: radio digital ad revenue reached $2.3B and reached 24.4% of total radio revenue.
2025–2026: radio has become the core channel in 62% of ad-supported audio listening (Q1 2026).
2026: digital radio sales expected to rise to $2.5B, led by programmatic and measurable inventory.
2025: iHeart reported stronger digital audio momentum, with podcast advertising and digital segments growing faster than broadcast spot categories in 2025 reporting.
whats_shrinking: 2025: SiriusXM self-pay subscribers declined to 32,927 vs 33,226 in 2024 (-299).
2025: Cumulus net revenue declined 10.3% year-over-year to $741.7M.
Longer-term: core radio advertising has been declining, even while digital gains partly offset it.
2025: iHeart reported broadcast spot pressure in its Multiplatform/AM-FM business despite growth in digital units.
recent_developments: 2025-12-31: SiriusXM 2025 filing shows total revenue $8.558B and subscribers 32,927 (down from 33,226 in 2024).
2026-02-09: RAB/Borrell reported 2025 digital radio revenue at $2.3B (25% of total), with average station digital sales improving.
2026-02-09: RAB/Borrell report also highlighted three-fourths of radio buyers still not fully adopting radio digital products.
2026-06-03: Nielsen/Radio Ink reported radio held 62% of ad-supported audio listening in Q1 2026; podcasts added 20% and streaming music 15%.
2026-06-18: iHeart launched AudioGraph to provide broadcast radio with identity-based targeting and outcome-based attribution at scale.
2026-01-15: NAB/Wood+P+BIA study estimated local broadcasting supported 2.46M U.S. jobs; approx. $1.19T GDP from local broadcasting.
outlook: From 2026 onward, aggregate industry growth is likely modest overall but uneven: pure broadcast spot activity remains weak, while stations and groups that can prove addressable, cross-platform performance should capture the upside, especially in local and national campaigns that blend radio reach with podcast and streaming context.
themes: Measurable radio: move from reach-only to addressable outcomes
Bundled radio + podcast + streaming offers
AI-driven sales enablement with stronger measurement discipline
Local advertising pressure despite robust audience penetration
High consolidation barriers in many markets, but selective scale advantages for strongest operators
one_sentence: In 2025–2026, US radio shows broad penetration, weak core ad growth, and faster gains in digital radio and podcast advertising tied to better measurement and targeting.

title: Rail Maintenance Services in the US
one_liner: Rail maintenance services in the US are a mature, safety-critical segment dominated by class-I rail operators and specialized service providers, with demand driven by freight intensity, aging rolling-stock programs and passenger-state-federal infrastructure spending.
overview: US rail maintenance demand follows rail traffic cycles: 2025 freight volume remained positive year-over-year, but intermodal softness and macro softness in certain freight subseries softened near-term service demand. Revenue is mostly tied to infrastructure and rolling-stock care, with major Class I carriers executing substantial in-house maintenance while still relying on specialist providers for advanced repairs, mobile services, painting/cleaning, and overhaul support. Federal grant programs and Amtrak’s continuing passenger-capital cycle remain important near-term demand catalysts for higher-precision maintenance activity and station/track-related work.

market_size.note: Estimated near-term level using IBIS baseline (2022 baseline 7,793m, near-flat projected trend to 7,900m by 2027)

maintenance_share.basis: share of operator revenue from maintenance and repair work

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes mainly from maintenance and repair of track and rolling stock (about 90.8% of 2022 industry revenue), including scheduled and unscheduled locomotive/car/track work, with smaller shares from railcar cleaning and freight arrangement/handling support (about 7.5%) and terminal/logistics-adjacent services (about 1.7%).

cost_structure.detail: Wages and labour-heavy service delivery are structurally high; 2022 total wages were 2,514m versus 7,793m revenue (~32.3% of revenue).

cost_structure.item: Materials, parts and mobile service infrastructure
cost_structure.detail: Heavy use of parts, wear items, safety consumables, and mobile/yard support capability across fixed and variable maintenance demand.

Safety-driven inspections and enforcement shape operating procedures; FRA FY2025 reported 4,005 cases with civil-penalty activity in Class I-related programs and $21.11m total final federal settlements.

cost_structure.item: Capacity management and project downtime risk
cost_structure.detail: Long repair windows, outage coordination and service reliability commitments drive premium pricing and fixed-cost scheduling risk.

current_dynamics: Freight activity in 2025 remained positive overall (AAR reported +1.5% full-year carloads and +1.5% intermodal units), while AAR noted mixed commodity and intermodal softness signals.
Class I carriers are maintaining high capital programs; BNSF planned a $3.8b 2025 plan with $2.84b directed to maintenance.
Carrier property spending remains substantial: Norfolk Southern 2025 property additions were 2,204m and management guided 2026 additions around 1.9b.
Federal grant and legislative demand is still active through CRISI and passenger-rail grant channels, supporting state and national network modernization work.
Safety compliance exposure is elevated in practice, with significant regulatory activity and penalties tracked in FRA FY2025 reporting.
whats_growing: Track modernization and preventive maintenance intensity where carriers announce durable capex programs.
Safety-related inspection, lifecycle monitoring, and modernization of older plant that supports asset reliability and regulatory posture.
Public passenger and corridor investment programs that require higher maintenance throughput.
Mobile and field repair capability to reduce asset downtime for shippers and intermodal flows.
whats_shrinking: Intermodal freight index weakness in late 2025 (BTS reported a 1.2% YoY fall in Freight TSI by Sep 2025, with a sharp 2.1% MoM dip that month).
Third-party maintenance spend share where Class I carriers expand internal teams and capability.
New business tied only to pure throughput expansion versus recovery-driven catch-up; throughput mix is stabilizing rather than rapidly expanding.
recent_developments: 2025-12-31: AAR weekly rail traffic for week ending 2025-12-27 showed 392,295 carloads+intermodal units (+0.7% YoY) and 2025 YTD totals up 1.5% in both carloads and intermodal units.
2025-11-13: BTS reported September 2025 Freight TSI at -2.1% MoM (136.2), with Rail TSI down versus year earlier.
2025-12-27: AAR RIO showed U.S. total carloads up 1.0% for 2025 and intermodal 1.5%, but signs of mixed momentum by commodity.
2025-01-23: BNSF announced a $3.8bn 2025 capital plan, with $2.84bn directed to maintenance, 11,400 miles surfaced/undercut and 2.5m ties replaced.
2025-02: Wabtec 2025 filing reported strong service-led order flow, including substantial locomotive orders and recurring service contracts.
2026: Amtrak FY26 legislative request includes $850m NEC grant and $1.577bn National Network annual grant ask, supporting major state passenger rail maintenance and infrastructure work.
outlook: Expect low-single-digit top-line movement in 2026 with volatility from transport-mode mix; maintenance demand remains stable to moderately positive as Class I operators replace ties/rails and refresh fleets, while service margins stay pressured by labour intensity, compliance burden, and slower near-term intermodal expansion.
themes: Steady maintenance demand despite modest freight growth
Safety regulation and inspection discipline
Infrastructure resilience and track-condition recovery
Carrier insourcing versus specialist-provider balance
Federal and state passenger-capital program tailwinds
one_sentence: Demand remains mostly tied to freight throughput and track/rolling-stock upkeep, while freight remains positive into 2025 but intermodal softness and safety/compliance pressure are keeping margin expansion limited.

title: Rail Transportation in the US
one_liner: U.S. freight rail is stabilizing on a mixed cycle, with industrial, grain, and coal demand lifting carloads while intermodal demand softens under slower consumer goods momentum.
overview: Freight rail in the U.S. remains a core long-haul transport backbone, serving energy, manufacturing, agriculture, automotive, and intermodal lanes across domestic and cross-border supply chains. 2025–2026 data show resilient freight generation outside of pure consumer-mix shifts, with stronger commodity and grain-related flows offsetting a weaker intermodal tone in parts of late 2025 and ongoing caution from lower goods demand.
how_it_makes_money: Per-unit freight charges for carload and intermodal transportation
Fuel and accessorial surcharge pass-throughs
Long-term shipping contracts, service commitments, and line-haul network access fees
Interline and logistics partnerships with ocean, trucking, and terminal operators
Ancillary rail logistics such as switching, terminal handling, and storage
cost_structure: High fixed network costs: track, bridges, signals, rolling stock, and terminals
Fuel/diesel volatility and pass-through management
Labor and operations costs (crew, maintenance, dispatch, safety)
Large maintenance and depreciation base requiring sustained capex
Insurance, regulatory compliance, and system modernization investments
Seasonality and idling dynamics that influence utilization and fixed-cost absorption
major_players: Soo Line-related Class I network (as reported in STB Class I filings)
current_dynamics: 2025-09: U.S. rail carloads for Jan–Aug 2025 were up 2.5% vs 2024, showing broad industrial persistence.
2025-12: Freight Rail Index was 4.4% below Nov 2024, while coal and grain carloads remained positive in many reporting segments.
2026-03: Total carloads in Feb 2026 were up 6.5% YoY and excluding coal up 6.3%, indicating non-coal freight resilience.
2026-03: U.S. labor-market data and manufacturing PMIs improved, lowering uncertainty around near-term industrial demand.
2026-01 to 2026-03: Intermodal remained elevated in absolute levels but showed mild softness relative to earlier 2025 momentum.
whats_growing: Coal carloads in Feb 2026 were up 6.9% YoY, with coal accounting for 26.6% of non-intermodal U.S. rail volume.
Grain carloads in Feb 2026 were up 21.8% YoY and at the highest February weekly levels since 1990.
Chemicals in Feb 2026 reached a record weekly average with carloads +3.3% YoY and strongest two-month totals.
US Class I Class rail carriers reported annual private investment of about $25 billion, supporting sustained asset refresh and corridor reliability improvements.
Intermodal volumes through Feb 2026 rose 1.5% YoY and weekly U.S. intermodal in February reached a February record.
whats_shrinking: Intermodal in Nov 2025 was softer in monthly growth terms with the freight index down 4.4% YoY.
US consumer-goods pressure in 2025 reduced the goods share in household spending in parts of 2024–2025.
November 2025 intermodal weakness and softer consumer flow remained a drag on short-horizon demand signals.
Some motor-vehicle and non-core segments showed mixed/weakening pace even as industrial flows improved.
recent_developments: 2025-09: AAR RIO reported Jan.–Aug 2025 U.S. carloads up 2.5% YoY and intermodal up 4.1% (9.47 million units).
2025-09: AAR RIO reported August 2025 total carloads up 0.7% vs August 2024 and intermodal up 5.2% (9.20 million).
2025-11: AAR RIO said the Freight Rail Index was 4.4% below Nov 2024 and highlighted mixed grain/coal strength with weaker intermodal tone.
2025-12: AAR weekly report for week ending 2025-12-27 showed combined North American rail traffic of 541,476 units, down 0.2% YoY.
2026-03: AAR RIO March 2026 reported February U.S. rail carloads up 6.5% YoY and total carloads excluding coal up 5.5% for Jan–Feb 2026.
2026-03: AAR RIO March 2026 reported U.S. intermodal in Feb 2026 at 280,687 per week, up 1.5% YoY.
outlook: Near term, 2026 appears to favor a moderate recovery path driven by manufacturing, chemicals, grain, and cross-border logistics if trade friction and consumer softness stay manageable. Intermodal is likely to be the swing segment: still large in absolute terms, but most sensitive to spending and tariff-driven inventory behavior. Capacity, workforce discipline, and fuel-cost planning are likely to stay central to profitability.
themes: Industrial-led freight resilience vs consumer-cycle softness
Rail intermodal is high-volume but volatile with consumer goods demand
Class I capital intensity drives continuous private capex demand
Safety and reliability remain structural strengths (accident and hazmat incident trends)
Energy mix and shipment concentration shift from coal to more diversified industrial commodities
Policy uncertainty and trade routes influence port-linked intermodal flows
one_sentence: By 2026, U.S. rail demand is increasingly led by industrial and export-oriented traffic, while intermodal remains sensitive to consumer demand and trade policy, and carriers prioritize cost control as labor, fuel, and network capacity pressures persist.

title: Railcar Manufacturing
one_liner: US railcar manufacturing remains a cyclical, order-driven market but moved back toward broader demand in early 2026 as rail freight volumes rose across key commodities.
overview: The US Railcar Manufacturing industry serves freight, passenger, and industrial logistics with durable steel and aluminum platforms that move coal, grain, chemicals, scrap, steel, and intermodal feedstock. Demand is dominated by railroad and industrial shipment activity and is highly volatile because orders are lumpy, fleets are long-lived, and operators time purchases around freight and macro cycles. Federal policy support and modernization of aging fleets can provide a floor, while energy, interest-rate, and consumer-demand swings create near-term uncertainty.

industry_notes: 2026 freight demand recovered in breadth: February and March carloads were up and were driven across multiple commodity groups.
First-quarter rail growth in 2026 was the strongest since 2019 in total carloads.

how_it_makes_money: New and rebuilt railcar sales to rail operators and logistics fleets.
Conversion and remanufacturing of existing cars (for remaining life extension, better product mix, and compliance upgrades).
Leasing, parts, repair, and service programs tied to owned and managed fleets.
cost_structure: Raw materials and components are a large share of manufacturing cost; FreightCar America notes material and component exposure is substantial.
Steel and aluminum cost volatility directly affects pricing and margin stability.
Manufacturing can benefit from integrated fabrication and supply control, but utilization swings push fixed-cost pressure during volume downturns.
Leverage and financing costs become relevant for firms with large lease fleets or balance-sheet-heavy capital programs.
current_dynamics: AAR freight indicators shifted from soft 2025 patterns toward broader 2026 recovery: Feb–Apr 2026 had consecutive month gains in carloads, rising breadth across commodity groups, and a stronger intermodal trend. At the same time, December 2025 showed unevenness, with intermodal deceleration and manufacturing still volatile, underscoring cycle risk despite improving rail activity.
whats_growing: 2026-02: AAR reported ~5.5% Y/Y growth in Jan-Feb carloads (1.76M units).
2026-03: AAR reported broad-based commodity gains and strongest Q1 freight levels since 2019.
2026-04: AAR reported 16 categories up in April and a strongest-in-years Q1 trend.
2026-02: U.S. freight rail fleet in storage reached 356,000 cars, 21.8% of 1.63M, indicating potential replacement potential ahead.
whats_shrinking: 2025-12: AAR noted weaker intermodal momentum in the December month and softer consumer-linked import pacing.
2025-Q1: ARCI-reported order cycle showed deliveries down ~22% vs prior quarter in at least one quarter sequence.
2025-2026: rail traffic remains commodity-sensitive with periodic softness in specific sectors (eg, periodic coal and vehicle-category volatility).
Order backlog remains volatile quarter-to-quarter, increasing execution risk for margin planning.
recent_developments: 2025-12: AAR Dec 2025 RIO reported total US rail traffic up 1.5% vs 2024, but intermodal down 3.4% in Dec and full-year momentum mixed.
2026-02: AAR Feb 2026 RIO showed 6.5% year-over-year February carload growth and 14 of 20 categories up.
2026-03: AAR Mar 2026 RIO showed 2026 YTD carloads up 5.5% and continuing broad-based strength.
2026-05: AAR May 2026 RIO reported a fourth straight monthly Y/Y carload gain and 16/20 categories rising.
2026-01: FreightCar America 2025 10-K showed 3,254 orders and 1,926 backlog at Dec 2025 (down from 4,245 and 2,797 in 2024).
2025-12/2026-01: FRA CRISI FY25-26 NOFO listed $2,039,246,480 available for rail infrastructure and safety awards.
outlook: 2026 looks like a transition from contraction optics to measured re-acceleration, with demand now wider than single-sector driven and backed by stronger manufacturing and rail-commodity breadth. The industry should benefit where manufacturers combine new-build exposure with conversion/aftermarket and leasing-linked service offerings, while pure new-build players remain exposed to order-cycle swings. Near-term upside depends on sustained freight demand broadening and stable freight rates; downside risks remain inflation/energy volatility, policy timing, and cyclic capital deferment by shippers.
themes: Demand quality is shifting from narrow to broader freight categories.
Replacement demand should dominate as long-haul fleets age and compliance requirements continue.
Order and backlog volatility remains a core structural risk.
Federal rail infrastructure and safety funding continues to support long-cycle project demand.
Supplier cost control is critical as steel, aluminum, and labor inputs stay unpredictable.
one_sentence: In 2025 rail traffic softened in spots but by 2026 the sector showed broader recovery in carloads, supporting a reacceleration in railcar replacement and conversion demand despite persistent macro volatility.
