Large operators are actively increasing recycling throughput via site modernizations, robotic sorting, and contamination-control upgrades to improve material capture rates and commodity quality.
Commodity and disposal economics remain strongly variable: recycling revenues still correlate with pricing of recovered materials, fuel, and logistics costs.

Federal and state policy activity is accelerating, with STEWARD and related recycling-focused legislative activity in the 119th Congress potentially shaping reporting, data, and grant/implementation conditions.
whats_growing: Public and private spending on recovery infrastructure (facility upgrades, sorting automation, and data/market infrastructure).
State and local program support for expanded access models, reflected in EPA map and planning work.
Recycling of higher-value, cleaner material streams and increased integration of organics pathways.
Shift from commodity-revenue dependence alone toward mixed-service models (materials + disposal + sustainability solutions).
whats_shrinking: Growth visibility from pure recycling-service expansion is modest versus earlier eras; expansion is more efficiency-led than volume-led.
Residual margins in low-quality mixed streams where contamination rates force disposal costs or lower recovery rates.
Standalone profitability of facilities dependent on highly volatile commodities (especially recycled plastics).
Any growth from unsustainable single-stream contamination if source separation quality does not improve.
recent_developments: 2025-02-05 — U.S. Senate Environmental Public Works Committee reported and favored STEWARD-related recycling legislation.
2025-11-20 — STEWARD Act passed the U.S. Senate without amendment by voice vote.
2025-06 — EPA updated the Recycling Infrastructure and Market Opportunities Map to version 2.0.
2025-12-31 — Republic disclosed 79 recycling centers in its US/Canada annual disclosures.
2025-12-31 — Waste Management disclosed 113 recycling facilities (51 single-stream) and 49 organics recycling facilities.

2025-2025 / 2026 — WM public sustainability/operations materials cite a 2022–2026 recycling facility modernization spending plan exceeding US$1.4B and major plant-level upgrades such as Cleveland facility expansion to 144,000 tons/year.
outlook: The industry outlook for 2025-2026 is cautiously positive: demand for recovered materials is structurally supported by waste-policy pressure and expanded recycling access, but near-term gains are likely incremental and heavily dependent on cost control, contamination reduction, and commodity-price resilience. Operators with balanced recycling, disposal, and energy linkages appear best positioned, while independent single-line MRF operators remain exposed to price swings and regional market constraints.
themes: Circular economy and material-security positioning
Automation and contamination control in MRFs
Public-sector recycling access investment
Commodity-price and fuel-cost risk management
Policy-driven data/reporting and infrastructure modernization
one_sentence: The industry is transitioning from incremental growth in tonnage to a phase of technology upgrades, policy pressure, and cost-control as operators expand throughput, improve sorting quality, and invest in access-oriented recycling infrastructure.

title: Refined Petroleum Pipeline Transportation in the US
one_liner: U.S. refined-products pipelines remain a core midstream link for fuel distribution, with growth increasingly tied to diesel, jet, and industrial demand rather than gasoline.
overview: Refined petroleum pipeline transportation remains a regulated, capital-heavy utility-style business moving gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and other liquid fuels from refiners to regional demand centers. The network is still expanding incrementally, with operators balancing tariff pressure, safety compliance, and shifting fuel mix as transportation demand moves from pure passenger-gasoline growth toward distillate and aviation-grade throughput.

key_stats.market_size: 2025-2026 demand proxy: 20.30 million bpd of U.S. total petroleum products consumption in 2025 vs 20.60 million bpd in 2026 (+1.5%); crude/marine/terminal-intensive flows stay demand critical for this segment.
key_stats.growth: 2026 outlook from EIA: motor-gasoline consumption expected to decline (~1% in 2026 and 2027), while distillate and jet are forecast to rise (~2% in both 2026 and 2027).
key_stats.network_scope: Refined products pipeline mileage (PHMSA hazardous liquid summary): 2025 65,067 miles (petroleum/refined products systems) and 2026 65,058 miles (slight near-flat network footprint).

baseline_2022.market_size: Baseline IBIS report notes U.S. refined petroleum pipeline transport revenue at approximately $9.665 billion (earlier period baseline).
baseline_2022.growth: Baseline historical CAGR in revenue was 4.85% (2003-2021); prior published outlook expected ~3.36% projected growth in 2025-2027 and ~3.8% projected growth to 2026.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is primarily earned through tariffed transportation fees and terminaling/storage charges on regulated and negotiated contracts, with additional contributions from optimization/marketing, blending, and product handling services.

cost_structure.fixed_vs_variable: High fixed-cost backbone with significant operating and replacement spend on pipes, pumping, metering, integrity programs, and safety systems.
major_cost_drivers: Property taxes and regulatory compliance obligations (including tariff and safety reporting).
cost_structure.pricing_dynamic: Tariffs/rate setting and contracted service terms can protect volume returns but still leave operators sensitive to throughput volatility and cost inflation.

current_dynamics: Demand mix is rotating: EIA forecasts support reduced gasoline share and comparatively stronger distillate and jet consumption.
Operators with broad network footprints continue to add short-haul connectivity and airport/inland access projects.
Pipeline mileage for petroleum/refined products remains largely stable while competitive pressure increases from road and other modes on shorter lanes.
FERC and PHMSA rule/reporting expectations keep tariff and safety/compliance execution central to operator economics.
whats_growing: 2026 distillate demand remains supported by industrial use and trucking freight momentum.
2026 jet-fuel demand is expected to increase with higher air-travel intensity.
Integrated players are expanding refined-product terminal and connectivity projects to capture regional flow and interchange points.
whats_shrinking: 2025-2026 gasoline demand growth is weaker from efficiency gains and modal substitutions.
Absolute petroleum/refined-products mileage is not expanding materially in 2025-2026 (PHMSA: 65,067 to 65,058 miles).
Cost sensitivity is rising as steel energy and compliance intensity keep network returns disciplined.
recent_developments: 2026-02-05: EIA STEO (Feb 2026) forecast higher total U.S. petroleum products consumption between 2025 (20.30 million bpd) and 2026 (20.60 million bpd), with gasoline softening and distillate/jet improving.
2026-02-24: ONEOK filed its 2025 Form 10-K; one filing shows 9,800 miles of refined-products pipelines and 1,526 MBpd refined-products throughput.
2026-02-27: Enterprise Products filed its 2025 10-K; enterprise transportation disclosures show ~14,199 MBpd equivalent pipeline volumes and 1,074 MBpd in refined/ petrochemical pipeline volumes.
2026-08-06: PHMSA updated hazardous liquid/refined-product mileage; petroleum/refined products systems remained near-flat at 65,058 miles.
2025-12-25 to 2026-01: Energy Transfer announced refocusing capex away from LNG expansion to existing gas pipeline backlog, signaling active capital rationing in midstream transport portfolios.
outlook: On a 2025-2026 horizon, pipeline demand is expected to trend modestly positive but with lower headline fuel-volume intensity than past cycles; operator returns will depend on tariff outcomes, network efficiency, and the ability to redeploy capacity toward heavier distillate and aviation-linked flows.
themes: Refinery-to-end-user connectivity
Tariff-led margin discipline
Transition from gasoline-led to distillate/aviation mix
Safety/compliance and network resiliency
one_sentence: Demand for gasoline transport remains structurally weaker while diesel/jet strength, tighter network planning, and tariff-driven pricing are reshaping the industry’s 2025-2026 growth mix.

title: Refrigerated Storage in the US
one_liner: Refrigerated storage is a high-capex cold-chain segment balancing modest capacity expansion with pricing pressure, while automation, fixed-storage contracts, and trade-linked infrastructure projects lift long-term resilience.
overview: US refrigerated storage supports food, agriculture, life sciences, and cross-border temperature logistics by holding goods in controlled environments and providing handling, consolidation, and shipment support. The 2025 USDA snapshot shows the system is larger than in 2021, but operator disclosures indicate continued demand stress from utilization softness and broader cost inflation. Growth now comes less from pure space need and more from service depth: automation, fixed commitments, and integrated import-export workflows.

market_size.2025: 3.99 billion cubic feet gross refrigerated capacity
market_size.2021: 3.73 billion cubic feet gross refrigerated capacity

growth.2025_2026_revenue_trend: 2025 operator disclosures show year-over-year declines in several reported revenue lines

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 report baseline references near-2022 full-year level: 2021 sector revenue USD 7.522 billion (IBIS snapshot context) and 2021 USDA capacity 3.73 billion cubic feet.
baseline_2022.growth: 2021-2026 projected growth: 3.6% CAGR (IBIS); historical 2005-2021 industry CAGR: 3.87%.

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn primarily from fixed storage commitments and rent/warehouse space pricing, plus handling and value-added services (cross-docking, order pick, temperature monitoring, compliance support, import-export execution).
cost_structure: Core costs are labor, power/utilities, facilities/maintenance, and transportation/handling support. Public filings and releases emphasize power and labor optimization, plus capital spend for automation/efficiency and emissions work to defend margins.
current_dynamics: Capacity and footprint expanded through 2025 while utilization and throughput softened for major operators at the 2025 quarter end.
Large players used automation, automation-heavy greenfield builds, and import-export rail/port integrations to compete on service reliability.
Private/captive logistics demand increased as public share fell (2021: 72% vs 2025: 62%), increasing pressure on the pure commodity storage model.
whats_growing: 2025-2026: US refrigerated capacity reached 3.99 billion cubic feet (USDA 2025), with facilities at 931.
2025 Q4: e-commerce was 16.6% of total U.S. retail (seasonally adjusted), supporting faster fulfillment and temperature-sensitive delivery networks.
Cross-border and rail-linked cold-chain infrastructure increased, such as new import-export hubs serving Canada-U.S.-Mexico food flows.
Automation, fixed contracts, and service bundling remain winners for operators with scale and capital access.
whats_shrinking: 2025 operator disclosures showed mixed to weak top-line momentum (for example Americold Q4 2025: $658.5m total revenue, -1.2% y/y).
Americold reported Q4 2025 throughput down 4.3% and economic occupancy near 76.1%, implying continued utilization compression.
Public warehouse dominance declined as private and semiprivate participation rose from 28% in 2021 to 38% in 2025.
recent_developments: 2025-03-25: We Store Frozen announced a new 180,000-square-foot Houston cold-storage facility, indicating continued new capacity build in high-growth domestic markets.
2025-04-01: Lineage announced acquisition of Bellingham Cold Storage, adding a multi-location regional network footprint.
2025-08-12: Americold opened a $100+ million Kansas City import-export hub with CPKC featuring 335,000 square feet and >50,000-pound container capability.
2026-02-19: Americold reported 2025 total revenue of $2.6 billion (down 2.4% y/y) and Q4 total revenue of $658.5 million (down 1.2% y/y).
2026-04-14: Americold reported a 21.0% Scope 1+2 emissions reduction from 2021 baseline and $23 million in 2025 energy-efficiency investments.
2026-06-09: Lineage announced construction of one of its largest and most automated refrigerated distribution centers in Hutchins, Texas, with expected completion by end-2027.
outlook: Near-term 2026 demand should remain positive in grocery, meal-prepared food, and trade lanes, but revenue quality will diverge by operator. Players with stronger fixed contracts, faster throughput, rail/port integration, and automation are positioned to gain share; operators unable to offset utilization and power/labor pressure will remain vulnerable.
themes: Capacity scale is rising, but utilization efficiency now matters more than pure footprint expansion.
Automation and advanced handling are becoming mandatory for competitive cost and service levels.
Trade and omnichannel food demand keep supply-chain reliability investments in focus.
Energy efficiency and emissions reduction are increasingly core operating priorities.
Industry structure remains concentration-biased, favoring large multi-region networks and fixed commitment models.
one_sentence: From 2021 to 2025, US refrigerated storage capacity increased to 3.99 billion cubic feet while major operators reported weaker 2025 utilization and revenue, making technology-led execution and contract quality the primary margin battleground in 2026.

title: Refrigeration Equipment Wholesaling in the US
one_liner: A niche but mature U.S. wholesale segment that remains tied to food, lodging, and commercial kitchen capex while shifting toward energy-efficient, low-GWP equipment and more digital distribution.
overview: The segment is centered on distributors of commercial refrigeration products and systems (excluding household refrigeration and A/C), and demand is strongly influenced by downstream spending by restaurants, grocery, and hospitality operators. Baseline IBIS reporting shows the market was around US$9.6 billion in 2022 with only moderate growth, and the latest visible trend is a shift to technology-enabled sales, faster product refreshes for refrigerant-efficiency compliance, and acquisition-led consolidation among regional players.

market_size.source: IBIS 2022 baseline file and projection language

baseline_2022.baseline_notes: IBIS baseline indicates relatively low growth, moderate but improving profitability, and concentration on downstream demand sensitivity.

how_it_makes_money: Primarily from distributing refrigeration equipment and related parts with gross margins driven by product sourcing leverage, plus value from service, technical support, installation support, and bundled credit-backed sales to installers and commercial operators.
cost_structure: Largest cost is product procurement from manufacturers, followed by inventory carrying cost, freight and logistics, workforce costs, and increasingly compliance-related carrying costs for higher-efficiency/Specialized refrigerant portfolios. Rising commercial electricity costs increase customer urgency for efficient equipment, while still challenging operators' budgets and slowing replacement cycles.
current_dynamics: Demand visibility is improving as foodservice continues recovery with still-cautious guest spending; restaurant sector sales were projected to recover to around US$1.55T in 2026 and remain a key downstream demand anchor. Energy and labor inflation are keeping replacement decisions selective, while firms are compensating through stronger digital channels (e-commerce, contractor apps) and portfolio expansion via acquisitions in HVAC/R distribution. Regulatory pressure on refrigerant efficiency and low-GWP transition is reshaping mix toward higher-value and more technical equipment lines.
whats_growing: 2025-11: HVAC/R distribution consolidation continued with Beijer Ref acquiring two U.S. regional refrigeration wholesalers, adding new territory.
2026-05: Watsco reported continued e-commerce growth and a broad rollout of A2L-related SKUs during 2026 Q1.
2026-07: Restaurant/economic demand backdrop remains positive with NRA framing 2026 foodservice sales at US$1.55T, sustaining commercial refrigeration replacement demand.
2026-08: Regulatory and sustainability messaging keeps commercial refrigeration energy-efficiency and refrigerant-transition capability in focus.
2026: DOE published/amended schedules for commercial refrigeration equipment standards and delayed effective-date actions, reinforcing long-duration compliance planning.
whats_shrinking: Margin headroom remains thin in a competitive, fragmented wholesaler market, limiting pricing power.
Unprofitable operators remain elevated in restaurants, increasing price sensitivity and extension-cycle negotiation pressure.
HCFC replacement overhang and legacy-stock management are compressing margins for non-compliant inventory pools.
Purely transaction-led growth is weak as customers prioritize capex discipline over broad discretionary expansions.
recent_developments: 2025-01-21 / 2025-03-07 / 2025-05-20: DOE commercial-refrigeration final rule cycle confirmed and delayed, with compliance timing extended and finalized standards framework reiterated.
2025-04-28: Watsco announced the acquisition of Jackson Supply Company (US$230M 2025 sales), adding 25 locations.
2025-11: Beijer Ref announced acquisitions of Key Refrigeration Supply and Dennis Supply to expand U.S. HVAC/R distribution reach.
2026-04-28: Watsco reported rapid digitization and A2L portfolio buildout as part of Q1 2026 strategy.
2026-07-23: EIA Electric Power Monthly data showed commercial electricity prices around 13.79 ¢/kWh in 2026 YTD and 13.41 ¢/kWh in 2025 benchmark.
2026-08-03: EPA ODS phaseout page updated; HCFC production/import restrictions remain core context for refrigeration portfolios.
outlook: The segment is likely to keep growing slowly through 2026–2027, with upside from foodservice and cold-chain modernization but with strong offset from operating-cost pressure and fragmented demand. Expect continued acquisition activity, digital channel gains, and portfolio migration toward compliant, efficient, and lower-emission solutions.
themes: Technology-led channel shift (e-commerce, contractor apps, data-driven tooling)
Regulatory-driven product mix shift toward low-GWP/high-efficiency refrigeration
Demand tied to foodservice/hospitality recovery cycles
Persistent margin discipline and inventory-management efficiency
Regional consolidation through buy-and-build among distributors
one_sentence: The industry is growing modestly in 2025–2026 on resilient restaurant and hospitality demand, but pressure on margins and higher operating costs are driving consolidation and efficiency-focused selling.

title: Refrigerator & Freezer Manufacturing
one_liner: US refrigerator and freezer manufacturing in 2026 is a mature, import-pressured market where housing-related demand and replacement cycles compete with high financing costs and tariff-related reshoring costs.
overview: The segment makes household refrigerators and freezers (commercial-grade units excluded). The latest public industry baseline remains the 2021 IBIS perspective, which still captures the core structural traits: limited product innovation scope, high import competition, and sensitivity to housing, credit, and household sentiment. In 2025-2026, that base is reinforced by elevated tariff pressure on steel-content appliances, still-positive but not accelerating housing and refinancing demand, and stronger consumer focus on operating-cost performance and connected features. Supply chains are increasingly regionalized as majors expand U.S. production claims and adjust sourcing toward tariff resilience.

market_size.year: 2021 data in provided baseline (separate 2022 point not published in that source)

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is primarily from selling finished major household refrigerators/freezers through appliance retailers, e-commerce channels, and builder/OEM channels; value creation also comes from premium model mix shifts (smart controls, energy-performance features), serviceable warranty/service offerings, and supply-chain efficiency from scale and domestic manufacturing footprint.
cost_structure: Direct materials (steel, compressors, insulation, electronics, refrigerant components) are the largest variable cost pool.
Labor and manufacturing productivity are meaningful but increasingly constrained by wage competition and need for automation.
Freight/logistics costs rise with global routing volatility and longer lead-time risk.
Import duties on steel-content appliances create additional landed-cost exposure when sourcing from countries with low-cost structures.
Regulatory and compliance costs rise with efficiency, safety, and labeling requirements even where policy review is reducing some mandates.
Working-capital carrying costs increase with pre-loaded inventories during tariff transitions.
current_dynamics: Demand remains linked to residential activity, with June 2026 private U.S. housing starts at 1,427,000 (SAAR) versus 1,399,000 in June 2025.
Credit conditions remain policy-sensitive: U.S. federal funds target remained 3.5%-3.75% after the June 17, 2026 FOMC meeting.
Household debt reached $18.8 trillion in Q4 2025, up $191 billion year-over-year (New York Fed).
Import tariffs on steel-derivative appliances continue to shape sourcing decisions, especially for products in HTS 8418.10.00.
Consumer sentiment improved in February 2026 but remains price-stressed; Index of Consumer Sentiment was 56.6 in Feb 2026 and February 2025 had been 64.7.
Whirlpool reported major appliance inventory/competitor strategy shifts around tariff pass-through and stated 2026 new-product volume plans.
The DOE signaled a 2026 deregulatory review of appliance energy mandates, affecting long-run compliance and product-design cost assumptions.
whats_growing: Replacement-led demand for reliable and connected units in energy-conscious households.
New-product cadence and connected/AI-enabled features (in-application diagnostics, smart assistants, app-based controls).
Domestic manufacturing/share narratives as majors emphasize U.S.-made positioning and tariff exposure management.
Channel diversification toward online and direct-to-consumer flow-through for premium SKUs.
Energy-utility-conscious purchasing in high-cost regions of the U.S. market.
whats_shrinking: Low- and mid-tier margin segments where imported, feature-light models compete heavily on price.
Export dependence, which remains vulnerable to exchange-rate and trade-policy volatility.
Margin expansion from standard products unless differentiation and regional sourcing offsets steel and component inflation.
Volume upside in non-urban, lower-income durables refresh cycles due elevated debt-service sensitivity.
recent_developments: 2025-06-23: Section 232 implementation notice added major appliance steel-derivative entries including HTS 8418.10.00 (combined refrigerator-freezers) and freezer categories for tariff coverage.
2025-03-26: Haier Smart Home reported 2025 full-year results and noted GE Appliances remained No. 1 in North America, with premium-brand revenue up 7%.
2026-02-20: University of Michigan February 2026 consumer sentiment release showed a flat-to-improving reading (Index of Consumer Sentiment 56.6) with high price concerns persisting.
2026-06-17: FOMC kept the policy rate at 3.5%-3.75% (in June 2026), leaving financing costs elevated for durable-good purchases.

2026-07-02: DOE issued proposed rules to end some appliance equipment mandates, including home appliance conservation rulemaking that has implications for future efficiency standard-setting and compliance costs.
outlook: The 2026-27 outlook is likely low-single-digit to flat unit growth for core US production, with replacement and energy-smart premiumization supporting selected segments while financing-sensitive demand and import competition pressure commoditized models. The strategic line of divergence is not total market size alone but mix: firms with localized manufacturing, stronger brand pull, and software-enabled after-sales value should defend margin better through 2026 and into 2027.
themes: Import policy shock transmission into source-cost parity
Housing-cycle demand sensitivity
Domestic manufacturing footprint as competitive moat
Energy-efficiency vs affordability tradeoff
Premium connected differentiation over commodity models
Tariff uncertainty and inventory timing discipline
one_sentence: Demand is expected to stay flat-to-down with modest price-sensitive replacement growth, while tariff changes, higher financing costs, and smart-energy differentiation determine winners among major players.

title: Regional Banks
one_liner: In 2026Q1, U.S. regional-bank-era players (defined as FDIC-insured institutions in the $50B–$500B asset band by the 2022 IBIS baseline) are operating in a sector that is growing in size and recovering earnings, while institutional count continues to shrink.
overview: US regional banks remain a core component of commercial credit intermediation through deposits, lending, and fee-based activity. FDIC’s 2026Q1 insured-institutions reporting shows stronger aggregate profitability and improved loan expansion, yet rising structural pressure from scale concentration, stronger compliance obligations above size thresholds, and persistent valuation sensitivity to rates.

growth.description: Q1 growth in reported total assets

market_size.period: 2021 revenue from baseline regional-bank profile (published February 2022)
market_size.note: Regional-bank baseline file snapshot used as historical comparator.

growth.period: Annualized 2016-2021 change in baseline profile revenue trend
growth.note: IBIS baseline indicates weak/corrective growth in the near-term pre-COVID-to-2021 period.

core_revenue: Interest income is primary, with 2026Q1 FDIC total interest income at 309,238.526 million USD and total noninterest income at 90,627.695 million USD.
Net interest income remained positive and loan activity continues to expand, indicating demand for credit, mortgages, and working-capital financing.
Fee income from payments, service charges, and other account/credit-related activities is increasing and helps offset margin softness.

2026Q1_revenue_mix_estimate.note: Based on FRED QBPQYTIY and QBPQYTNIY point values: 309,238.526 / (309,238.526 + 90,627.695).

cost_structure.margin_dynamics: NIM on FDIC Q1 2026 data is 3.31%, down 8 basis points from prior quarter.
cost_pressure_drivers: Labor and compliance intensity at smaller- to mid-size lenders remains elevated.
Technology and fraud/safety modernization costs are rising even as digital channels expand.
Credit loss/allowance management is a key non-discretionary earnings control.

current_dynamics.balance_sheet: 2026Q1 total assets reached 26,145,182.573 million USD, with deposits at 20,547,677.086 million USD.
current_dynamics.profitability: Net income rose to 80.5 billion USD in 2026Q1 vs 77.7 billion USD in 2025Q4.
current_dynamics.institutions: Reporting institutions declined from 4,338 in 2025Q4 to 4,278 in 2026Q1.
current_dynamics.credit_quality: Q1 2026 noncurrent rate was 0.98079% versus 0.96414% in 2025Q4, with net charge-offs easing vs Q4.

whats_growing: 2026Q1 net income rose to $80.5B (+3.6% q/q from 2025Q4).
Total assets increased to 26,145,182.573 million USD in 2026Q1 (+3.51% q/q vs 2025Q4).
Total deposits increased to 20,547,677.086 million USD in 2026Q1 (+2.34% q/q).
Total loans and leases increased to 13,692,552.539 million USD in 2026Q1 (+1.59% q/q vs 2025Q4).
Total noninterest income increased to 90,627.695 million USD in 2026Q1 (+5.8% q/q).
whats_shrinking: Institution count declined to 4,278 in 2026Q1 from 4,338 in 2025Q4.
Net interest margin eased to 3.31% in 2026Q1, down 8 bps.
Total interest income declined to 309,238.526 million USD in 2026Q1 from 316,557.391 million USD in 2025Q4.
recent_developments: 2026-05-27: FDIC press release reported 2026Q1 ROA of 1.26% and aggregate net income of $80.5B for 4,278 insured institutions.
2026-05-27: FDIC Q1 2026 release highlighted NIM of 3.31% (down 8 bps q/q) and a continued institution consolidation trend.
2026-05-30: FDIC QBP-FRED-linked data release shows 2026Q1 noninterest expense at 159,847.359 million USD and institutions at 4,278.
2025-12-31: FDIC Q4 2025 release reported industry ROA 1.24% and $77.7B net income (4,336 institutions), with full-year 2025 net income at $295.6B.
2026-02: FDIC released 2026 stress-testing economic scenarios for covered institutions above the $250B threshold.
outlook: Through 2026, regional-bank economics are expected to remain resilient if credit demand holds, but near-term upside is capped by margin compression and continued consolidation. Growth is more likely in scale-efficient lenders with stronger digital channels and stronger deposit/friction economics than in subscale franchises.
themes: Credit growth continues in commercial real estate and consumer lending while fee income rises.
Industry concentration rises as smaller institutions disappear or merge.
Margin pressure remains the primary profitability drag despite improving net income.
Regulatory intensity is structurally higher for banks above $50B and especially above $250B asset bands.
Credit quality is stable but requires persistent monitoring in slower-growth and rate-sensitive portfolios.
one_sentence: The segment is showing a 2026Q1 rebound in income (with ROA near 1.26% and net income around $80.5B) but faces margin pressure (NIM down 8 bps) and slower consolidation-resistant growth as the number of active banks declines.

title: Reinsurance Carriers in the US
one_liner: US reinsurance demand remains high as insurers push more risk transfer and alternative capacity into reinsurance programs, while pricing at top layers is softening gradually.
overview: Reinsurance carriers in the US continue to act as a risk-financing layer for insurers, ceding catastrophe, casualty, and specialty exposures through treaty and facultative structures. The market is global in distribution and increasingly fed by offshore and capital-markets sources, with Bermuda and major global reinsurers remaining central counterparties. US primary insurers are still heavily exposed to secondary peril and wildfire-driven volatility, which keeps underwriting decisions conservative despite broad signals of softening.

key_stats.market_size: USD 614 billion (traditional reinsurance capital USD 500bn at YE2024 + ILS capacity estimated USD 114bn in 2025)
key_stats.growth: Top non-IFRS17 reinsurers’ GPW among largest non-IFRS17 players grew 3.5% (from USD 87.6bn to USD 90.7bn); dedicated traditional reinsurance capital rose 6.8% from USD 468bn (YE2023) to USD 500bn (YE2024).

baseline_2022.growth: 4.4% in 2022; projected CAGR 1.25% for 2022-2028 in the legacy profile

how_it_makes_money: Premium income from reinsurance underwriting (gross and net earned), retrocession spread and treaty/facultative risk transfer fees; plus net investment income on fixed-income-heavy portfolios and other insurance service income.
cost_structure: catastrophe and reserve volatility, especially in secondary perils and U.S. catastrophe events
policy acquisition, commissions, and distribution costs
underwriting expenses and reserve volatility (including adverse development)
investment performance risk from fixed-income and credit exposure
current_dynamics: 2025–26 is characterized by stable-to-improving capitalization, selective softening at higher attachment points, stronger investment income support, and continued concentration of loss risk in climate-driven events; AM Best and Swiss Re both describe the market as profitable but still sensitive to large catastrophe years.
whats_growing: Global ILS/alt-capacity expansion, with ILS estimated at USD 114bn in 2025
US/market demand for large catastrophe placements and alternative capital-backed solutions (e.g., cat bonds and sidecar-style flows)
Selectivity in underwriting and diversification into more primary/specialty insurance-adjacent reinsurance solutions
Top non-IFRS17 reinsurance GPW trend to USD 90.7bn (from USD 87.6bn)
whats_shrinking: Price relief and moderate softening are emerging at higher layers in property reinsurance, not yet broad-based across all lines
Reinsurance segment gross premiums declined in recent company-level 2026 quarter examples while insurance segment growth stayed stronger
High-volatility US casualty and workers-comp pressure is compressing underwriting leverage for parts of the book
US line-rate momentum for auto and some short-tail segments cooled after prior surge
recent_developments: 2025-09-02: AM Best issued a global reinsurance review noting two straight years of strong results and solid performance through first-half 2025 despite weather losses likely above USD 100bn.
2025-08-19: AM Best reported dedicated traditional reinsurance capital up to USD 500bn at YE2024 and described 144A cat bond issuance as a record in both 2024 and 2025.
2025-08-19: AM Best estimated ILS capacity to rise to USD 114bn in 2025 and noted 144A issuance of USD 16.7bn through June 2025.

2026-01-20: AM Best market outlook for Global Non-Life Reinsurance remained 'stable,' with a shift from the hard-peak conditions after Jan 2023 renewals toward moderated but still profitable underwriting.
2026-03-19: Swiss Re reported global insured catastrophe losses in 2025 at USD 107bn and estimated USD 148bn as an adjusted 2026 baseline year with peak scenarios up to USD 320bn.

2026-03-31: A US reinsurance/public insurer filing reported reinsurance segment gross premiums down 9% quarter-over-quarter while insurance segment premiums rose 5%, with renewal premium rates up 6.6% in 2026.
outlook: Steady 2026 outlook through 2027 is for a more normalized market with continued disciplined underwriting, modest rates trend easing at upper layers, and continued dependence on capital resilience and loss management after major weather cycles.
themes: capital depth supports underwriting discipline
catastrophe-driven volatility remains the core risk driver
alt-cap and ILS as meaningful capacity supplements
high-quality reinsurers expanding in select property/casualty layers
social inflation and litigation/cost pressures in lines such as casualty
continued globalization of capital and reinsurance pipelines
one_sentence: By 2025-26, reinsurers are using stronger capital and disciplined terms to absorb climate-driven catastrophe pressure, even as rate cuts and slower exposure growth trim near-term margin expansion.

title: Relaxation Drink Production
one_liner: A niche functional beverage segment producing melatonin, L-theanine, and botanical formula drinks for sleep, stress relief, and calmness through convenience, grocery, and online channels.
overview: The US category remains small versus mainstream beverages but has become more strategic because demand for daily wellness solutions is broadening beyond traditional energy drinks into calming and wind-down use cases. IBISWorld’s baseline view describes strong growth from a low base, rapid formula experimentation, and pressure on margins from competition and potential regulatory shifts. In 2025–2026, category momentum is increasingly connected to adjacent nootropic, sleep-support, and alcohol-alternative functional beverages, while FDA and supplement-safety scrutiny is pushing stronger ingredient transparency, labeling, and quality systems. Channel exposure is improving in convenience chains and health-oriented grocery/online platforms, but operators remain dependent on premium shelf access and repeat trial.

key_stats.market_size: USD 286.3 million (IBISWorld forecast base, 2026)
key_stats.growth: 1.5% CAGR (IBISWorld style projection, 2021–2026)
key_stats.secondary_industry_context: North America functional beverages estimated at USD 58.01 billion in 2025 and USD 61.56 billion in 2026 (Mordor), with USD 6.12% CAGR through 2031

baseline_2022.market_size: USD 269 million (derived from IBISWorld 2021 USD 265.2 million at 1.53% annualized growth)
baseline_2022.growth: USD 269 million implied from 2021 to 2022 using 1.53% annualized progression

how_it_makes_money: Producers sell ready-to-drink relaxation beverages and shot formats with premium wellness positioning, primarily through convenience stores, supermarkets, retail pharmacies, and digital channels. Revenue is mixed across direct bottle sales and recurring buyer behavior driven by habit stacking (nighttime or stress-use routines), while launches in adjacent functional formats and higher margin SKU extensions (shots, adaptogen blends, non-traditional actives) improve wallet share.

cost_structure.ingredients: High and variable due to actives, flavor systems, and compliant sourcing of botanical/biochemical components
cost_structure.packaging_and_co-packing: Material and fill costs for cans/bottles remain significant, especially with small-batch innovation cycles
cost_structure.distribution: Retail shelf access, logistics, and placement intensity are expensive because category visibility is critical
cost_structure.marketing: Heavy trial-driven spend across digital, in-store activation, and influencer channels
cost_structure.compliance_and_quality: Rising burden from ingredient documentation, testing, labeling controls, and potential recalls/reformulations

current_dynamics: Category growth is strongest where brands combine relaxation claims with lifestyle positioning (sleep, stress, alcohol moderation, focus) and clear formats that fit impulse retail. Big functional-beverage economics are shifting from novelty to volume discipline, making distribution architecture and retail breadth decisive. Regulatory pressure remains a structural cost and speed brake, especially around label clarity, ingredient lawfulness, and caffeine/supplement messaging.
whats_growing: Niche functional blends that move beyond single-ingredient melatonin claims
Shot and convenience formats with immediate-consumption positioning
Distribution expansion into mainstream grocery/convenience clusters and online fulfillment
Cross-over demand from alcohol-alternative and nootropic hydration positioning
whats_shrinking: Standalone legacy CBD-only relaxation narratives without broader routine-value
Early-stage micro-players without scale to secure national retail shelf access
Low-trust products vulnerable to adverse labeling or ingredient-quality incidents
recent_developments: 2025-10-30: Recess completed a $30 million Series B led by CAVU and expanded to support national growth in relaxation/wellness positioning.
2025-07-01: BRĒZ reported a four-product launch, said it entered over 461 Sprouts stores, and cited US$28 million in 2024 revenue with US$13 million in Q1 2025.
2026-04-03: FDA issued a national food-safety alert against Addall XR Shot/Addall products after finding undeclared/dangerous ingredients in convenience-store distributed sleep-support products.
2026-06-29: FDA Human Foods Program added caffeine-content labeling and Healthy claim topics to 2026 guidance priorities.
2026-07-20: Sleep-supplement market reporting tracked US$3.33 billion for the US market in 2026, with continued movement toward targeted, multifunctional sleep-support formats.
outlook: Near-term outlook is positive but uneven: category demand is rising with sleep and stress concern, while pricing power depends on brand trust and shelf velocity. Producers with strong trial engines, distribution, and robust compliance systems are best placed to compound. Structural upside is in combining relaxation efficacy cues with cleaner labeling, simple formats, and stronger quality controls; downside is execution risk from category crowding and tighter enforcement.
themes: Functional beverages as a mainstream wellness platform
Sleep-and-stress support moving into routine consumption occasions
Regulatory tightening around label integrity and ingredient safety
Convergence of functional relaxation and alcohol-alternative beverages
Shift toward premium distribution and repeat-retail economics
one_sentence: US relaxation-drink producers are transitioning from early category experimentation to a more distribution-led, category-platform market inside the broader functional beverage expansion.

title: Religious Organizations in the US
one_liner: Religious organizations remain a large, donation-dependent service category in the U.S., with 2025 nominal revenue up but real gains muted and participation trends mixed.
overview: In this industry, revenues are almost entirely tied to religious and philanthropic donations rather than consumer sales, so household income and donor confidence remain the primary demand signals. The IBIS baseline from 2022 described this as a mature, moderate-growth category, and 2025–2026 data still show broad participation in religious activity without sustained acceleration from younger adults. Pew’s 2024–2026 findings indicate a stable-but-fragmented religious landscape: significant engagement among older cohorts and major faith traditions, persistent growth of non-affiliation, and renewed visibility of religion in public-role debates. The result is a sector with resilient headline funding but constrained expansion in core in-person engagement metrics.

key_stats.market_size: $151.58 billion (2025 religious-destination giving, nominal)
key_stats.growth: +2.4% nominal from 2024 to 2025; -0.2% inflation-adjusted (2025)
key_stats.supporting_scale_1: $617.20 billion total U.S. charitable giving in 2025 (+5.7% nominal; +3.0% real)
key_stats.supporting_scale_2: 40% of U.S. adults participated in religious services at least monthly in 2023-24 (in-person or online), while 37% said they are members of a house of worship
key_stats.supporting_scale_3: 1,603.3 thousand jobs in NAICS 8131 Religious Organizations in 2025 (BLS via FRED)

baseline_2022.market_size: $129.6 billion (estimated 2022 level, derived from IBIS 2021 $127.75bn baseline and 2021–2027 growth trajectory)
baseline_2022.growth: +1.44% annualized baseline growth path (IBIS projected 2021–2027)

how_it_makes_money: Primarily voluntary contributions: weekly/periodic tithes and offerings, member pledges/subscriptions, and online donations. Secondary income includes gift campaigns, event fundraising, space/event rentals, and affiliated mission revenues; in many organizations, donations from individuals remain the dominant share of annual revenue.
cost_structure: Cost base is staff and clergy compensation, facility operations (rent/mortgages, utilities, maintenance), service programming, digital and media streaming infrastructure, compliance/administration, insurance and risk management, and local outreach support. Variable costs rise with attendance-program intensity while fixed costs remain high in legacy building-heavy models.
major_players: Evangelical Protestant and non-denominational megachurch networks
Mainline and historically Black Protestant congregations
Islamic, Hindu, Buddhist, and other non-Christian congregational systems
current_dynamics: 2023-24 Pew RLS reporting: 37% of adults identify as members of a church, synagogue, temple or mosque, and about 40% participate in services at least monthly by any channel.
Pew’s 2025 attendance metrics still show 33% attending in-person monthly+, with 16% watching weekly online/TV and 18% attending only in person infrequently.
2025 Giving USA showed religious giving at $151.58B, with growth constrained in real terms despite nominal gains.
2026 Pew ATP showed opinion movement: 37% of adults said religion is gaining influence in public life (largest share since 2002), while 61% still said it is losing influence.
whats_growing: Digital and hybrid participation remains resilient (in-person plus online/TV attendance).
Nominal charitable flow to religion rose from $146.54B in 2024 to $151.58B in 2025.
Household giving participation remains central and still the single largest demand driver for the sector.
Engagement in religious services is increasingly multi-channel rather than purely in-person.
whats_shrinking: Real (inflation-adjusted) giving to religion was flat-to-down in 2025 despite nominal gains.
Religious participation intensity (especially among younger adults) remains relatively low versus historical norms.
Perceived cultural centrality of religion is mixed, with 61% still saying influence is declining in 2026 despite some visibility gains.
A larger non-affiliated share (22% in 2024 Gallup preferences data) continues to pressure headcount growth in traditional membership pathways.
recent_developments: 2024-02-26: Pew reported 37% of U.S. adults are members of a house of worship and 40% participated in religious services monthly by in-person or online means.
2024-02-26: Pew reported one-third attend services in person at least once a month, 16% watch weekly online/TV, and 7% watch virtually bi-monthly.
2024-06: Giving USA 2025 estimated total U.S. charitable giving at $592.50B for 2024 and religion receiving $146.54B.
2025: Giving USA 2026 estimated total U.S. charitable giving at $617.20B for 2025 and religion at $151.58B (+2.4% nominal, flat real).
2025-03: Gallup reported 2024 religious preferences at 45% Protestant/nondenominational Christian, 21% Catholic, 10% other religion, 22% not affiliated.
2026-04-06: Pew ATP found 37% of adults say religion is gaining influence in American life and 61% say it is losing influence.
outlook: Short to medium term, growth is likely modest and more about efficiency, retention, and channel mix than scale expansion. The most likely positive outcome is a continuation of nominal resilience in donation inflows supported by macro-income and digital convenience; the primary downside risk is real-giving drift if inflation and donor fatigue persist among financially constrained households. Organizations with strong community retention, hybrid engagement, and multi-generational relevance are best positioned versus attendance-dependent models.
themes: Donation-driven economics vs. attendance dependence
Aging donor and attendee base
Digital worship normalization
Intergenerational affiliation drift
Policy and church-state positioning
High fixed-cost real estate and staffing exposure
one_sentence: In 2025–2026, the industry held scale through strong donor sentiment, while Pew’s 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study still showed only 40% of adults participating in services monthly and 37% identifying as house-of-worship members.

title: Remediation & Environmental Cleanup Services in the US
one_liner: The US remediation and environmental cleanup market in 2026 remains federally anchored while PFAS and legacy contamination compliance are pulling faster private-sector demand growth.
overview: The U.S. remediation market is still concentrated in site and building cleanup, with growth supported by federal cleanup authorities and private redevelopment, while fixed-price contracts and project complexity keep margins dependent on scope control. Baseline industry size is still near the 2022 level in IBISWorld terms, but newer market trackers show a 2026 US estimate near USD 24.4 billion with stronger PFAS-driven activity and continued policy-driven demand volatility.

key_stats.additional_note: Projected US market CAGR is 6.8% for 2026-2033.

how_it_makes_money: Most revenue is earned through fixed-price remediation, environmental engineering, hazardous-material response, and emergency cleanup project contracts.

Public-sector contracts remain a core base (EPA Superfund-related and other federally funded remediation programs), while private projects rise with redevelopment, mining, manufacturing, and energy-related industrial activity.
Project economics are driven by site characterization, permitting, treatment/disposal, emergency mobilization, and post-remediation validation/reuse services.
Recurring value is generated via maintenance, compliance, and follow-on cleanup or closure activities after major incidents and legacy-site response work.
cost_structure: Majority of costs are labor, field mobilization, sampling, and analytical testing.
Specialized equipment, disposal logistics, and contractor coordination add meaningful fixed costs regardless of margins.
High contract-performance risk exists under fixed-price models when timelines, subsurface conditions, and permitting outcomes change.
Compliance reporting, health/safety systems, and liability controls are mandatory overhead across both public and private workstreams.
current_dynamics: 2026 is defined by a policy transition: EPA and related programs are tightening PFAS controls and funding, while DOE remains a large federal cleanup spender. EPA’s FY2026 planning signal keeps national cleanup activity meaningful but with budget re-shaping through Superfund tax financing and targeted program shifts, and PFAS infrastructure actions are expanding technical demand for sampling, treatment, and disposal solutions.
whats_growing: PFAS-driven drinking-water treatment and removal capacity demand is rising with EPA’s 2026 rulemaking and grant actions.
Private-site redevelopment and redevelopment-ready remediation is becoming the faster-growth use case in the market.
Emergency and resilience-focused cleanup demand remains elevated by climate-event pressure and insurance-driven risk management.
Advanced characterization and treatment technologies are gaining share as utilities pursue compliance and cost-controlled remedies.
whats_shrinking: Purely routine remediation volume growth is less visible than policy-driven or incident-driven spikes.
Projects exposed to narrow fixed-price execution risk are becoming more margin-volatile as scope changes and schedule shocks hit contract economics.
Some standalone program lines in EPA’s FY26 structure moved toward lower direct appropriated spending, increasing dependence on tax-based and targeted grant pathways.
recent_developments: 2026-05-18: EPA announced nearly $1.0 billion in new PFAS-related drinking-water actions and two proposed PFAS drinking-water rules.
2026-04-14: EPA launched PFAS OUT and set a target to engage about 3,000 systems (~2% of systems) with known PFOA/PFOS issues.
2026-05-19: EPA announced $77.257 million in EC-SDC funding for California PFAS cleanup planning, testing, and infrastructure.
2026-05 (EPA FY2026 budget framing): EPA reported Superfund budget authority of about $282.7 million (with Superfund tax-receipt transition mechanics) and about $330.6 million total trust-fund level.
2026-06 (FY2026 request package): DOE requested $8.092751 billion for Environmental Management cleanup, down about 5% from FY25 enacted levels.
outlook: For 2026-2028, the US market is likely to grow moderately (high single digits from 2025 to 2026) with mixed public/private momentum: strongest upside from PFAS, brownfield redevelopment, and natural-disaster-driven response, offset by funding reclassification risk and fixed-price execution pressure.
themes: PFAS lifecycle controls and drinking-water compliance
Federal cleanup spending resilience through EPA and DOE channels
Superfund mechanism transition and tax-funded cleanup financing
Emergency response demand from climate and industrial incidents
Private redevelopment conversion of brownfields and former industrial lands
Competition and risk pricing in fixed-price cleanup contracts
one_sentence: The industry combines public-sector programs (Superfund, EPA cleanup, DOE Environmental Management) with private land redevelopment, emergency response, and water/industrial contamination work, and remains highly sensitive to regulatory funding cycles.

title: Remodeling in the US
one_liner: In the US, residential remodeling is a fragmented but resilient service business powered by aging housing stock, home-equity financing, and steady demand for upgrades to living space and energy performance.
overview: Residential remodeling follows national housing affordability and interest-rate dynamics closely. NAHB shows industry activity gaining momentum in 2026-27, while the 2025 NAR Remodeling Impact Report estimates homeowners spent US$603.0 billion on home remodeling in 2024. Sector structure is dominated by smaller firms, yet demand is increasingly distributed through national DIY/pro channels and digital lead ecosystems.

market_size.definition: Estimated total US home remodeling spending (NAR).

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from full-project remodeling, labor plus materials execution, kitchen/bath/roof/project completion services, and retrofit-related work. In the 2025 NAR owner survey, 29% hired a professional for the whole job, 24% hired labor only, and another 24% did the job themselves; financing commonly used home-equity credit lines (54%) and savings (29%).

cost_structure.labour_and_subcontracting: Labor and skilled-trade capacity are the largest controllable costs and are highly volatile with local labor-market tightness.
cost_structure.materials_and_products: Procurement and systems/equipment components are major variable costs, with material inflation elevated through mid-2025 and still elevated in 2026.
cost_structure.business_pricing_pressure: NAHB reports trade contractor cost burden easing from 36% of revenue in 2021 to 30% in 2024, while average net margin reached 6.3% and gross margin 29.9% in 2024 (highest levels in the long run).

major_players: The Home Depot (major home-improvement pro channel and supply scale)
Lowe's (pro-focused home-improvement retailer with large US footprint)
Angi (major homeowner-to-contractor sourcing platform, over 300 million projects)
NAHB member local remodelers (fragmented operator base; typically small and project-led)
current_dynamics: The NAHB/Westlake Royal Remodeling Market Index stayed above break-even for 24 consecutive quarters through 2025, with Q4 2025 at 64. Home improvement spending is gaining share inside residential construction. Growth is supported by home-equity financing and aging-in-place demand, while high mortgage rates and material/labor inflation remain key downside risks.
whats_growing: Kitchen, bathroom, and full-home renovation demand remains a dominant mix.
Aging-in-place and accessibility-related remodeling (56% of remodelers report increased requests).
Statewide demand concentration in high-growth states (for example, Michigan +15.9% change in Q4 2025 according to NAHB SPR data).
Pro-led renovation segments and contractor-facing service channels.
whats_shrinking: Whole-job DIY is not dominant for larger-value projects; consumers still split work with professionals on larger jobs.
High interest-rate friction and policy uncertainty are suppressing some new-build spillover demand into remodeling.
Margin resilience is constrained as labor and materials remain elevated versus historical norms.
recent_developments: 2025-04-09: NAR estimated US homeowners spent US$603.0B on remodeling in 2024.
2025-02-25: NAHB projected single-family starts to grow 0.2% in 2025 and +4.0% in 2026 while noting mortgage rate sensitivity.
2026-01-15: NAHB reported Q4 2025 RMI at 64, with better leads and backlog indicators.
2026-02-18: NAHB said residential remodeling expected +3.0% in 2026 and +2.0% in 2027, and RMI has stayed above 50 for 24 quarters.
2026-04-10: NAHB published Remodelers’ Cost of Doing Business highlights with 2024 average net margin 6.3% and gross margin 29.9%.
2026-05-05: NAHB SPR showed Q4 2025 leading state shares: California 7.9% ($22.11B), Texas 7.0% ($19.7B), Florida 5.5% ($15.3B).
outlook: NAHB's 2026 framing points to moderate short-term expansion in remodeling with a +3.0% expectation for 2026 and +2.0% in 2027 (inflation-adjusted), alongside longer-run targets of +19% by 2030 and +32% by 2035 versus 2026 levels, but execution remains exposed to labor shortages, mortgage affordability, and input inflation.
themes: Aging housing stock and lock-in effects keep owners upgrading existing homes
Energy-efficiency and accessibility retrofits remain structural demand drivers
Fragmented local contractor market with heavy subcontractor dependence
Scale effects from large material-retailer ecosystems (Home Depot, Lowe's) in pro channel
Digital matchmaking and lead platforms increasingly important in customer acquisition
one_sentence: US remodeling is growing again in 2026 on a modest path while still carrying pressure from mortgage conditions, labor gaps, and material-cost volatility.

title: Rendering & Meat Byproduct Processing
one_liner: U.S. rendering processors convert inedible animal byproducts into feed proteins, fats, and industrial/energy inputs, with growth now tied to livestock throughput, biofuel margins, and trade-policy-linked demand.
overview: The U.S. rendering & meat byproduct processing industry remains a mature, low-margin, high-volume segment that sits downstream of meat and poultry slaughter and upstream of animal feed, fertilizer byproducts, and oleochemical/energy uses. Baseline IBIS framing shows moderate scale and modest growth from a stable domestic demand base, with exports and feed demand still the key scale multipliers. In 2025–2026, the business mix is increasingly influenced by policy-driven renewable fuels (especially biodiesel, renewable diesel, and SAF-related feedstock economics), biofuel credit timing, and trade channel shifts rather than broad end-consumer shocks.

key_stats.market_size: US IBIS-style industry revenue around $4.9 billion in 2026 (model outlook from the IBIS baseline)
key_stats.growth: 0.8% CAGR from 2021 to 2026 in the IBIS projection

baseline_2022.market_size: about $4.7 billion (IBIS baseline era, with 2022 treated as near-flat continuation from 2021, prior to 2025-26 policy-driven shifts)
baseline_2022.growth: roughly flat to low-single-digit in 2021–2022; modeled 2021–2026 trajectory was +0.8% CAGR

how_it_makes_money: Captures and processes animal byproducts from slaughter plants, food service, and related streams, then sells into: 1) animal nutrition (feed and pet food inputs), 2) fertilizers and agricultural additives, 3) rendered fats/greases for industrial and biofuel feedstock markets, and 4) specialty ingredients (e.g., protein/ collagen-adjacent outputs in broader portfolios). Profitability depends on conversion yield, offtake mix by product line, and energy/capital costs.

cost_structure.main_inputs: Collection/handling network, yield recovery, and feedstock variability from upstream livestock processing volumes
cost_structure.processing: Labor, utilities/steam energy, and plant maintenance for rendering/sterilization
cost_structure.logistics: Outbound transport and inbound residue collection from multi-point feed supply
cost_structure.quality_and_compliance: Testing, food/animal safety controls, and regulatory compliance
cost_structure.market_risk: Commodity-cycle impacts from feed and fuel economics, and short-cycle changes in biofuel economics

current_dynamics: Recent data in 2025–2026 shows mixed pull-through: steady-to-higher livestock product availability supports byproduct supply, while renewable-fuel demand is policy-sensitive and operationally volatile. EIA reporting shows 1Q25 biomass-based diesel production weakness from tax-credit uncertainty, followed by biofuel trade and export rebalancing once policy clarity improved. USDA 2026 livestock outlooks show pork and turkey production elevated versus prior periods, which supports rendering feedstock availability, while beef trade has shown more uneven quarterly movement. The operational model is therefore still supply-linked, but less constrained by end-consumer demand and more by upstream throughput and energy-policy profitability.
whats_growing: Animal meal and oil feed demand linked to higher poultry/pork throughput in 2026 livestock outlooks
SAF/renewable fuels demand chain integration, especially where waste-derived feedstocks qualify under low-carbon pathways
Industrial biofuel byproduct flow as renewable diesel and SAF capacity utilization improves
Export participation in higher-margin downstream channels where policy support and logistics permit
whats_shrinking: Margins pressured when federal biofuel credit timing is uncertain
Biodiesel output growth relative to renewable diesel/other biofuel balance
Any high-cost plants when output mix shifts to lower-margin categories
Purely domestic growth momentum without policy support in energy-linked outlets
recent_developments: 2025-06-04: EIA reported 1Q25 renewable diesel and biodiesel production fell sharply (biodiesel around 60,000 b/d, lower due to federal credit uncertainty).
2025-05-06: EIA reported U.S. SAF production capacity and output rising, with Other Biofuels production roughly doubling from Dec 2024 to Feb 2025.
2026-03: EPA RFS March 2026 final-rule response projected BBD production of 4.5 billion gallons in 2026 and 4.7 billion gallons in 2027, with roughly 70–75% domestic feedstock use.
2025-05-07: EIA showed U.S. renewable diesel and SAF exports in 2H25 averaged ~50,000 b/d (about 20% of production), with Canada and Europe as main destinations.
2026-06-17: USDA LDP-M-384 adjusted 2026 meat outlooks including beef forecast 25.438 billion lb and pork forecast 28.0 billion lb for 2026.
outlook: Near-term outlook is moderate expansion with uneven profitability. The structural tailwind is higher throughput in pork and poultry chains and deeper biofuel integration, while the key drag remains policy and input margin volatility. Expect continued selective consolidation and strategic positioning toward higher-margin end uses (specialty feed/industrial channels) rather than pure commodity throughput growth.
themes: Livestock-demand proxy: rendering revenue tends to follow meat throughput and slaughtering activity
Policy sensitivity: renewable-fuel credits, equivalence rules, and RFS updates materially shift economics
Trade sensitivity: biofuel byproduct exports and import competition in lean-processing channels
Operational resilience: stable, incremental growth in a mature sector through efficiency and product mix
one_sentence: Demand stays tied to livestock and poultry throughput and a volatile biofuel policy cycle, while capacity and supply-chain consolidation keep the industry low-growth but still expanding in selected niches.

title: Renters' Insurance
one_liner: US renters' insurance remains a small but resilient personal lines market driven by rental demand, climate risk awareness, and low-to-mid ticket digital distribution.
overview: Renters' insurance underwrites personal property and liability risk for occupants of leased housing, typically via HO-4 policies for tenants and HO-6 for condo unit owners. Premium size has historically been much lower than homeowners’ policies, making demand sensitive to rent affordability and risk perception. New 2025–2026 indicators show renters are increasingly exposed to affordability and disaster risks, while policy ownership remains below full penetration. The competitive field is increasingly digitized, with carriers relying more on online channels for quotes, binding, and claims workflows.

key_stats.market_size: 2026: about US$4.2 billion (US$4.055 billion in 2021 baseline with low single-digit growth trajectory)
key_stats.growth: 2021-2026: +0.5% CAGR (IBIS-style projection)

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: about US$4.1 billion (near the 2021 level reported in baseline dataset, with low growth trajectory)
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: about 0.5% CAGR implied in the 2021-2026 IBIS outlook

how_it_makes_money: Premium collection from HO-4 (tenant/renters) and HO-6 (condo) homeowners-property lines is the core. Some carriers use bundling with auto/personal lines, liability endorsements, and optional riders; investment income on float is a secondary income stream.
cost_structure: Losses and loss adjustment are the largest variable cost, followed by commissions and policy administration. Core fixed costs include underwriting, fraud/claims analytics, cloud and compliance operations, and catastrophe reserving/capital costs in severe-weather markets.

current_dynamics: Demand is being supported where rental occupancy remains strong, while cost pressure rises from weather-driven risk repricing and high affordability sensitivity; at the same time, digital self-serve platforms keep conversion cheaper and broaden penetration among digitally active renters.
whats_growing: 2025-10-23: Zillow reports 48% of surveyed renters have renters insurance, up slightly in recent consumer polling context.
2026-07-28: Q2 2026 rental vacancy remains elevated in many regions (7.3% nationally), supporting a large renter universe.
2026-05: Federal Reserve housing report shows 23% of renters fell behind on rent at some point in 2025, reinforcing value-focused purchasing behavior.
2026-08-14 to 2026-08-12: NAIC regulator meeting activity continues on homeowners/renters-related market data, indicating active reporting and data modernization in this market.
whats_shrinking: Renters without coverage remains high versus full penetration, with large uninsured segments.
Regulatory and catastrophe-cost pressure in high-risk areas is likely compressing margins where risk pools are concentrated.
Low premium pricing in some channels remains hard to sustain as catastrophe frequency and repair costs rise.
recent_developments: 2025-10-23: Zillow article reports 48% of renters have renters insurance; only 32% said landlord requirement is mandatory.
2025-10-23: Same article reports average quoted renters premium around US$276/year (US$23/month).

2026-07-28: Census Housing Vacancy Survey shows Q2 2026 rental vacancy at 7.3% with homeownership at 65.0%.
2026-04-30: California 2025 P&C market-share filing shows continued concentration in large national carriers, implying ongoing scale pressure in retail insurance distribution.
outlook: Expect low-single-digit revenue growth overall through 2026–2027, with growth concentrated in digital-first acquisition and retention bundles rather than headline premium expansion. Renters' coverage demand is structurally supported by still-large rental tenure, but margins remain vulnerable where climate risk and claims volatility rise.
themes: Digital-first retail and comparison-channel competition
Affordability sensitivity in renter households
Climate-risk pricing and underwriting tightening in hazard-prone ZIPs
Consolidation and scale advantage among large P&C groups
one_sentence: The industry serves mostly tenants and condo owners through HO-4/H0-6 policies, with modest near-term growth as renter concentration eases and competition in distribution keeps price pressure high.

title: Repossession Services
one_liner: The U.S. repossession industry secures creditor collateral after borrower delinquency, with auto loans remaining the dominant source of demand and subprime financing as the key volume multiplier.
overview: The U.S. market is small but highly cyclical, with activity tied to consumer credit conditions and vehicle affordability. Auto lending remains the core engine: NIADA and CFPB data show continued stress in used/new vehicle financing, while NY Fed and CFPB reporting confirm continued growth in household debt and ongoing use of third-party recovery channels.

key_stats.market_size: US$1.20 billion in 2025 (Kentley)
key_stats.growth: The 2026 report snapshot shows approximately 1.0% five-year CAGR; from official 2022 employer-firm data (US$1.16bn) to 2025 (US$1.20bn), total growth is about 3.4% (~1.1% CAGR).
key_stats.concentration: Top 4 companies held 15.8% market share in 2025
key_stats.vehicle_recovery_share: Vehicle repossessions were historically 50.2% of revenue in 2021

baseline_2022.growth: From 2022 to 2025, official revenue moved from US$1.16bn to US$1.20bn (about 1.1% annualized)

how_it_makes_money: Recovery assignment fees from lenders and finance companies for repossession execution.
Storage/impound and transportation fees while assets are held and moved.
Platform and workflow coordination fees paid by lenders/forwarders for case management.
Remarketing-related revenue through auction preparation, transfer, and sale support.
cost_structure: Labor and field operations are the core cost driver (tows, repossession agents, skip tracing operations).
2022 official expense data indicate US$731 million in industry expenses (Census/FRED RSEESTFITEF32561491).
Vehicle, fuel, towing, compliance, and insurance/bonding costs remain structurally high.
2025 benchmark data points indicate professional services are a small but visible line item (2.7% of operating expenses).
current_dynamics: 2025Q4: NY Fed Household Debt and Credit context shows high and persistent household debt levels, supporting sustained collateral-recovery demand.

2025-01-23: CFPB’s Repossession in Auto Finance report confirms the auto market scale (~US$1.64 trillion in 2024Q3 context) and that third-party forwarder use has become important.
whats_growing: 2026-06: Subprime vehicle financing share increased year-over-year (used: 20.60%, broad subprime: 15.75%).
2026-02: NIADA noted slower decline or plateau in auto delinquencies compared with earlier spikes, creating a steady workflow for recovery agents and forwarders.
2026-06: Average used-car loan duration and amounts rose (67.73 months, US$27,070), increasing long-tail payment strain potential.
2026-02: Auto loan originations in 2025Q4 increased versus 2024Q4 (US$180.8bn vs US$175.1bn), supporting replacement-cycle recovery demand.
whats_shrinking: 2026-02: 2025Q4 auto-originations slipped versus Q3 (US$180.8bn vs US$183.9bn).
2026-06: Repo-ready delinquency growth is not accelerating broadly as sharply as in stress years, limiting a sharp boom in repossession volume.
2026-06: Higher financing costs keep lenders more selective, increasing underwriting discipline and moderating default growth.
recent_developments: 2025-01-23: CFPB released the Repossession in Auto Finance report, citing a US$1.64 trillion auto-loan market (2024Q3 context) and persistent data gaps in precise repossession volume.

outlook: Expect controlled but persistent growth through 2026 with elevated debt balances and slower borrowing costs not enough yet to materially ease payment stress. The rebound risk is to the downside in defaults if credit quality weakens further; upside comes from sustained subprime exposure and longer-duration auto financing.

Subprime expansion and credit score erosion
Third-party forwarding and remarketing infrastructure
Operational/legal compliance intensity
Technology-enabled skip tracing, tracking, and assignment routing
one_sentence: In 2026, repossession demand remains moderate-to-steady as U.S. household debt and auto-credit stress stay elevated while high borrowing rates prevent a sharp rise in defaults.

title: Residential Cleaning Service Franchises
one_liner: Recurring home-cleaning franchises serving U.S. households through subscription visits, one-off deep cleans, and maintenance add-ons.
overview: IBIS baseline data from Jan 2022 shows a small but steadily growing U.S. residential cleaning franchise business, and recent franchise-industry evidence in 2026 points to continued expansion in home services through branded, recurring, and tech-enabled models.

baseline_2022.growth: 2.4% annualized (projected to 2026)

how_it_makes_money: Recurring cleaning contracts are the core model, with regular visits and repeat schedules generating predictable monthly revenue.
Average-unit economics are supplemented by one-off services (move-in/out, deep cleans, seasonal specialty cleaning).
Cross-selling of green, maintenance, and home-upkeep services improves customer retention.
Franchise systems monetize via startup fees, royalties, and marketing/technology support fees layered on unit operations.
cost_structure: Labour is the largest variable cost; janitorial/home-cleaning roles are labor-intensive and wage-sensitive.
Janitors and building-cleaner wage benchmarks indicate mid-2024 pressure on service payroll planning.
Chemical supplies, equipment, transport, insurance, and worker safety/HR costs are major operating line items.
Recurring local and national advertising, software/dispatch tooling, scheduling systems, and platform fees add fixed operating drag.
Typical franchisee startup/ongoing cost bands remain wide: Molly Maid (2026 FDD basis) $144,150–$203,950 startup; Cleaning Authority total units 241 franchised in 2026 context.

2026-04-09: FRANdata reported franchised home-services unit growth averaging 3.7% CAGR between 2021 and 2024.
2026-04-09: IFA noted 11% of 2025 new concepts were in home services and maintenance categories.
2025-12-31: Molly Maid disclosed 430+ U.S. franchise locations.
2026: The Cleaning Authority was listed with 244 total units (241 franchised).
whats_growing: Recurring-service subscriptions and retention-led pricing
Green/low-chemical service positioning
AI-assisted scheduling, CRM, and route efficiency
Subscription bundles and upsell programs tied to seasonal home maintenance
whats_shrinking: Purely transactional, one-off cleaning sales without retention programs
Pure price-based competition from independent operators
Customer willingness for discretionary add-on spending when housing maintenance budgets are constrained

2025-07: U.S. population aged 65+ reached 18.9% in 2025 Census QuickFacts, supporting outsourcing demand from older households.

2025-12-31 / 2026: Cleaner chain disclosures showed active expansion at Molly Maid and The Cleaning Authority unit levels.
outlook: Near-term growth is expected to be steady rather than explosive: the segment remains resilient and need-based, but competition and wage pressure should keep margins disciplined while favoring better-managed, branded, and tech-enabled operators.
themes: Labor cost management and retention are central to franchise unit health.
Trust and recurring engagement beat one-shot lead conversion.
Convenience and time-sensitivity drive demand more than pure price.
Tech efficiency (dispatch, reviews, routing, AI support) becomes a key moat.
Green credentials and reliability messaging increasingly influence premium segments.
one_sentence: The U.S. residential cleaning franchise segment remains demand-resilient on recurring household service contracts, with 2025–26 momentum concentrated in convenience, trust, and tech-enabled operations.

title: Residential Intellectual Disability Facilities in the US
one_liner: Residential services for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities are shifting toward Medicaid-funded community-based care, while aging demographics and workforce strain define operating outcomes.
overview: The industry provides residential, supervisory, medical coordination, and life-skill supports for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities. The 2022 IBIS baseline shows a $35,512m market, Medicaid-linked demand, and a long-running transition from larger institutions to smaller, local group-home and supported-living settings. Current policy and demographic signals in 2025–2026 reinforce that shift: greater HCBS rebalancing, tighter federal reporting expectations, and a rising older-adult population.

market_size.value: $35,512m (2022) and approximately $39,200m (2026 estimated from IBIS 2022 baseline applying 2.50% CAGR to 2027)
market_size.growth: 2.50% CAGR projected 2022-2027; HCBS share rising from 86.6% (2022 baseline) to 86.8% historical in 2024 and 87.0% target for 2027

key_stats.growth: n/a

baseline_2022.market_size: $35,512m revenue; $2,592m profit; 18,477? no, 2,592m profit is as provided in IBIS block (2022)
baseline_2022.growth: Revenue CAGR 2.81% from 2005-2022; projected 2.50% CAGR 2022-2027; profit margin around 7.3% in 2022 and around 7.30% projected by 2027

how_it_makes_money: Primary payers are Medicaid and Medicare via ICF/IID-authorized residential and home/community-based service financing; secondary revenue includes private health insurance reimbursements and limited philanthropy/government grants. Federal spending for Medicaid/Medicaid-matched LTSS and HCBS capacity remains the dominant demand enabler, including ARP-related Medicaid HCBS investments. Baseline reports also show significant reliance on private pay for out-of-pocket gaps when coverage is incomplete.
cost_structure: Labor is the dominant cost driver: 24/7 supervision, nursing/clinical support, and care-coordination staffing. Indirect care expenses include provider compliance, incident management systems, transportation, lodging and food, and residential operating overhead. 2024 workforce data indicates high turnover pressure (37% average DSP turnover in 26 participating states) and wage compression, which increases training/recruitment costs and service instability.
major_players: State developmental-disability systems administering Medicaid HCBS/ICF-IID capacity
Private nonprofit provider networks (for example, Elwyn and Easterseals residential/IDD service systems)
Direct Support Professional agencies and vendors (3,936 agencies represented in NCI-IDD workforce reporting, 2024)
State Medicaid plans and managed-care arrangements that design and rate service delivery
current_dynamics: 2026 policy momentum is strongest around HCBS quality and access requirements: CMS tracks HCBS share growth and continues monitoring state waiting-list and quality reporting, while CMS set delayed enforcement for selected grievance-system requirements through 2027-12-31. Enrollment and use are still moving out of institutional settings, but workforce shortages in direct support roles remain an operational bottleneck and are pushing labor costs up even as providers raise wages.
whats_growing: HCBS share of Medicaid LTSS users is trending up (86.6% baseline in 2022 to 87.0% target in 2027 and 87.2% target in 2028).
US population aged 65+ reached 18.9% in 2025 V2025 estimates, increasing indirect demand for family substitution and substitute long-term services.
The direct support workforce in IDD settings is large (344,179 DSPs in survey period, 2024) and becoming more formalized through reporting and quality frameworks.
Residential IDD provider presence remains concentrated in smaller home-like and supported-living settings, reducing dependence on large institutions.
whats_shrinking: In Medicaid long-term services data, institutional LTSS users declined from 1,769k in 2019 to 1,456k in 2021 (MACPAC trend).
The share of facility models based on large institutional settings is under policy and consumer pressure from the HCBS rebalancing framework.
Turnover and staffing constraints have reduced the number of providers that can accept new referrals in some states (1 in 4 agencies reporting this at least part-time in 2024; down from 38% in 2023).
