2025-12: NCI-IDD State of the Workforce infographic (survey year 2024) reported 344,179 DSPs and 37% average turnover, with 26% agencies turning away/referrals in 2024 versus 38% in 2023.

2024-07: BLS long-term-care employment data showed residential ID/mental health facilities are a distinct job category, with HCBS and home/community settings collectively larger than institutional settings.
2024-09-09: Medicaid published CMS-2442-F applicability updates, including 2026/2027 compliance dates for several HCBS person-centered and reporting requirements.
outlook: Short-term growth should remain moderate-positive through 2027, led by HCBS rebalancing and supportive Medicaid policy targets rather than abrupt institutional expansion. Price/margin pressure is likely to stay elevated because labor supply constraints and rising training, retention, and compliance burdens outweigh utilization upside. The most important 2026-27 inflection is provider execution: states that improve direct support staffing, wage competitiveness, and data-driven person-centered planning should win share.
themes: HCBS rebalancing over institutional care
Aging-demographic tailwinds
Workforce retention as a structural cost risk
Medicaid compliance and quality-measure expansion
State-level variation in waiver implementation and access
one_sentence: The sector in 2026 continues steady expansion in community settings, but profitability is constrained by labor intensity, staffing turnover, and compliance overhead tied to Medicaid HCBS rules.

title: Residential RV & Trailer Park Operators
one_liner: The U.S. residential RV and trailer park operator segment remains a retirement-led, recurring rental real-estate niche where scale-focused operators in 2025-26 are trading higher operational leverage for tighter cost control and portfolio cleanup.
overview: The sector is centered on leasing RV and manufactured-home sites, with stable long-duration occupancy from residents and repeat travel demand from seasonal users. In the latest company-level disclosures, leading operators report high occupancy and positive same-store NOI while simultaneously running disposal/asset-replacement programs and debt de-leveraging through 2025-26.

key_stats.market_size: $8.599 billion annual revenue (2022, NAICS RV parks and camps, Service Annual Survey; all establishments, employer firms)
key_stats.recurring_mix_signal: Major public operator disclosures still show a high share of annual revenue (e.g., 92% annual sources at ELS)
key_stats.establishments_proxy: 7,985 NAICS 7212 establishments in Census profile references (latest public snippet)

how_it_makes_money.primary_revenue: Lot/site rental from annual MH and RV residents, plus annualized home-site and marina/RV membership revenue
how_it_makes_money.secondary_revenue: Transient RV and seasonal stays, utility reimbursements, and amenity-related charges
how_it_makes_money.industry_evidence: ELS reported core MH +4.1%/5.5% and core RV+mria +4.1% growth in 2025, with more than 90% of revenue from annual sources in the same filing context.

major_cost_components: On-site labor and property management staffing
Utilities, grounds care, and common-area operations
Repairs, site upgrades, and infrastructure renewal
cost_structure.pricing_pressure: ELS 2026 guidance points to property operating expense growth in the 2.2%-3.2% range versus property revenue growth around 4.0%-5.0% (mid-point 4.5%), implying margins remain sensitive to labor and inflation inputs.
cost_structure.margin_notes: Industry operators emphasize high-share annual occupancy as the profitability anchor versus higher-variance transient segments.

current_dynamics: 2026 guidance from ELS shows continued core income growth while projecting controlled expense growth (property operating expenses +2.2% to +3.2%).
Sun reported 2025 same-property NOI strength (5.7%) and major balance-sheet repair through debt reduction and sale of non-core properties.
ELS and Sun both reported high core occupancy in 2025 (ELS 94%; Sun 97.9% excluding transient and high MH+RV same-property occupancy).
2026 macro backdrop remains inflationary, with BLS labor and unemployment data still reflecting a relatively soft but non-recovered labor market.
Mortgage-rate environment (6.69% 30-year FRM in Aug 2026) continues to influence affordability-sensitive residential alternatives.
whats_growing: Retiree and aging-household demand: 18.9% of U.S. population age 65+ in 2025.
Long-stay segments with annualized occupancy remain the strongest revenue anchor.
Consolidation and portfolio optimization among public operators (acquisitions plus selective disposals).
Same-store NOI management and ancillary service monetization in larger REIT portfolios.
whats_shrinking: Margin sensitivity to financing conditions as rates remain elevated.
Transient-heavy segments are structurally less stable than annual residential occupancy.
Higher operating costs (labor and utility/maintenance intensity) remain a structural drag; operators are explicitly flagging expense management.
Smaller independent operators face greater pressure from capital-market discipline and rising compliance/technology expectations.
recent_developments: 2025: ELS reported core MH rental growth of 5.5% and core annual RV/marina rental growth of 4.1%.
2025: Sun said it repaid about $3.3 billion of debt, reduced net debt/TTM recurring EBITDA to 3.4x, and completed the Safe Harbor portfolio simplification strategy.
2025: Sun acquired 11 MH and 3 RV properties for $457.0m, repurchased 32 UK freehold ground-lease interests, and sold non-core properties.
2026-03: ELS 2026 shareholder materials showed guidance of core property operating revenue +4.5%, property operating expense +2.7% (midpoint) and income from property operations +5.7% (midpoint).
2026-07: BLS CPS reported U.S. unemployment of 4.1%.
2026-08-06: Freddie Mac PMMS 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.69%.
outlook: A modest, uneven 2026-27 expansion path appears likely, led by operators with diversified annual and growth-capable transient portfolios. Consolidation, de-leveraging, and disciplined property-level operations should keep high-quality operators resilient, while financing pressure and labor intensity likely keep valuation and execution risk elevated.
themes: Aging-demographic demand supports long-stay occupancy
Annualization versus transient mix rebalancing
Operator consolidation and simplification
Cost discipline versus inflationary input costs
Housing-affordability substitution toward alternative home formats
one_sentence: After pandemic normalization, operators entered 2026 with stronger occupancy and same-store NOI, but demand quality is increasingly tied to age demographics, housing affordability pressures, and high short-term financing costs.

title: Respiratory Protection Equipment Manufacturing
one_liner: US respiratory-protection manufacturing has shifted from pandemic-driven demand toward compliance-led, higher-specification replacement demand with stronger approval and quality controls.
overview: The industry remains small versus broader PPE but is structurally durable because respirator requirements are embedded in core occupational-safety rules across construction, healthcare, mining, firefighting, military, and industrial facilities. A 2025 US market benchmark from recent research places this segment around USD 3,988.4 million, while the 2022 IBIS baseline period already showed steady but low single-digit growth and rising compliance-driven demand for fit, serviceability, and accessory replacement. Key near-term pressure now comes from regulatory churn and approval-list maintenance rather than purely from health-event shocks, with market-share gains increasingly tied to reliability, comfort, and auditability.

key_stats.additional_note: US was US$ 3,988.4m in 2025 and is forecast at 8.8% CAGR through 2033 by 2026-2033 outlook.

growth.source: IBIS forecast path in baseline report

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is led by respirator hardware (APR/PAPR/SCBA and filtering facepiece models) and replenishment channels: filters, cartridges, canisters, battery assemblies, hoses, seals, and maintenance kits; operators improve margin with premium features (electrical/power systems, end-of-life indicators, workflow software aids) and longer service relationships with regulated enterprises.

cost_structure.materials: High-grade filtration media, polymer components, battery and electronics are the largest variable input buckets and remain volatile at approval-cycle highs and lows.
cost_structure.regulatory_and_quality: NIOSH/CEL status assurance, testing support, and documentation burden are fixed-to-semi-fixed costs that rise whenever certification rules or approval status changes.
cost_structure.sales_and_support: Commercial mix is weighted toward direct sales to industrial distributors and safety procurement channels plus technical support for fit-program compliance documentation.
cost_structure.margin_profile: Mature market with stronger margins on high-spec reusable and specialized systems, weaker pressure in commoditized disposable low-cost models vulnerable to substitution and price competition.

current_dynamics: Demand is no longer dominated by emergency stockpiles; it is increasingly driven by routine OSHA/Federal enforcement readiness, fit-program integrity, counterfeit-risk control, and the need to keep NIOSH approval status current. The most immediate competitive advantage is now tied to certification discipline, comfort-driven adoption, and accessory replenishment lock-in.
whats_growing: 2025-2026: Demand for reusable respirator ecosystems with cartridges, alarms, and battery/maintenance programs is growing relative to basic disposable models.
2025-2026: Certified-list hygiene and compliance documentation needs are increasing as users tighten procurement controls.
2025-2033: Supplied-air respirator segment appears as the faster-growing US segment in recent market outlooks.
2025-2026: Replacement/consumable cycles are strengthening where downstream firms standardize end-of-life management and fit/maintenance programs.
whats_shrinking: 2025: COVID-era overhang in temporary emergency demand is normalizing versus 2020-2022 surge conditions.
2025-2026: Lowest-tier, commodity respiratory devices face tighter scrutiny and reduced share due certification churn and counterfeit awareness.
2025-2026: Pure low-margin, one-time purchases are shrinking versus bundled solutions that include monitoring, fit support, and recurring replacements.
recent_developments: 2025-06-30: NIOSH CA 2025-1097 removed 801 3M respirator approvals from active use immediately.
2025-09-25: NIOSH CA 2025-1101 removed one Pure Environments respirator approval.
2025-07-01: OSHA published a proposed update to 29 CFR 1910.134 in the Federal Register addressing medical-evaluation requirements in respiratory programs.
2025-02-18: NIOSH CEL guidance page was refreshed to reinforce approved-device lookup and counterfeit prevention practices.
2026-04-15: OSHA Top 10 Most Frequently Cited Standards page was updated and continued to include respiratory protection in the top-10 enforcement list.
2026-04: FDA released draft guidance (docket FDA-2025-D-7121) on premarket/compliance expectations for NIOSH-approved air-purifying respirators.
outlook: The base expectation is for moderate to above-moderate growth with a strong skew to regulated, high-specification demand rather than commodity expansion. The industry’s best growth path is likely from recurring replacement economies, digitalized maintenance fitment programs, and customer segments that are risk-averse on NIOSH compliance and inspection outcomes.
themes: Compliance-led demand engine
Certification volatility and product lifecycle hygiene
Technology upgrades for comfort, alarms, and end-of-life indicators
Higher attach rates from consumables and service programs

title: Restaurant & Hotel Equipment Wholesaling in the US
one_liner: The industry supplies restaurants and hotels with capital equipment, fixtures, and store hardware, with demand tied to hospitality traffic, renovations, and foodservice modernization.
overview: The industry is a fragmented B2B distributor base serving foodservice operators, hotels, and noncommercial foodservice venues. After the pandemic shock, demand has rebounded in waves and is increasingly driven by operators prioritizing menu/experience upgrades, beverage-led traffic growth, and energy-efficient equipment. Recent 2025-26 data show resilient but selective capex: operators add capacity where returns are clear, while independent operators and lower-margin segments remain cautious.

key_stats.market_size: 2026 est. US industry market size: $42.6bn (IBIS baseline projection)
key_stats.growth: 2021-2026 baseline rebound CAGR: 5.8% (IBIS) and 2026 top-100 foodservice equipment dealer sales up 4.72% in 2025 vs 2024 (FE&S)

baseline_2022.market_size: $34.0bn (derived from IBIS baseline 2021 level $32.148bn and 5.8% annualized rebound path to 2026)
baseline_2022.growth: 5.8% annualized baseline path

how_it_makes_money: Primary revenue comes from wholesale sales of restaurant and hotel equipment (largest product segment), with secondary revenue from store fixtures and related service labor, consultation, and installation support. Gross margin is held through product mix, supplier terms, and bundled retrofit/specialized service offerings.
cost_structure: Key costs are supplier COGS/price pass-through, labor for sales and service delivery, warehouse and logistics fixed costs, credit financing carry costs, and energy/technology inputs; operators’ own cost pressures (food, labor, energy, insurance) also directly weaken order frequency and contract timing.
major_players: Great Lake? Hotel Supply-related and adjacent regional equipment groups in FE&S 2026 Distribution Giants sample
current_dynamics: Demand is still cyclical and operator-sensitive: restaurants are expanding but under margin pressure, while hotels are improving traffic and RevPAR in 2026 with still-lingering demand/supply gaps versus pre-pandemic levels. The 2025-2026 period shows rising labor costs, tighter execution pace, and selective capex, with stronger opportunities in segments that can improve throughput, beverage mix, and efficiency.
whats_growing: 2026: Restaurant and foodservice sales projected at $1.55T, with modest real growth (1.3%) and a return to hiring.
2025 to 2026: Top 100 foodservice equipment & supplies dealers report sales of $16.49bn (+4.72% vs 2024).
2026: U.S. hotel RevPAR +5.7% and occupancy +0.8% in Q2 as demand growth (1.7%) outpaced supply (0.4%).
2026: Hotel sector travel demand remains supported by events outlook and domestic activity, with strong RevPAR momentum in multiple U.S. markets.
Shift to energy-saving combinations, installation-integrated solutions, and technology-enabled operations is increasing in deal-to-deal prioritization.
whats_shrinking: 2025: operators reported high macro volatility and 42% of restaurants not profitable, sustaining capex discipline.
Uncertainty from tariffs and cost inflation in 2025 reduced confidence in smooth expansion plans for many dealers.
CBRE 2026 notes occupancy still below 2019 norms across location types, with weaker post-Covid operating baseline in some segments.
Independent restaurant demand has been described as mixed to slower in parts of 2026 despite resilient broader dining demand.
Labor access and service wage pressures continue to constrain faster, labor-intensive restaurant upgrade cycles.
recent_developments: 2026-02-12: NRA press release reported 2026 restaurant sales forecast at $1.55T with operators adding over 100,000 jobs; real sales growth expected at 1.3%.
2026-04-01: FE&S 2026 Distribution Giants reported top-100 foodservice equipment and supplies dealers sales of $16.49bn (+4.72% year-over-year).
2026-01-27: AHLA 2026 State of the Industry signaled hotel guest spending expected near $805bn in 2026 (+1.7% vs 2025) and continued demand recovery framing.
2026-07-29: CBRE reported U.S. Q2 2026 hotel occupancy +0.8% yoy and RevPAR +5.7%, ADR +4.4%; hotel demand momentum improved.
2026-02: NRA reporting emphasized 42% of operators were not profitable in 2025, reinforcing margin sensitivity in equipment demand.
outlook: 2026 remains a measured recovery scenario for this industry: demand conditions are improving but uneven, with operator profitability and capex timing the main governors. The most constructive trajectory is tied to restaurants and hotels investing in higher-velocity modernization (digitalization, energy efficiency, high-margin beverage-driven concepts) while avoiding broad discretionary expansion.
themes: Hospitality demand-led equipment replacement cycles after uneven 2025
Margin pressure and cautious capex create winner-take-share among service-led dealers
Energy-efficient and combination equipment positioning gains importance
Talent and installation capability become strategic differentiators
Consolidation via distribution M&A and local geographic share gains
one_sentence: In 2026, restaurant and hotel equipment wholesaling is recovering from prior volatility as demand shifts toward efficiency-oriented upgrades despite persistent cost inflation at operators.

title: Restaurant Construction
one_liner: Restaurant construction remains a small but resilient U.S. construction niche in which most demand comes from remodels, expansions, and conversion projects supported by steady foodservice spending and constrained by high costs.
overview: The industry remains tightly linked to downstream restaurant demand: NRA expects total U.S. restaurant and foodservice sales to reach $1.55T in 2026 and foodservice spending to represent a larger share of household food outlays, with 56.3% of food expenditures in 2025 going to food-away-from-home. At the same time, construction activity is softening broadly, with Census reporting nonresidential construction spending at $2.1665T total in June 2026 and first-half 2026 construction activity below first-half 2025 by 3.5%. ENR’s 2026 first-quarter report shows costs rising in 2025 (steel +11.9%, skilled labor +5.7%, common labor +4%, CCI +3.6%, BCI +4.2%), reinforcing a sustained margin squeeze for restaurant operators and their buildout budgets.

2026: off-premises formats (takeout and delivery) driving kitchen/process and back-of-house adaptations in existing footprints.

2026: operators face ongoing softness in lower-income demand pockets due to constrained discretionary spending.

title: Retail Store Fixture Dealers
one_liner: Retail fixture dealers supply shelving, displays, counters, and shop fittings to retailers for store launches, remodels, and brand-facing shop design.
overview: Retail Store Fixture Dealers acquire store fixtures and display systems from manufacturers (wood products, laminates, plastics, metal systems, and lighting components) and resell to nonstore and storefront retailers. Demand depends on retail spending, retailer expansion, remodeling intensity, available square footage, and price sensitivity, while competition from used fixtures and online sourcing remains structurally high.

key_stats.market_size: US market size: $5.7 billion (2026 projection from baseline 2021 IBIS-style profile); 2021 historical level: $5.103 billion.
key_stats.growth: IBIS baseline projects +2.1% annual growth for 2021-2026; retail environment indicates continued stress from closures/downsizing in discretionary formats despite resilient core demand.

baseline_2022.market_size: $5.2 billion (2022 proxied from 2021 baseline level of $5.103 billion and low-single-digit IBIS baseline trajectory).
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 era was broadly mid-single to low-single digit implied annual growth versus 2021 rebound, while the broader post-pandemic trend moved from volatile reset to softer expansion.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is primarily from direct fixture sales (shelving, racks, displays, counters, mannequins, cases, signage fixtures, and accessories), with add-on margin from design support, installation assistance, fulfillment reliability, and repeat purchase of consumables and replacement modules. Dealer economics are driven by turnover velocity, product mix (commodity fixtures vs. high-spec displays), and margin discipline under heavy price competition.

cost_structure.primary_costs: Inventory purchases from upstream wood/plastic/metal suppliers, import lead-time risk, freight and warehousing, and showroom/branch operating costs.
cost_structure.operational_costs: Sales staffing, specification support, customer service, installation coordination, and credit terms tied to retailer project cycles.
cost_structure.pricing_pressure: Competition from used-fixture channels, online channels, and value-focused buyers compresses realized margins and forces tighter terms.

major_players: Orbus Visual Communications Group (Nimlok and group brands)
LSI Industries (Display Solutions: JSI, EMI, CBH)
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 backdrop is mixed: U.S. retail activity is growing (Census data show broad retail expansion through 2025 and into 2026), but the store-format mix is shifting toward grocery, convenience, discount, and fitness with ongoing churn in specialty/apparalel channels. Fixture demand is therefore less about net square-foot growth and more about quick-cycle, modular, and brand-consistent refreshes in active formats.
whats_growing: Q1 2026 retail demand held momentum with total retail sales up 1.5% q/q and e-commerce rising 9.8% from 1Q2025.
2026 activity in grocery, dollar/discount, and convenience-heavy operators is stronger, supporting practical fixture refresh and replacement cycles.
Store openings plus backfilling of closed space are supporting selective fixture demand for replacement formats rather than large luxury-scale build-outs.
Buyers increasingly evaluate suppliers on speed, modularity, and design-to-install capabilities, not only product price.
whats_shrinking: Physical store footprints in discretionary and specialty retail categories remain under pressure from closures and format rationalization.
Higher used-fixture availability and online sourcing increase downward pricing pressure on standard SKUs.
Demand share for very high-end custom pieces is flattening versus value-oriented, standardized and portable fixture solutions.
recent_developments: 2025-08-19: Census reported 2Q2025 e-commerce sales at $304.2 billion (+1.4% q/q); total retail sales $1,865.4 billion (+0.4% q/q); e-commerce share 16.3%.
2025-12-31: Census advance release showed December 2025 retail and food services sales of $735.0 billion, essentially unchanged from November.
2026-03-10: Census Q1 2026 reported total retail sales $1,929.0 billion (+1.5% q/q) and e-commerce $326.7 billion (+2.7% q/q), with e-commerce share 16.9%.
2026-03-19: NRF forecast 2026 U.S. retail sales growth at 4.4% (to $5.6T in core definition).
2026-05-04: CoStar: U.S. retail vacancy expected to peak in the mid-4.4% range in 2026, with elevated near-term move-outs in some categories.

2026-Q1: JLL reported stronger opening activity from discount and grocery operators (e.g., Dollar Tree +400, Aldi +180, Starbucks +175) alongside closures (GameStop 470, Francesca's 457, Eddie Bauer 175).
outlook: By 2026, fixture dealers are positioned for low-single-digit growth only: demand recovers in resilient, value-led retail formats while pressure persists from consolidation, used goods, and margin compression. The segment’s winners are expected to be service-rich dealers with fast fulfillment, modular designs, and portfolio support across openings, closures, and concept refreshes.
themes: Omnichannel retail increases fixture relevance for experiential, localized merchandising.
Store churn shifts fixture business toward short-cycle projects and modular systems.
Value formats and discount/grocery expansion outperform premium and slower specialty formats.
Competition from used fixtures and online channels keeps price-to-quality pressure high.
Material and transport cost volatility encourages leaner SKUs and standardized components.
one_sentence: The industry is a low-margin, demand-flexible B2B segment tied to retail capex, with growth in 2025-2026 coming mainly from high-turnover value formats and omnichannel stores while specialty footprints and expensive custom work stay pressured.

title: Retail Trade in the US
one_liner: U.S. retail and food services remain in a high-volume but moderating cycle, with $768.6B in June 2026 sales and sustained strength in nonstore channels.
overview: The latest Census advance release on 2026-07-16 shows 2026-06 U.S. retail and food services sales of $768.6B (seasonally adjusted), up 0.2% from 2026-05 and up 6.7% from 2025-06. The same series shows 2026-1Q e-commerce sales of $326.7B, with e-commerce at 16.9% of total retail in 2026-1Q, up from 16.0% in 2025-1Q and 16.7% in 2025-Q4 (revised). The Census sector table for 2026 reports total retail-and-food-services sales of $4,420,287M, up 5.1% from 2025.

growth.note: IBIS baseline: Revenue increased by 3.8% in 2022; 2022 margin around 3.2%

how_it_makes_money: Buying power with suppliers, then selling goods at retail margin across core formats (grocery, auto, general merchandise, e-commerce).
Capturing incremental income from marketplace and online channels, fulfillment speed, and repeat purchase ecosystems.
Supplementary income from loyalty, financial services, advertising, and platform/network effects at scale.

major_costs: Cost of goods sold and promotion-driven margin pressure
Labor intensity across stores, warehouses, and call-to-delivery chains
Logistics and fulfillment including shipping, reverse logistics, and network costs
Store occupancy, utilities, and last-mile technology

current_dynamics: June 2026 growth was modest month-over-month, suggesting consumer spending normalization after stronger spring pace.
Nonstore retail remained a structural growth engine with high year-over-year growth.
Food services and gasoline-linked categories continue to create sharp month-level swings depending on travel and energy conditions.
Top retailers continue to expand scale advantages through omnichannel capture and fulfillment productivity.

whats_growing.note: Strong MoM momentum despite broad retail moderation
Volatile but still high absolute movement in the latest monthly estimate
Lifestyle demand and high-ticket replacement demand supportive

whats_shrinking.note: Category weakness persists in late-cycle discretionary spend
Pressure from discounting and online substitution

recent_developments: 2026-07-16: Census MARTS reported 2026-06 total retail and food services sales at $768.6B, up 0.2% MoM and up 6.7% YoY.
2026-07-16: The same release revised 2026-05 sales to $766.9B and revised 2026-05 growth from 0.9% to 1.0%.
2026-07-16: U.S. e-commerce for 2026-1Q was $326.7B, with share at 16.9% of total retail.
2026-06-17: 2026-04 (May 2026 release): Census reported 2026-04 sales of $757.1B and 0.5% MoM growth (revised March at 1.6%).
2025-12 (revised): Quarterly Census data show 2025-Q4 e-commerce share at 16.7% of total retail sales.
outlook: 2025-2026 data imply continued total-sales growth but likely moderation in monthly momentum, with structural upside concentrated in omnichannel, delivery, and inventory/service operations rather than broad in-store expansion. Near-term winners should be efficient operators that combine high-frequency essentials with scalable digital fulfillment; margin improvement is likely only where wage, shrink, rent, and freight costs are tightly managed.
themes: Omnichannel normalization: physical stores plus digital-first conversion
Scale concentration: largest retailers gaining share across grocery, auto, and general merchandise
Labor and fulfillment productivity as margin battleground
Rising digital share despite macro volatility in discretionary categories
Volatility transmission from fuel/energy and travel into adjacent retail categories
one_sentence: Market breadth is still broad, but growth is concentrated in digital and everyday essentials while pricing, wage, and concentration pressures keep margins under stress.

title: Retirement & Pension Plans in the US
one_liner: The U.S. retirement industry is still growing in assets but continues to shift away from defined-benefit sponsorship toward more portable defined-contribution and IRA accumulation.
overview: The US retirement ecosystem now has two clear engines: very large public and private retirement asset pools that are expanding, and a still-large but structurally pressured defined-benefit segment with funding risk concentrated in legacy plan promises. Defined-contribution, 401(k), and IRA balances keep broadening access, while defined-benefit access remains comparatively constrained in private-sector employment settings, reinforcing the shift toward employer/employee portable arrangements.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: U.S. retirement assets reached $49.1T at year-end, with $14.2T in defined-contribution plans, $10.1T in 401(k) plans, and $19.2T in IRAs.
key_stats.growth: 2025: Total retirement assets rose 11.2% year-on-year; 2025: state and local pension assets increased 8.46% from 2024 to $6.49T.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: $914.7B in industry revenue for Retirement and Pension Plans (IBISWorld baseline).
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: -0.08% CAGR in revenue over 2003-2022 (IBISWorld baseline metric basis).

how_it_makes_money: This industry is driven by employer and participant contributions plus investment gains on plan assets, with returns and contribution pacing directly determining annual industry performance.

major_costs: Employer/plan sponsor contribution obligations, especially for DB promises
Market volatility and funded-status volatility in portfolio performance
Administrative, recordkeeping, custody, fiduciary, and compliance costs borne at plan level
Increased liabilities from benefit shortfalls and funding make-up when contributions lag or asset returns weaken
cost_structure.notes: Plan service fees and custody/asset-management fees are often captured in adjacent financial-service segments rather than this industry's own revenue definition.

major_players: California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS) — largest defined-benefit public pension in the U.S., over $500B in managed assets (2025-26 public updates)
California State Teachers' Retirement System (CalSTRS) — $415.4B in assets as of June 30, 2026
Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) — government insurer and key backstop for single-employer and multiemployer plans
State and local public pension systems — 37M participants and $6.49T in pension assets in 2025
Pooled Employer Plan (PEP) sector — growing pooled platform adoption, 244 PEPs in 2023 with $11.8B assets and 1.2M participants (latest available administrative bulletin)
current_dynamics: A structural migration is underway from DB-centric employer commitments toward DC/IRA-based accumulation models that reduce sponsor liability and improve portability, while macro and labor demographics preserve demand for long-horizon retirement income infrastructure.
whats_growing: Defined-contribution and IRA wealth is the dominant growth lane, with 2025 ending at $49.1T in retirement assets.
State and local pension funding scale is rising with 2025 assets at $6.49T, up 8.46% from 2024.
Private and public retirement market participation remains broad, with private-sector retirement access at 72% in 2025 and 70% in DC.
whats_shrinking: Defined-benefit availability is constrained, with DB access only 14% of private-sector workers in 2025 versus 70% DC access.
Purely sponsor-funded certainty from traditional DB promises is weakening as employers prioritize liability predictability over legacy pension design.
recent_developments: 2025-03-25: BLS reported retirement benefits were available to 72% of private industry workers (70% DC access, 14% DB access).
2026-02-23: EBSA reported 2.6 million plans in scope (156M workers/retirees/families covered), including 801,000 private retirement plans, with about $13.8T in assets.
2026-03-27: ICI Q4 2025 data were cited at $49.1T total retirement assets, with DC at $14.2T and 401(k) at $10.1T.
2026-05-14: Census reported 2025 state and local public pension assets at $6.49T, up 8.46%, with 37M participants.
2026-06-09: SSA projected OASI reserve depletion in 2032Q4 and combined OASI+DI benefit sufficiency through 2034, then 83% payable.
2026-01-27: PBGC FY2025 showed over $6.4B paid to 926,000 retirees in single-employer plans and $6.2B in SFA support.
outlook: Short-term expectations are for continued asset growth in retirement systems alongside continued reprioritization toward flexible DC/IRA frameworks; however, defined-benefit underfunding risk and benefit adequacy stress from aging demographics and labor transitions will keep pressure on sponsor policy design and benefit guarantees.
themes: DB-to-DC structural migration
market-driven investment performance sensitivity
rising pension scale in public systems
demographic aging and delayed retirement readiness
infrastructure backstops (PBGC, Social Security solvency signal) shaping sponsor behavior
