current_dynamics: Federal Reserve industrial production remained positive into late 2025, with the manufacturing index near stability and still supportive of industrial protection demand.
Construction spending in June 2025 was 2,136.2B SAAR, below June 2024, with residential and nonresidential activity mixed.
OSHA increased targeting of high-injury establishments in 2025 and continues digital injury-data submission requirements, reinforcing safety compliance spend.
Public and private distributors reported mixed 2025 earnings outcomes, indicating customer-specific budget discipline despite continued need for mandated PPE.
Tariff, labor, and interest-rate pressures were repeatedly cited as cost risks in 2025/2026 filings.
whats_growing: Safety and compliance budgets that tie to mandatory hazard-control and recordkeeping workflows.
Digital procurement and fulfillment capabilities (API/API-like reporting, e-commerce replenishment, inventory portals).
Higher-value service layers such as VMI, vendor-managed programs, and field technical support.
whats_shrinking: Pure commodity-volume growth in generic safety consumables under stronger price pressure.
Residential construction-linked demand pockets that showed softness versus 2024.
Low-touch replacement sales where buyers consolidate toward larger MRO platforms.
Margins where transport, labor, and energy inputs rise faster than list price gains.
recent_developments: 2025-05-20: OSHA updated inspection targeting to prioritize establishments with high or rising injury and illness rates.
2025-04-17: OSHA released 2024 workplace injury and illness data from 370,000 Form 300A summaries and over 732,000 Form 300/301 records.
2025-06-02: Census reported total construction spending at $2.1524T SAAR for April 2025.
2025-08-01: Census reported total construction spending at $2.1362T SAAR for June 2025, 2.9% below June 2024.
2025-10-23: MSC reported FY25 net sales of $3,769.5M, down 1.3% year over year.
2026-02-03: Grainger reported FY25 net sales of $17.9B and 2026 guidance range $18.7B–$19.1B.
outlook: The near-term outlook is stable with low single-digit demand growth through 2026, largely defended by regulation and ongoing industrial safety requirements. Growth is expected to come mainly from service differentiation, digital workflow integration, and higher-touch solutions rather than broad list-price expansion. Risks remain tied to construction softness, tariff-driven costs, and sustained wage/freight inflation.
themes: Compliance pull from OSHA and mandatory reporting frameworks
Industrial safety digitization and workflow analytics
Low- to mid-single-digit structural growth
Cost inflation and operational cost control
Concentration pressure from broad MRO competitors in adjacent categories
one_sentence: In 2025–2026, US safety equipment and supplies distributors were supported by stable mandatory-demand dynamics, but faced persistent margin pressure from higher logistics, labor, and compliance-related operating costs.

title: Salad Dressing Production
one_liner: US salad dressing production remains a mature, ingredient-led packaged condiments category with stable demand and limited room for broad volume expansion.
overview: US salad dressing production is a mature packaged-food subsegment with relatively high brand concentration and low supplier concentration but strong niche entry from natural/clean-label players. Industry fundamentals still show slow growth in core volume, with demand increasingly dependent on packaging innovation, shelf-ready convenience, and ingredient quality positioning. Channel demand is split between grocery and foodservice, while macro food spending data suggests continued room for packaged serving condiments as part of a larger food-at-home and food-away-from-home mixed basket. Baseline IBIS context remains useful: growth has been low and price competition historically suppresses margin recovery, while product innovation is the main lever for upside.

key_stats.market_size: USD 3.5 billion (US salad dressings & mayonnaise proxy estimate for 2024/2025-2026 cycle); IBIS-style US dressing baseline around USD 3.246 billion in 2021
key_stats.growth: IBIS-style projection to 2026 implies ~1.3% annualized; broader US sauces, dressings & condiments projected at 4.77% CAGR (2026-2033) in an adjacent-data proxy

baseline_2022.market_size: USD 3.246 billion (2021 baseline proxy for early-2020s level, adjusted to 2022 context in this brief)
baseline_2022.growth: approximately 0.0% annualized over the 5-year period into 2021; 2021 was expected to be weak, near -1.2%

how_it_makes_money: Produces and sells packaged dressing formulations into retail grocery channels (mass and specialty), including core flavors and shelf-stable/range variants
Supplies foodservice and restaurant-related demand where dressings are used as accompaniments, marinades, and portioning sauces
Competes on SKU breadth, flavor/packaging differentiation, promotions, and brand trust rather than fast volume expansion

major_inputs: vegetable oils and oils-vinegar blend components
dairy/egg/fermented bases where recipe architecture uses protein-rich formulas
vinegar, herbs, spices, stabilizers, and packaging films/containers
processing, blending, shelf-life management, and distribution logistics
key_cost_pressures: cost of goods inflation and freight/supply volatility
high retail trade and promotional pressure in grocery channels
cost_structure.gross_margin_context: category margins historically pressured by retail price competition despite modest premiumization gains

current_dynamics: As of 2026 the category is stabilizing after years of discount pressure: macro food spending reached USD 2.51 trillion in 2025, with food-away-from-home at 56.3%, while grocery/retail channels still carry the largest direct packaged-volume load. Growth is concentrated in differentiated variants (clean labels, transparent ingredients, elevated dairy/protein positioning, small-portion packs, and brand-led line extensions) while legacy commodity formats face tighter price realization. Consumer preference migration toward cleaner labels and recognizable ingredients is reinforcing reformulation and premiumization.
whats_growing: Natural/clean-label and ingredient-forward salad dressing launches
Premium and shelf-stable niche launches at specialty channels
Smaller and meal-friendly pack formats tied to at-home recipes and meal kits
Foodservice-linked premium dip/sauce usage in higher-income channels
whats_shrinking: Purely commoditized formulations without clear flavor or ingredient differentiation
Unit-price upside in legacy channels without reformulation or packaging advantage
Mature base-share growth in traditional grocery staples
recent_developments: 2026-07-15: Conagra reported FY2026 full-year net sales of $11.3 billion and announced 2027 guidance, with foodservice up 8.1% in Q4.
2026-06-11: USDA ERS reported total U.S. food spending at $2.51 trillion in 2025; food-away-from-home was 56.3% of total spending.
2026-03-12: Marzetti launched its Simply Dressed line (ranch, Caesar, vinaigrettes, etc.), replacing prior SKUs and emphasizing simple, recognizable ingredients.
2026-02-17: Primal Kitchen launched three shelf-stable creamy dressings made with grass-fed dairy and positioned them as a premium, ingredient-led growth move.
2025-06-17: Kraft Heinz announced it would not launch new FD&C color products in the U.S. and plans full U.S. removal of remaining FD&C colors by end-2027.
outlook: Near-term outlook through 2026 remains constructive but modest: category volume is not expected to accelerate materially, while margin recovery depends on successful premiumization and mix shifts rather than broad base-price increases; producers with credible ingredient narratives and stronger retailer relationships should gain share within a low-growth total market.
themes: Health and transparency-led reformulation
Premiumization over broad penetration
Channel balancing between grocery and foodservice
Retail differentiation via smaller formats and convenient packaging
Moderate restructuring and cost-control focus after sustained input inflation
one_sentence: The US category is shifting from value-driven, high-discount sales toward cleaner labels, smaller portions, and premiumized refrigerated or specialty dairy-free/functional variants as households rebalance grocery and foodservice spending.

title: Sand & Gravel Mining in the US
one_liner: US sand and gravel mining is a high-volume, low-margin infrastructure and industrial input business split between construction aggregates and industrial (largely frac-sand) demand.
overview: US sand and gravel mining links directly to construction activity, transport infrastructure, and oil-and-gas extraction. 2025 USGS data show construction outputs falling modestly while industrial sand remains volatile and tied to rig activity and frac-sand substitution, so demand quality has become more segmented than broad-based. The industry remains concentrated by geography, transport corridors, and vertically integrated operators with downstream logistics exposure.

market_size.year: 2021 (latest detailed IBIS historical point in 2022 baseline file)
market_size.note: IBIS baseline lists 2021 revenue and projects forward to 2027

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is generated mainly from sale of graded sand and gravel by destination use (concrete aggregates, road base, fills, asphalt aggregate, well-plugging/well-packing sands) and increasingly through integration into asphalt, ready-mix, and concrete channels. Price is per-ton material value plus logistics premiums for nearby extraction-to-site delivery.
cost_structure: High transport and fuel intensity from pit-to-market movement
Significant stripping, blasting, and processing costs (crushing, washing, sizing, storage)
Permitting and land-access risk in extraction counties
Energy and maintenance costs for heavy-quarry equipment
Compliance costs from silica dust and environmental controls
Weather sensitivity (flooding, seasonal access, wet conditions)
major_players: Vulcan Materials (10-K 2025: nation’s largest supplier of construction aggregates, mainly crushed stone, sand and gravel)
Martin Marietta Materials (IBIS/SEC-referenced as a major US aggregates operator with nationwide quarry/mine footprint and aggregate-dominant economics)
CRH (aggregates as core business; substantial US quarry network and sand-and-gravel integration)
Cemex US (large U.S. quarry and ready-mix network supporting aggregate-based construction demand)
current_dynamics: Construction sand and gravel remained large in scale in 2025 but showed modest volume softness versus 2024, with signs of uneven recovery across regions.
Industrial sand and gravel continued to be driven by frac demand, but oversupply and lower rig activity reduced both tonnage and realized value.
Import dependence on a few origins remains concentrated, creating supply-chain exposure even though the nation remains largely net-exporting in industrial sand.
Corporate consolidation and integration into infrastructure-adjacent materials platforms accelerated in 2026 with major transaction activity.
whats_growing: Shift toward durable, integrated supply platforms that combine quarry output with asphalt and ready-mix demand channels.
Infrastructure and utility-adjacent demand around transport, grid, and resilient construction continues to support baseline consumption of construction aggregates.
Regional concentration in high-growth metro and rebuilding corridors where freight and proximity advantage dominate pricing.
whats_shrinking: Industrial sand and gravel tonnage (-7.7% in 2025) and value (-16% in 2025) due to frac-market normalization.
Short-run construction output softness in 2025 relative to 2024 in aggregate consumption patterns.
Apparent flexibility in recycled aggregate alternatives for some road/pavement streams, limiting pricing power in portions of market.
recent_developments: 2026-02-05: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 data reported construction sand and gravel output at 870 million tons and $12.6B in 2025.
2026-02-05: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 estimated industrial sand and gravel at 120 million tons and $4.5B in 2025, with imports down and exports up.
2025-09: CRH disclosed plans to acquire Arcosa for $8.5B, reinforcing U.S. aggregate platform consolidation and infrastructure positioning.
2026-02-17: Vulcan Materials reported 2025 full-year outcomes in a U.S. filing/release cycle, continuing its aggregate-led strategy.
2026-01: USGS reports for aggregates highlighted weaker 2025 industrial fracking-linked demand intensity and concentration risks in key inputs.
outlook: Near-term outlook is mixed: construction remains demand-critical but not uniformly expanding, while industrial sand is likely to remain cyclical with oil-and-gas activity and rig pace. Operators with logistics advantage and integrated downstream channels should outperform on margins despite muted top-line growth.
themes: Demand split between construction scale and frac-cycle volatility
Geography and transport as key competitive moat
Concentration in quarry footprints and aggregate destinations
Safety/environment compliance (especially crystalline silica) as a rising cost and operating constraint
Consolidation toward vertically integrated materials groups
one_sentence: In 2025, US mine output of construction sand and gravel was 870 million metric tons and industrial sand and gravel was 120 million metric tons, with value stability overall but clear demand divergence between the two subsegments.

title: Sandwich & Sub Store Franchises
one_liner: A maturing sandwich franchise category where unit pruning and convenience-led growth are replacing simple expansion.
overview: This segment covers franchised U.S. operators centered on made-to-order sandwiches, wraps, soups, sides, and ready-to-go service formats. The competitive structure is still large but polarized: one legacy icon faces double-digit operational pressure from shrinking units while several peers post steady opening pace and stronger average unit economics. Growth now comes less from indiscriminate unit count and more from stronger traffic per store, convenience channels, and disciplined multi-unit development.

key_stats.market_size: $29.8 billion in 2024 U.S. sandwich-segment systemwide sales for leading chains (Subway, Panera, Arby’s, Jersey Mike’s, Jimmy John’s, Firehouse Subs, McAlister’s)
key_stats.growth: Sector-wide direction in 2026 is modest; franchising-level forecast is +1.6% output growth, while unit trends are mixed (Subway down, growth-oriented operators up).

baseline_2022.note: IBISWorld estimate referenced in industry franchise commentary

how_it_makes_money: Franchise units and territory rights create upfront revenue through franchise and development fees.
Ongoing system revenue is driven mainly by royalties on sales plus marketing fund contributions.
Operators depend on high-frequency meal occasions across lunch, dinner, and off-premise channels.
Delivery, pickup, loyalty, and catering increasingly add mix and margin versus dine-in only sales.
cost_structure: Food and labor remain the largest variable cost blocks, with inflation pressure visible in menu pricing decisions.
Occupancy/occupancy carry and buildout intensity (modernization/remodels) pressure returns on entry.
Most systems levy sales-based royalties plus brand-level advertising and support contributions (e.g., Firehouse model includes royalties and marketing support fees).
Digital ordering channels lower friction for demand but add commissions and technology management costs for operators.
current_dynamics: Competition has shifted from scale-by-growth to scale-by-AUV and execution quality.
Subway’s contraction has accelerated relative to the rest of the sandwich segment.
Firehouse is explicitly using incentive programs to accelerate multi-unit development and improve regional density.
Franchise-sector data still supports expansion in value despite macroheadwinds, but QSR output growth is expected to be only moderate.
whats_growing: Developers favor operators with stronger unit economics and local scale potential.
Firehouse’s 2026 incentive structure (up to $100k per unit in target programs) aims to pull growth into 2026.
Chains with stronger digital/off-premise workflows and healthier/larger-format menus are attracting stronger traffic.
New international initiatives (e.g., Mexico expansion plans for Firehouse) show selective geographic expansion.
Jersey Mike’s momentum continues, with reported rapid 2024 unit base increase in QSR category reporting.
whats_shrinking: Subway continues meaningful footprint contraction: 729 U.S. closures in 2025 and cumulative multi-year decline.
Legacy high-dependency franchise systems face pressure from higher labor, labor-stability, and remodel costs.
QSR output growth is forecast below double-digit pace, limiting broad-category expansion.
Some slower-volume formats are becoming vulnerable relative to peers with ~$1.0M+ AUV levels.
recent_developments: 2026-05-06: Subway closed 729 U.S. stores in 2025, leaving 18,773 locations.
2026-04-01: Firehouse Subs announced development incentives through 2028 to speed franchise expansion.
2026-04-30: Subway FDD reported 3,417 U.S. unit decline versus 2021.
2025-05-27: RBI and Foodplay announced a Mexico growth plan to open 100 Firehouse Subs in five years.
2025: QSR50 data showed Subway at 20,133 U.S. units with Subway down 443 units, while Jersey Mike’s and other peers grew.

outlook.trajectory: Likely 2026–2027: consolidating in lower-productivity nodes and expanding best-performing operators, with mixed but positive net output at franchise-market level.
outlook.opportunity: High-execution operators can capture share through stronger convenience, speed, and AUV.
outlook.risk: Macroeconomic softness and persistent operating-cost inflation can keep closures elevated among weak operators.

themes: Consolidation over pure expansion
AUV-first growth model
Digital convenience and off-premise demand
Franchisee quality over pure franchise density
Cross-market international expansion in selected brands
one_sentence: U.S. sandwich and sub store franchising remains large but increasingly selective, with legacy brands contracting footprints and faster growers pressing for higher value per store.

title: Sanitary Paper Product Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US sanitary paper is a stable but pressured market where aging demand supports growth in incontinence and adult care products while diaper demand is softer.
overview: Sanitary paper manufacturing includes toilet paper, facial tissues, diapers, feminine care wipes, and related consumables. The market is relatively mature, with modest headline growth, but company results increasingly depend on the mix shift toward premium performance products and the ability to manage raw-material and transport costs.

market_size.2025: US$27.5bn+ (tissue-related store sales context for US sanitary paper retail proxy)
market_size.2026: US$14.4bn+ (toilet and tissue category base signals suggest continued scale around prior estimate range)

capacity_and_scale.2025: 5,766 paper manufacturing establishments (NAICS 322, Q4 2025, reported in 2026 BLS IAG release)
capacity_and_scale.2025_2026: paper manufacturing employment roughly 356.6k (all employees), with 253.8k production and nonsupervisory employees in 2026 Q4 reports

baseline_2022.growth: 1.52% CAGR projected for 2022–2028

how_it_makes_money.revenue_mix: Volume-driven sales of consumable paper products sold primarily through mass retail, grocery, and drug channels.
how_it_makes_money.pricing: Mostly low-to-mid premium mass-market pricing, with some margin upside in value-added absorbency, texture, and brand-led differentiation.
how_it_makes_money.repeat_demand: Recurring household and institutional replenishment behavior supports durable baseline demand despite low category growth.

cost_structure.2025_2026_raw_materials: pulp, recovered fiber, and resins remain the largest cost line and are most sensitive to global supply and tariff shifts
cost_structure.2025_2026_labor: paper manufacturing hourly earnings in the US around US$33.55–US$33.95
cost_structure.2025_2026_energy_and_freight: natural gas and transportation volatility continues to compress margins in many quarters

major_players: Private label leaders in US supermarkets
current_dynamics: US births were 3,606,400 in 2025 (down 1%), reducing long-term diaper demand momentum.
US population age profile is shifting up, with 18.9% aged 65+ in 2025, supporting incontinence and adult care consumables.
Trade exposure remains a material earnings risk; import competition and tariff sensitivity are recurring in 2025–2026 commentary.
Labor and manufacturing cost floors are elevated versus 2022, while productivity gains are uneven across producers.
Large brands are balancing premium launches with private-label share pressure.
whats_growing: Adult care and incontinence-related sanitary paper categories through 2025–2026 demographic support.
Premium performance positioning in tissue and wipe formats (absorbency, softness, comfort claims).
Capacity and efficiency investments, including dedicated absorbency-line expansions.
whats_shrinking: Standard diaper growth versus 2022-level demand patterns.
High-volume commoditized SKUs where price competition is intense.
Margin resilience in lower-technology paper formats reliant on expensive pulp inputs.
recent_developments: 2025-11-12: Edgewell announced sale of its feminine care business to Essity for US$340M, with closing planned in 2026.
2026-02-18: KP Tissue reported FY2025 revenue of US$2,203.4m, up 7.5%, and announced new TAD line expansion in Memphis in 2026.
2026-04-09: US births reached 3,606,400 in 2025, down 1% from 2024.
2026-06-15: Tissue market tracking showed US toilet tissue segment around US$14.4bn and broader US tissue sales context above US$27.5bn.
2025-12-31: Public filings in the sanitary consumer segment (P&G, Kimberly-Clark) continued to cite import and input-cost pressure as key risks.
outlook: For 2026–2028, US sanitary paper is expected to stay steady to lightly growing, with upside likely concentrated in differentiated adult-care and premium paper formats while commodity-grade diaper and basic tissue segments face tighter pricing and higher cost volatility. Strategic winners will be those with stronger fiber-cost hedging, efficient wet-forming capacity, and better route-to-store execution in mass retail.
themes: Aging population demand shift
Cost-volatility management
Private-label vs national-brand competition
Import exposure and tariff sensitivity
Fiber sustainability and recycling quality signals
Performance-paper innovation (softness, absorbency, strength)
one_sentence: The sector is defined by steady volume demand in household and personal care tissues, with margin performance increasingly driven by pulp, energy, and logistics volatility.

title: Satellite TV Providers in the US
one_liner: Satellite TV in the US is in structural decline, but operators are shifting to hybrid satellite-plus-streaming models and tighter cost control.
overview: The industry has moved from broad TV households coverage toward a mixed model where DBS is a shrinking but still material part of total pay-TV distribution. Baseline IBISWorld data show a mature, contracting market, while 2025-2026 data show accelerating pressure from streaming alternatives. In this cycle, provider strategy is less about growth in total subscriptions and more about defending a smaller installed base through packaging, pricing, and churn management.

market_size.note: IBISWorld baseline revenue snapshot for the U.S. satellite TV providers industry.

growth.source_note: EchoStar March 31, 2026 10-Q shows Pay-TV subscribers down from 7.397M to 6.632M.

baseline_2022.baseline_notes: IBISWorld baseline also reported low-growth trajectory and profit compression in the mature phase of the cycle.

how_it_makes_money: Monthly subscription bundles under DISH TV and SLING TV, with a mix of basic, premium, sports, and specialty channels.
Pay-per-view and event-based purchases for live or premium content.
Advertising and commercial insertion on select video products as a supplemental monetization source.
Receiver/installation equipment sales, hardware leasing, and service activation economics.
Programming carriage economics: revenue is sensitive to content licensing terms and channel bundles.
cost_structure: High programming and content carriage costs, including contract-based per-subscriber economics.
Satellite network operations and maintenance: uplink/downlink systems, transponder/satellite capacity, and network support.
Installation, service support, and field/customer acquisition activity.
Marketing and churn-retention spend, especially when ARPU is pressured.
Depreciation/amortization on fleet and infrastructure assets.
major_players: vMVPD/OTT competitors encroaching on the same households: YouTube TV and Hulu + Live TV
current_dynamics: DBS remains a shrinking delivery method: TVB measured DBS share at 8.5% of TV households in May 2026, down from 10.5% in February 2026.
Total traditional pay-TV demand continues to soften; Q1 2026 data show continued losses across traditional pay-TV categories.
Large satellite operators are blending linear satellite with streaming-enabled products to defend base while targeting lower-ARPU churn-sensitive cohorts.
Programming negotiations and carry-cost pressure remain a central operating variable for margin.
whats_growing: Hybrid consumption behavior: DBS households with stronger streaming overlays and flexible streaming add-ons are being pursued.
The share of ad-supported and flex-offer models is rising relative to pure premium linear packages in provider portfolios.
Operator consolidation and distribution bundling are accelerating as scale economics matter more than standalone acquisition growth.
whats_shrinking: Subscriber base at leading DBS operators: EchoStar Pay-TV fell from 7.397M (2025-03-31) to 6.632M (2026-03-31), a 10.3% drop.
Pay-TV segment service demand remains down despite tactical efforts; segment service revenue fell 10.4% QoQ in EchoStar’s March 2026 quarter.
Satellite household share in TV mix is falling (TVB May 2026: DBS 8.5%).
Industry-wide Q1 2026 showed 2.03M total pay-TV net subscriber losses and weaker conversion from pay-TV to vMVPD.
recent_developments: 2025-07-02: AT&T sold its remaining 70% stake in DirecTV to TPG.
2025-?12-31: TVB baseline trend work shows the broad decline in traditional cable/satellite penetration through 2025, with DBS continuing to fall.
2026-03-31: EchoStar reported 6.632M total Pay-TV subscribers (4.845M DISH TV, 1.787M SLING), down YoY.
2026-03-31: EchoStar reported Pay-TV ARPU of $110.19 in Q1 2026 and service revenue of $2.262B, both under pressure from subscriber mix and volume decline.
2026-05-29: LightReading (via Moffett data) reported the U.S. pay-TV market lost 2.03M subscribers in Q1, with traditional + vMVPD both negative.
2026-05: TVB monthly survey showed DBS share at 8.5%, down from 10.5% in Feb and continued decline from prior quarters.
outlook: Given 2025-2026 evidence, satellite providers are likely to remain in managed decline: headline subscriptions fall, ARPU drifts sideways to lower levels as mix shifts, and profitability becomes execution-sensitive across programming costs and churn. The path to stability is likely hybridization, selective bundling, and infrastructure efficiency rather than top-line growth.
themes: DBS-to-streaming transition within the same household
Content cost inflation with limited pass-through ability
Retention through pricing architecture and lower-friction entry/upgrade tiers
Ad-supported monetization as a counterbalance to declining linear bundles
M&A and ownership changes as strategic resets (e.g., DirecTV ownership change)
one_sentence: Declining satellite share, rising content costs, and stronger OTT substitutes are forcing providers to trade scale for retention-focused, lower-cost bundles while preserving profitable customer cohorts.

title: Satellite Telecommunications Providers in the US
one_liner: US satellite telecom providers are moving from niche fixed-capacity operators toward integrated LEO broadband and direct-to-device services as competition with terrestrial networks intensifies.
overview: The industry has shifted from a slow, capital-heavy model toward higher-capacity LEO networks, wireless backhaul, and satellite-cellular convergence. US providers are expanding into underserved geography, enterprise resilience, and niche mission-critical government use, while facing aggressive launch and regulatory execution pressure. Baseline performance was modest through 2022, but 2025–26 filings and FCC actions show accelerating structural change with larger constellations, direct-to-device pilots, and tighter milestone scrutiny for new entrants.

scale_indicators.metric: Amazon Leo Gen1 deployment milestone target

how_it_makes_money: Capacity leasing and resale of transponder / gateway bandwidth to broadcasters and telecom carriers.
Wholesale interconnection and private network links for enterprises with high geographic coverage requirements.
Consumer and SME satellite broadband subscriptions, often bundled with terminal hardware and support.
Government and defense service contracts (secure communications, emergency and maritime/aviation coverage, mission continuity).
Aviation and industrial mobility services that use mobile/air/ground backhaul where fiber or cable is impractical.
cost_structure: High fixed-cost profile: space segment build and replenishment, satellite launch campaigns, ground gateway and terminal manufacturing.
Capital intensity and financing risk are elevated, with operating leverage highly sensitive to launch delays and capex timing.
Large recurring cost base for spectrum rights, regulatory compliance, insurance, and mission operations.
major_players: Iridium, Globalstar, Ligado (satellite mobile service participants and petition participants in 2025–26 FCC proceedings)
current_dynamics: 2025-26 activity is driven by mega-constellation expansion and direct-to-device capability, with Starlink still dominant in scale and throughput growth.
Regulatory momentum is concentrated in spectrum access and orbital-licensing decisions, especially for MSS/direct-to-cell authorizations and launch-milestone enforcement.
Enterprise/government demand remains the revenue anchor while consumer satellite broadband share is still comparatively smaller than terrestrial broadband.
Competition is increasingly between satellite operators and carrier-level backhaul substitutes rather than only between satellite incumbents.
whats_growing: Direct-to-cell and satellite-terrestrial integration pilots moving toward commercialization (e.g., SpaceMobile, Starlink SCS/Cellular workflows).
Higher-capacity constellations and faster replacement cycles to sustain service quality in remote and high-latency-sensitive use cases.
Government, defense, and emergency communications demand as backup and mobile resilience use-cases expand.
Enterprise and industrial backhaul where terrain, mobility, or disaster resilience limits terrestrial alternatives.
whats_shrinking: Suburban/urban consumer dependence on pure satellite broadband as terrestrial networks densify.
Pure commodity-style resell-only models with weak scale, fixed margins, and limited technology differentiation.
Slow-walk growth in pure legacy MSS offerings exposed to spectrum and interference constraints.
recent_developments: 2025-11-30: EchoStar disclosed about 7.5 million wireless subscribers as of 2025-12-31 in FCC filing context.
2026-01-09: FCC authorized SpaceX to add 7,500 Gen2 Starlink satellites, increasing total Starlink authorization to 15,000 for global service expansion.
2026-02-13: Starlink reported more than 10 million active users in the US, up from 2+ million in Nov 2025.
2026-02-10: AST SpaceMobile deployed BB6 with large LEO phased-array payload and continued its rollout program toward initial space-based cellular service in selected markets.
2026-04-19: AST SpaceMobile reported a Block 2 BB7 satellite loss from a low-orbit insertion issue and filed for replacement support under launch/insurance arrangements.
2026-07-30: Amazon Leo milestone pressure remained central in FCC discussions; interim-milestone deadlines and spectrum-priority consequences remained active constraints.
outlook: Through 2027, US satellite telecom is likely to keep growing where terrestrial coverage is expensive or unreliable and where mobility resilience is mission-critical; however, winner outcomes depend on launch execution, cost discipline, spectrum efficiency, and the pace at which direct-to-device services transition from pilot to reliable commercial volume.
themes: Cellular-satellite convergence and direct-to-device service models
Milestone-driven rollout discipline for newer constellations
Spectrum regime complexity in L-band/Ka-band and MSS bands
Reliability and resilience demand from defense and critical infrastructure
Backhaul/complement vs replacement role relative to terrestrial fiber and 5G
one_sentence: The US market is in a scale-up phase driven by Starlink and emerging direct-to-cell constellations, even as high costs, launch pacing, and spectrum constraints keep margins uneven across operators.

title: Sawmills & Wood Production in the US
one_liner: U.S. sawmills and wood preservation convert logs into lumber and related building products, with revenue tied most directly to construction activity.
overview: The industry remains structurally tied to new housing, repair/remodel spending, and downstream building demand, while also dependent on imported input economics and tariff conditions for softwood lumber. Recent official indicators show muted housing starts, relatively high import-price sensitivity, and stable but not strongly expanding domestic production activity, consistent with a mature, cycle-dependent wood-products market.

market_size.note: IBIS forecast level referenced as the latest industry estimate in the baseline report context.

growth.note: IBIS baseline projection for industry revenue decline; wood-product manufacturing output index rose from 95.204 (2024) to 95.379 (2025), showing slight near-term production stability.

establishments.value: 16,141 private and 5 local gov establishments in wood product manufacturing

how_it_makes_money.description: The sector earns from sale of sawn hardwood and softwood lumber, beams, boards, treated products, and by-products to home builders, lumber dealers, repair/remodel customers, and downstream wood-product manufacturers.
how_it_makes_money.pricing_mode: Commodity pricing with significant exposure to regional market swings, especially softwood lumber benchmarks and import-cost movements.

cost_structure.labour: Production and non-supervisory hourly earnings were around USD 25.15 in June 2026 for wood product manufacturing, with stable but elevated payroll intensity.
cost_structure.energy_and_fuel: Drying, finishing, and kiln operations remain cost-sensitive to industrial energy and utility prices.
cost_structure.raw_materials: Log procurement quality and availability remain central; imported softwood pricing and duty treatment materially affect feedstock economics.
cost_structure.regulatory_and_duty_compliance: Post-2025 Section 232 measures on wood-product imports increase administrative and sourcing complexity.
cost_structure.capital: High capital intensity in mill modernization and throughput reliability encourages selective capex and selective expansion.

major_players: {'name': 'Weyerhaeuser', 'evidence': 'Operates large U.S. and Canadian wood product facilities with significant structural lumber, OSB, engineered wood, and plywood capacity; reported 2025 wood-products net sales of USD 4,957 million.'}

{'name': 'West Fraser', 'evidence': 'Operates 28 lumber mills and major OSB/plywood/MDF/LVL/other wood facilities as of Dec 2025; cites U.S. housing demand and tariff uncertainty as a central demand/cost factor.'}
{'name': 'Canfor', 'evidence': 'North American Q4 2025 results indicate elevated U.S. softwood duties continued to pressure demand and operating performance.'}
current_dynamics: Demand is being held between two forces: slower new-home start growth on the demand side and domesticization pressure from wood-product tariffs on the supply side, while downstream channels (repair/remodel and nonresidential replacement demand) remain comparatively steadier.
whats_growing: Demand for repair, maintenance, and upgrade applications in the housing stock remains a relative stabilizer despite new construction softness.
Domestic production planning is increasingly emphasizing tariff-aware procurement and supply diversification.
whats_shrinking: New residential starts declined to 1,177,000 SAAR in May 2026 (down 8.7% vs May 2025).
Tariff-driven pricing and sourcing volatility are reducing volume certainty for commoditized lumber sellers.
recent_developments: 2025-10-06: White House section 232 proclamation process on wood products initiated with findings of domestic-sector stress.
2025-10-14: Tariff framework on softwood timber and lumber made effective under Section 232 terms.
2026-03-05: Canfor Q4 2025 report flagged elevated U.S. softwood duties and tariffs as continuing demand pressure.
2026-06-16: Census reported U.S. housing starts at 1,177,000 SAAR (down 8.7% y/y).
2026-06-16: Census reported 1,413,000 housing permits SAAR (down 0.2% y/y from May 2025).
outlook: Near-term growth is more likely to be modest than strong. Domestic demand support from repair/remodel channels may offset weak new-housing momentum, while duty-related import competition management could keep some capacity utilization support intact but not restore broad demand growth unless rates and housing affordability improve.
themes: Housing-cycle sensitivity
Trade-policy-driven margin volatility
Domestic capacity discipline and selective capex
Industrial production stability with weak end-demand
Wage productivity management in a mature manufacturing segment
one_sentence: In 2025-2026, construction-led demand weakened as housing starts slowed, while trade duties and wood-price volatility increased operating uncertainty for domestic sawmills.

title: Scaffolding Contractors
one_liner: Specialized contractors that erect, shoring, dismantle, and increasingly engineer access and protection systems for elevated construction and maintenance work.
overview: Scaffolding contractors provide temporary access structures, lifting/hoisting systems, and related site support for new building, retrofit, and infrastructure work rather than building complete projects themselves. The industry is cyclical and price-sensitive, with activity driven by project starts in nonresidential and public infrastructure markets. Competition is high, but firms that combine engineering support, fast mobilization, and strong OSHA-compliant operations capture more durable margin opportunities.

growth.2025_2026_total_construction_spending: 1.4% CAGR equivalent increase from $2,136.2B in 2025 to $2,166.5B in 2026

baseline_2022.market_size: $4.712 billion (nearest reported baseline anchor in provided dataset)
baseline_2022.growth: +1.2% CAGR outlook in the provided 2021-2026 baseline trajectory; short-term demand in 2021 showed 4.6% annualized growth in the prior five-year period

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes primarily from erection/dismantling of scaffolding, shoring, temporary hoisting, and related access/protection work billed by project scope and labor intensity, with some operators packaging inspections, engineering, and safety support into bundled jobs.

cost_structure.labour: high share of project cost due to skilled crews and labor safety requirements
cost_structure.fleet_equipment: capital tied up in scaffold systems, components, and transport/maintenance
cost_structure.mobilization_logistics: short-notice trucking, crane coordination, and downtime risk on delayed projects
cost_structure.compliance_and_risk: OSHA-compliant design/inspection burden, workers’ compensation, and liability controls
cost_structure.pricing_pressure: high competition and narrow project-level margins in residential and retrofit work

current_dynamics: Demand is increasingly bifurcated: U.S. construction spending remains resilient overall while housing and some traditional office segments cool, and firms win more projects by adding engineering, mobilization speed, and integrated safety/inspection capabilities. Public infrastructure and institutional work are better supported than discretionary segments, but project pacing remains exposed to funding release timing.
whats_growing: 2026 nonresidential activity is supported by infrastructure and institutional categories where project momentum is stronger than in single-family housing
AIA July 2026 points to a commercial rebound in selected segments, especially data-center-linked activity, despite broader weakness
IIJA-funded transport and highway programs continued to progress with substantial reported obligations, helping scaffold demand in public infrastructure.
Safety-linked differentiation is increasing as operators with strong 1926.451 compliance, inspection, and access planning are preferred.
whats_shrinking: NAHB reported total 2025 housing starts of 1.36M, down 0.6% from 2024, indicating weaker broad residential stimulus for labor-intensive exterior projects
NAHB reported May 2026 housing starts at 1.18M SAAR, down 15.4% from May 2025, with multifamily down 40.2%
AIA forecasts show K-shaped weakness in nonresidential categories: office and manufacturing construction outlook remained soft in 2026
High labor and materials costs plus borrowing-cost sensitivity continue to pressure smaller operators
Margin expansion is constrained by high price competition and the need for certified staffing
highway and public programs remain uneven by geography
recent_developments: 2026-08-03: Census released June 2026 construction spending of $2,166.5B and private nonresidential at $745.3B (0.1% month-over-month versus revised May)
2025-08-01: Census reported June 2025 total construction spending of $2,136.2B and private construction at $1,621.9B

2026-07-20: AIA July 2026 forecast signaled a K-shaped nonresidential building outlook, with commercial and institutional strength tied partly to data-center-driven demand and weakness in other segments
2026-06-16: NAHB reported May housing starts fell to 1.18M SAAR, down 15.4% from the prior month’s year-over-year pace
2026-05-01: Brock Group announced acquisition of a Florida scaffolding business to expand its Southeastern footprint
2025-03-25: ASCE report card kept infrastructure as critical, with a $3.7T national gap remaining despite improving grades, implying prolonged public capital needs
outlook: In 2026, market direction is moderate growth rather than a broad acceleration: scaffolding demand should continue in commercial/industrial retrofit, public infrastructure, and selective data-center and institutional projects, while housing-related and discretionary commercial segments remain volatile. Operators with lower labor turnover, stronger safety governance, and bundled access-system offerings should defend margins better than pure labor-only players.
themes: Safety-compliance as a qualification moat (OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451 requirements are increasingly project-gated)
Capital-cycle sensitivity (demand follows nonresidential, municipal and infrastructure spending signals)
Service diversification through shoring, hoisting, and access-management bundles
Geographic and sector concentration risk across states and subsectors
Labor + cost volatility amplifying pricing discipline needs
one_sentence: Scaffolding contractors are a service-led niche tied to nonresidential construction and repair cycles, with demand now split between stronger institutional/commercial work and weaker housing while safety and cost-control remain central.

title: Scale & Balance Manufacturing
one_liner: Scale and balance firms build precision weighing systems for industrial logistics, process control, and scientific measurement, with demand driven by production, trade, and compliance intensity.
overview: The industry combines industrial, commercial, and lab-scale products tied to manufacturing output, freight activity, and regulatory-grade measurement. In 2022, U.S. revenue was about $1,168m, with industrial scales and balances the largest segment and an early-2022 baseline where profitability and margins were improved relative to prior volatility; industry performance remains linked to downstream industrial and logistics strength.

growth.market_growth_note: 2026 estimate applies IBIS baseline growth path from 2022.

baseline_2022.notes: Baseline from the provided industry file: revenue 1,168m (2022), CPI-adjusted IBIS 2022 currency, CAGR 0.70% (2002-2022), projected 1.21% CAGR to 2028.

how_it_makes_money: Sells precision industrial weighing hardware: truck scales, weighbridges, platforms, bulk and process control systems.
Sells high-accuracy laboratory balances and analytical solutions used in regulated quality/validation environments.
Earns recurring service revenue from calibration, software connectivity, maintenance, replacements, and spare parts.
Captures value from integration into workflow systems (inventory, routing, dimensioning, compliance reporting) where software + service increases switching costs.
cost_structure: Precision component costs (electronics, load cells, mechanical frames), with some pressure from commodity-linked input costs.
Skilled manufacturing labor and engineering costs for calibration, reliability, and industrial-grade certifications.
Regulatory/compliance burden for legal-for-trade accuracy requirements and documentation.
Aftermarket support and service network costs; freight/logistics costs tied to hardware distribution and installation.
Price pressure on low-end models from lower-cost import channels.

current_dynamics.demand: Industrial production was stable month-on-month in June 2026 but growing in 2026 on a broader quarter basis (4.0% annualized), while 2026 transborder freight reached $153.4bn in May, supporting truck and process weighing need.
current_dynamics.capacity: ISM data for June 2026 still show manufacturing expansion overall, though production softened versus May; industrial demand remains uneven across sectors.
current_dynamics.trade_and_currency: The broad trade-weighted dollar appreciated in Q1 2026 after a weaker 2025, improving import competitiveness of finished foreign scales and pressuring low-end domestic replacement demand.

whats_growing: High-end industrial truck and process systems linked to compliance-heavy logistics and freight operations.
Laboratory and precision measurement demand tied to biotech, pharma, and quality-control workflows.
Connected/revenue-recurring solutions (software, remote diagnostics, in-motion weighing, inventory integration).
whats_shrinking: Low-value commodity scales where price competition is highest and NTEP-compliant differentiation is lower.
U.S. export market share for generic low-margin products when the trade-weighted dollar appreciates.
New export-order momentum in sub-industries with slower global demand, where ISM export-order indexes remained below expansion in 2026.

outlook: For 2026, the industry is better positioned where manufacturers deliver precision, industrial ruggedness, and compliance-enabled digital integration than in commodity-only scales. However, continued currency strength and import penetration from major scale-producing hubs keep pricing pressure high in lower-margin channels. Expect modest top-line expansion with clearer divergence between premium/high-regulation and low-value commodity segments.

Trade competitiveness versus domestic premium differentiation
Regulation-led durability and legal-for-trade compliance
Freight/logistics intensity and truck-scale modernization
High-accuracy lab and quality-control instruments as resilient demand pockets

title: Scheduled and Charter Bus Services in the US
one_liner: US scheduled and charter bus transportation is recovering through intercity demand and longer utilization runs, but fleet numbers are shrinking as larger operators consolidate.
overview: The industry serves a dual market: private or public-sector charters and scheduled intercity travel. After the 2020-2022 rebound cycle, activity has remained uneven by segment: charter remains a core service, while scheduled intercity operators are increasingly central in corridor recovery and substitution to driving. Evidence from 2025 data shows higher vehicle productivity, stronger fleet utilization, and continued participant participation in the federal Intercity Bus Atlas, while cost pressure remains concentrated in fuel, wage labor, maintenance, and compliance.
how_it_makes_money: Revenue is earned mainly from charter contracts (school, group, corporate, civic, and tour travel), scheduled intercity fares (including airport/port/corridor service and city-pair routes), packaged tours/sightseeing, commuter and shuttle contracts, and secondary shuttle/last-mile support trips; survey data in 2025 shows large variability by fleet size in service mix.
cost_structure: Primary variable costs are fuel and labor, with second-order effects from maintenance, insurance, finance, tolls, and compliance. In 2025-2026 data, diesel and gasoline remained materially relevant in operating cost models; transit-industry wage data for NAICS 485 remained elevated (about $27.17/hr in Mar 2026 rising to $28.03/hr by Jun 2026), while motorcoach workforce scale stayed high at 77,176 jobs in 2025.
current_dynamics: Intercity scheduled coverage remains fragmented but expanding in digital feed participation, with over 40 ICBA providers represented in the June 17, 2026 update.
2025 Census data shows bus operators increasing utilization (passenger miles, miles run) even as the total number of companies declined, indicating scale concentration.
Fuel costs in 1H 2026 were volatile but not uniformly higher than 2025, reinforcing route-level fare sensitivity and selective add-on pricing.
Transit-sector recovery in 2025-2026 (bus + demand-response rebound cited by APTA) supports short-haul intercity and group mobility demand spillover.
whats_growing: Passenger miles and motorcoach miles run grew in 2025.
Intercity carrier participation and mapped scheduled network detail in federal ICBA datasets.
Fleet productivity: passengers per vehicle and utilization moved higher versus 2024.
Operational consolidation with large carriers absorbing more service volume.
whats_shrinking: Carrier count declined, indicating exits among smaller operators.
Margin headroom in low-yield fixed schedules where fuel and staffing are high.
Purely traditional scheduled models outside major corridors remain pressured versus charter and platform-linked intercity offerings.
recent_developments: 2026-06-17: BTS Intercity Bus Atlas update showed participation from over 40 scheduled intercity bus carriers.
2026-05-20: ABAF released 2025 Motorcoach Census; US motorcoach operators at 1,769 carriers and 49,543 motorcoaches.
2026-03-03: BTS reported February 2026 regular gasoline at $2.91/gal and diesel at $3.72/gal nationwide.
2026-02-03: BTS reported January 2026 regular gasoline at $2.81/gal and diesel at $3.52/gal nationwide.
2025-05-14: APTA reported U.S. ridership recovery to 85% of pre-pandemic levels, with bus mode recovering to 86% of 2019.
outlook: The near-term outlook is moderate recovery with continued consolidation: volume growth likely continues in intercity and charter demand pockets, while smaller operators face margin strain and substitution pressures. Profitability is expected to improve mainly through utilization and route/asset density, not broad fare inflation.
themes: Consolidation and operational scale
Intercity network modernization
Charter + scheduled portfolio mix
Fuel-sensitive economics
Labor and operator shortages
Regional corridor growth
