title: Shaving Razor Manufacturing
one_liner: U.S. shaving razor manufacturing is a mature, concentrated wet-grooming niche where incumbents defend share through premium systems while low-cost imports and subscription-led direct brands pressure margins.
overview: IBIS’ 2022 baseline shows a small U.S. razor manufacturing base with modest long-term expansion, high concentration, and continued pressure from imports and substitute channels. Recent 2025–2026 disclosures show major incumbents still expanding revenue at low rates, with P&G’s FY26 Grooming net sales up 4% and guidance for FY27 held to 1%–3% all-in growth, while Edgewell reported FY25 razor-related sales weakness and positioned for an organic-growth rebound in 2026.

key_stats.market_size: 2026 global razor market USD 12.06B (baseline projection: 2025 USD 11.62B, 2026 USD 12.06B, 2027+ forecast in the same tracking framework).
key_stats.growth: 2026–2031 global razor market CAGR 3.90%; P&G FY26 Grooming net sales +4% versus FY25; Edgewell FY25 Wet Shave net sales -0.8% while the company guided for FY26 organic improvement.
key_stats.industry_baseline_anchor: IBIS baseline: 2021 market size USD 2.511B with 2021–2026 projected CAGR 1.71%.

baseline_2022.market_size: USD 2.511 billion (IBIS baseline in 2021 currency, reported in shaving razor manufacturing base period).

how_it_makes_money.2026: Manufacturers earn from razor handle/system sales plus high-margin recurring replacement cartridges/blades; disposable and value SKUs remain demand-stabilizing but carry lower margin and lower long-run retention value.
how_it_makes_money.drivers: Premium cartridge systems and brand-led lock-in in 2026 remain core profit pools, while private-label and imported value offerings capture price-sensitive demand.

cost_structure.materials: 2025–2026: plastic and steel input volatility remains a major structural headwind in wet razor manufacturing cost models.
cost_structure.marketing: 2026: major players increased marketing and promotion intensity (P&G cited higher marketing-related SG&A reinvestment in FY26 quarter disclosures).
cost_structure.tariffs_and_operations: 2025: Edgewell reported gross margin pressure from unfavorable mix and inflation/tariff effects despite productivity offsets.

major_players: Edgewell Personal Care (Schick, Wilkinson Sword, Billie, Hydro systems)
Dollar Shave Club and Harry's (DTC and import-heavy competition; not part of the IBIS domestic manufacturing set)
Private-label / club and retailer programs distributed through mass and ecommerce channels
current_dynamics: 2026 data shows incumbents still growing on pricing and portfolio mix while net-volume gains are weak in mature markets; North American premium wet-shave volume remains challenged by grooming-behavior shifts and alternative channels. Global razor demand is still rising, but the competitive battleground is moving toward digital distribution, sustainability, and cost efficiency.
whats_growing: Subscription and recurring-replenishment models around shaving categories
Higher-value cartridge/refill and multi-function system pricing, even as volume is less robust
International growth and online channels relative to mature domestic wet-shave replacement demand
whats_shrinking: Purely price-driven domestic razor volume in mature male-shave demand pools
Pure disposable, low-involvement purchase behavior where consumers trade down or switch to alternatives
US-margin headroom from legacy manufacturing economics without stronger premium differentiation
recent_developments: 2025-11-13: Edgewell reported FY25 net sales of USD 2,223.5M (-1.3%); Wet Shave net sales were USD 1,218.9M (-0.8%), while saying it expects a return to organic growth in FY26.
2025-11-13: Edgewell reported signing a USD 340M sale of Feminine Care, signaling portfolio focus toward grooming/skin categories.
2026-01: Mordor Intelligence updated its razor market baseline, projecting global razor size at USD 12.06B in 2026 from USD 11.62B in 2025.
2026-07-29: P&G reported FY26 net sales of USD 87.0B (+3%) and Grooming net sales of USD 6,918M (+4%), with grooming organic growth seen as restrained in Q4.
2026-07-29: P&G gave FY27 guidance of 1%–3% all-in and 1%–3% organic company-wide growth, indicating a continued low-growth environment for the broader category.
outlook: For the near term (2026–2027), expect restrained top-line gains, a premium-versus-value split in favor of incumbents with stronger portfolios, and continued margin sensitivity to input costs and brand-building spend; long term, consolidation around stronger brand ecosystems and sustainable materials is likely to dominate U.S. razor manufacturing economics.
themes: Premiumization versus value erosion
Recurring replacement economics in wet-shave systems
Subscription and digital-first go-to-market models
Volatile commodity and logistics costs
North America volume stagnation versus international recovery
Sustainability pressure on plastic-heavy product mix
one_sentence: In 2026, the industry is moving through low-single-digit value growth as domestic scale stays concentrated and competition shifts toward cartridges, refillable systems, and recurring replacement economics.

title: Sheep Farming in the US
one_liner: A small, fragmented U.S. livestock segment where lamb drives most value while wool remains structurally weak.
overview: U.S. sheep farming remains a niche but stable part of livestock agriculture, with producers increasingly focused on lamb and mutton returns while wool income declines. Inventory has edged lower into 2026 and production shifts are visible month-to-month, while processing channels and trade remain important for balancing domestic gaps. The sector is still dominated by smaller, often part-time operators rather than a few large integrated firms.
how_it_makes_money: Revenue is led by lamb and mutton sales to processors, grocery, and foodservice channels.
Secondary revenue is derived from wool/hair clipping, pelt and by-product sales.
A minor share of revenue comes from live-animal sales and value-added channels such as specialty fibers.
cost_structure: Feed and forage costs remain a major and cyclical cash-flow item.
Labor costs rise when operators scale operations and must attract replacement workers.
Processing and slaughter costs are sensitive to capacity at federally and non-federally inspected facilities.
Animal health, predator loss, and climate-related forage variability directly affect margin volatility.
major_players: U.S. sheep operators (50,378 enterprises in 2022; increasingly small and part-time in structure)
Regional lamb slaughter and processing plants (federal and state-inspected channels)
Wool and pelt marketing handlers that monetize clipped and sheared fiber
Domestic and international trade channels for lamb and mutton on a carcass-weight basis
current_dynamics: Flock size slipped in 2026 while market inventory stayed comparatively resilient.
Wool value is compressing, while lamb/mutton remains the principal commercial output.
Monthly lamb and mutton slaughter volume has shown high volatility from 2025 into 2026.
ERS outlooks in mid-2026 indicate firmer lamb price expectations despite near-term output softness.
whats_growing: 2026 data show lamb and mutton still positioned as the primary revenue source versus wool.
Market lamb share within inventory rose, with market lambs/market sheep around 94% of market inventory in January 2026.
Lamb price outlook for 2027 improved, supporting cash-flow planning for finishing systems.
whats_shrinking: Total sheep and lambs inventory fell 1% from 2025 to 4.99 million head in January 2026.
Shorn wool output declined 5% from 2024 to 2025, to 20.5 million pounds.
Wool price declined from 2024 to 2025 ($1.43 to $1.40 per lb).
Monthly lamb and mutton production weakened in early 2026 compared with 2025 (June 2026 down 11% from June 2025).
recent_developments: 2026-01-30: USDA NASS reported total sheep and lambs at 4.99 million head on Jan 1, 2026 (down 1% from 2025).
2026-01-30: NASS reported 2025 lamb crop 3.03 million head and shorn wool 20.5 million pounds (-5% from 2024).
2025-05-22: NASS Livestock Slaughter reported April 2025 lamb and mutton production 12.8 million pounds (+13% from April 2024).
2026-06-25: NASS Livestock Slaughter reported June 2025 vs June 2026 lamb and mutton production at 9.4 million pounds (-19% YoY).
2026-07-23: NASS Livestock Slaughter reported June 2026 lamb and mutton production at 10.4 million pounds and sheep slaughter 175,900 head (-7% YoY).
2026-05-19: ERS reported lamb/Sheep prices rose in Apr-May 2026 and lifted the 2027 slaughter lamb forecast to $252.50/cwt.
outlook: Near-term US sheep farming is expected to remain structurally small but financially pressured in wool, while lamb remains supported by stronger price expectations in ERS/USDA outlooks; the 2027 forecast points to lower total output variability but continued sensitivity to processing and inventory trends.
themes: Inventory drift with value-chain rebalancing
Shift from wool toward meat-led profitability
Monthly slaughter volatility and timing risk
Regionalized, fragmented production base
Foodservice and retail lamb demand dependence
one_sentence: In the 2026 period, U.S. sheep farming sits near 4.99 million head, with weaker wool economics and volatile monthly lamb-mutton production offsetting long-term structural resilience.

title: Sheet Metal, Window & Door Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: Fabrication-heavy domestic makers of metal windows, doors, and architectural sheet-metal components are tied to housing and commercial construction while facing volatile aluminum/steel costs.
overview: The U.S. Sheet Metal, Window & Door Manufacturing segment (NAICS 332321) covers metal-framed windows, doors, trims, and related architectural metal products. Demand is primarily tied to residential and commercial construction cycles, with the segment also benefiting from renovation and retrofit activity. Because production is highly material-intensive, profitability is sensitive to aluminum and steel price movements and freight/energy dynamics, while automation and capacity expansion are the main levers for competitiveness.
how_it_makes_money: Sells metal-framed windows, doors, and associated architectural metalwork to construction supply chains (new residential, multifamily, and commercial projects).
Captures value through customized fabrication, project-based production, and margin capture via material procurement, conversion/assembly quality, and installation-ready delivery.
Derives additional growth in replacement and renovation channels where customers buy to update energy performance, weather resistance, and security.
Some players move up/down the value chain with glazing, tooling, or adjacent component capabilities to improve gross margin.
cost_structure: Material cost is the dominant variable component: purchased metal, glazing partners, coatings, and fastening/packaging costs heavily influence unit economics.
Labor is significant in fabrication and finishing, and most firms report ongoing hiring and expansion needs.
Energy, transport, and fixed plant overhead create high operating leverage, making volumes and mix critical for margin.
Raw metal costs are managed through product mix, hedging/contract pricing, and all-in pricing formulas where pass-through is possible.
major_players: Manhattan Steel Door and Window Co.
current_dynamics: Residential permitting and starts remain the main demand engine, though permits in 2026 have cooled more than starts.
Residential construction activity is still positive in 2026, while nonresidential construction spending remains mixed and below prior-year totals in some segments.
Aluminum pricing volatility is a key margin variable, with one large U.S. aluminum processor reporting all-in U.S. aluminum up sharply in 2026 versus 2025.
Manufacturers continue capacity upgrades and automation in 2026 as volume and labor needs rise.
Tariff risk is viewed as a sector-wide constraint, especially for imported components and downstream pricing.
whats_growing: Residential construction demand remained positive in 2026, with June 2026 housing starts at 1,427,000 SAAR.
Capacity expansion and facility investments are expanding among leading manufacturers.
Sales and production growth are strong among surveyed manufacturers in 2024-2025 windows/doors reporting, with volume expansion and broader product innovation.
Demand for higher-specification fenestration products tied to replacement/energy goals remains supportive.
whats_shrinking: Nonresidential construction remains the weaker leg of demand; annual 2025/2026 comparison was negative in nonresidential spending in core category terms.
Raw-material premium exposure remains a persistent downside because metal inputs are volatile under tariff and logistics stress.
Some lower-margin segments tied to price-sensitive retrofit/repair demand face tighter project economics.
Import cost uncertainty and trade friction remain a drag on working-capital and procurement planning.
recent_developments: 2026-07-17: U.S. Census reported June 2026 privately-owned housing starts of 1,427,000 SAAR and housing starts up 3.5% versus June 2025.
2026-06-27: U.S. Census Construction Spending release (February 2026) shows 2025 private nonresidential and private total construction data, with continued uneven monthly movement across categories.
2026-03-31: SEC filing from a major U.S. aluminum processor reported average all-in U.S. aluminum price US$5,495/ton in Q1 2026 vs US$3,339/ton in Q1 2025.
2025-05-29: Window + Door Top Manufacturers report showed average 2024 volume growth at 2.2% YoY and revenue growth at 3.7%, with many firms reporting expansion activity.
2026-06-16: Reuters/industry coverage reported LME aluminum spot retreating from the 2026 peak (US$3,854/mt peak to US$3,418/mt on June 15), reflecting temporary tariff-geopolitical de-risking.
outlook: Near-term growth is expected to be moderate and uneven: resilient residential demand supports volume, while nonresidential softness and metal-price risk keep margins volatile; best performers are likely those with tighter procurement, automation, and stronger replacement-market positioning.
themes: Residential construction sensitivity
Raw-material inflation management
Tariff and trade-policy risk
Automation/capacity scaling
Volume diversification into replacement and retrofit demand
one_sentence: The industry is relatively stable into 2026, with new-home construction and replacement demand supporting volume, while material cost spikes, tariff exposure, and selective labor constraints pressure margins.

title: Sheet Music Publishers
one_liner: US sheet music publishing is moving from a print-first niche toward controlled digital channels, with consolidation around major catalog and platform players as free alternatives pressure price and unit volume.
overview: US sheet music publishing is a small, concentrated, low-growth segment that is transitioning from physical sales toward digital licensing, downloads, and platform-distributed learning workflows. IBISWorld’s last published baseline shows industry revenue at $242.4m in 2021 and a projected decline to $216.5m in 2026. In 2025-26, recorded music economics continued shifting toward streaming subscriptions, while legal digital sheet music platforms increased scale, intensifying competition for standalone print-focused publishers. Institutional buyers (schools, ensembles, worship groups, retailers) and licensed catalog depth remain the key support for revenue stability, but volume pressure from inexpensive or free alternatives remains persistent.

key_stats.market_size: 2026: $216.5m projected US market size (from IBIS projection); 2026: $11.5b US recorded music overall (RIAA)
key_stats.growth: 2021-2026: -2.2% CAGR projected by IBISWorld; 2025: free digital and low-price substitutes remain a major demand drainer
key_stats.businesses: 2021: 94 enterprises; 2026: 79 (IBIS projected) and trending fewer operators

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: approx. $237.8m (estimated from 2021 published base of $242.4m and the 2021 -1.4% decline path in the baseline report)

how_it_makes_money: Majority economics come from catalog monetization across three channels: (1) licensed digital sheet downloads and app playback/reader workflows, (2) printed music books and individual pieces sold via retailers and direct channels, and (3) rights-related licensing arrangements tied to downstream uses by schools, ensembles, venues, and media buyers. Platform operators also monetize with subscription upgrades and recurring learning bundles, while publishers earn from long-tail catalog access and controlled licensing rather than one-time unit spikes.
cost_structure: Fixed costs include editorial and engraving/transcription labor, digital formatting, rights administration, and platform hosting; variable costs include copyright clearances, cloud delivery, and sales/commercial channels. Material, printing, and warehousing costs decline with digital substitution, but compliance, rights metadata, piracy control, and publisher-merchant relationships remain high and increasingly systemized expenses.
current_dynamics: In 2025-26, consumer behavior and music workflow time remained focused on digital channels, while institutional buyers continued to value legal, organized curriculum catalogs for classrooms and ensembles. RIAA’s 2025 US figures show streaming-led growth and high paid-subscription engagement, reinforcing substitution away from ownership-centric digital purchases. Concurrently, Musicnotes’ March 2026 updates show continued scaling of legal digital catalog and app-based consumption. Major publishers are responding through catalog consolidation and platform-level distribution synergies; Wise Music’s 2025 education-division sale and the Hal Leonard–Muse Group combination indicate strategic separation of music publishing versus adjacent education and software layers.
whats_growing: 2025-26: legal digital sheet music ecosystems and subscription-style usage models; catalog aggregation around strong title libraries and school-ready materials; institutional demand from ensembles, worship, and music programs; platform-enabled discoverability in search, instant delivery, and device playback.
whats_shrinking: Print-first unit sales and small independent print-run publishers with narrow catalogs; free-displacement channels and hobbyist substitution behavior (tabs, user-generated alternatives); low-margin standalone stores and thin operators as concentration rises.
recent_developments: 2026-03: Musicnotes updated its profile to 500,000+ licensed digital sheet music/guitar tablature titles and 9 million customers, indicating continued digital scale at a legal platform.
2026-03: RIAA 2025 year-end results showed US recorded music at $11.5b with paid subscriptions up to 106.5m accounts, highlighting continued shift to subscription music consumption.
2025-01: Wise Music Group sold its Digital Education division to Achieve Partners, signaling re-concentration on core music-publishing assets.
2025-05: NEA announced 1,474 awards totaling $36.79m for arts in all 50 states, reinforcing federal arts-policy support for arts programming and education access.
2026-05: U.S. Census reported public school per-pupil spending at $17,619 in FY2024, with state/ local finance pressure still shaping discretionary arts buying power at schools.
2023-12: Hal Leonard’s advised merger with Muse Group with Francisco Partners reflected continued consolidation and expansion of content ecosystems around major catalog players.
outlook: The industry is likely to keep shrinking in aggregate through 2026-2027, but the composition is becoming more defensible for operators with deep licensed catalogs, efficient digital fulfillment, and education/community channels. The near-term path favors fewer firms with stronger rights operations and platform workflows, while small publishers remain exposed to margin squeeze and catalog commoditization.
themes: Digital substitution intensity
Catalog concentration
Institutional demand anchor
Education-program sensitivity
Piracy and free alternatives pressure
Legal platform migration
one_sentence: The industry is shrinking and consolidating, with catalog-heavy digital distribution leaders and software-enabled channels growing faster than print-dominant legacy models.

title: Sheet-Metal Roofing Manufacturing
one_liner: U.S. sheet-metal roofing remains a specialized, durability-led manufacturing niche where demand is driven by re-roofing replacements, industrial-commercial construction, and material performance value.
overview: Baseline IBIS data show sheet-metal roofing as a small but steady U.S. manufacturing segment (about USD 1.237 billion in prior baseline reporting) with long-cycle, low-volatility demand quality and strong dependence on construction spending. In 2025–26, demand signals are mixed: residential permitting softened slightly from June 2025 to June 2026, while housing starts edged up and nonresidential commercial activity stabilized, supporting industrial commercial reroof demand. The domestic supply chain has gained support from tighter steel-mill capacity and federal domestic-content policy, while input inflation from steel and energy remains a structural headwind.

key_stats.market_size: USD 1.3 billion (IBIS-style projected 2026 revenue for sheet-metal roofing manufacturing)
key_stats.growth: 0.5% annualized growth to 2026 (IBIS projection 2021-26)

baseline_2022.market_size: USD 38,592.2 million (Sheet Metal Work, NAICS 332322, sector output proxy from FRED)
baseline_2022.growth: +29.4% vs 2021 (29,841.5 million to 38,592.2 million; broad NAICS proxy, not a pure roofing-only filter)

how_it_makes_money: Manufactures and sells sheet-metal roofing materials and assemblies (galvanized steel, aluminum, coated panels, edge systems, fasteners) to builders, fabricators, roofing contractors, and distributors.
Margins improve on higher-specification products (long-life, high-durability systems, premium coatings, fastener/edge systems) and retrofit-focused specification sales.
Revenue is tied to construction project timing and is often cyclical across new-build and reroof replacement cycles.
cost_structure: Raw materials are the largest cost element: steel and aluminum input prices are highly influential and linked to domestic/global steel market conditions.
Specialized fabrication, coating, and finishing add fixed and variable manufacturing costs with low substitution flexibility in the short run.
Labor and installation-support economics remain relevant because localized fabrication/engineering and technical lead times are key to project margins.
Freight and handling costs are meaningful due to bulky goods and the project-installed nature of roofing systems.
Distribution and channel management costs rise when distribution channels become unstable or when channel restructuring occurs.
major_players: Carlisle Construction Materials (Drexel Metals, Carlisle SynTec, Versico, Weatherbond, Metal-Era ecosystem)
current_dynamics: Demand is relatively resilient in re-roofing, while new construction remains the more rate-sensitive leg.
Steel upstream conditions show upward pricing pressure even as mills report tighter utilization and stronger market conditions.
Nonresidential construction spending was mixed through 2026 and not strongly expanding in near-term snapshots.
Domestic-content policy increases attention to U.S.-sourced steel, manufactured products, and infrastructure-grade components.
Energy-efficiency positioning (cool roofs, reflective envelopes) is increasingly integrated into commercial and institutional roofing proposals.
whats_growing: Reroofing activity in mature commercial and institutional buildings due to lifecycle replacement and aging stock.
Cooling/energy-performance positioning of metal systems (cool-roof and high-reflectance/low-heat-transfer designs).
Domestic steel and U.S. manufacturing content preference in federally supported infrastructure and public-sector construction programs.
Demand for systems with longer service life and premium performance attributes (fire/wind/hail resilience).
whats_shrinking: Pure new-construction-led growth versus replacement demand, especially in higher-rate environments.
Pure price-based competitiveness versus substitute roofing systems in highly price-sensitive projects.
Margin expansion without operating discipline due persistent input-price volatility and installation/distribution bottlenecks.
Industry-level differentiation as more firms compete on volume and short-cycle channel share.
recent_developments: 2026-07-17: U.S. Census reported June 2026 private housing units authorized at 1,367,000 (down 2.3% vs revised May 2026), with housing starts at 1,427,000 (up 3.5% vs June 2025).
2026-08-03: U.S. Census reported total construction spending at $2,166.5B in June 2026, below $2,237.7B in June 2025.
2026-07-27: Nucor reported higher average selling prices and a second consecutive quarter of record steel-mill shipments.
2025-10-29: Carlisle reported solid commercial re-roofing demand despite weaker new-construction conditions.
2026-06-05: Kingspan increased planned U.S. roofing investment commitment to $1 billion over five years.
2026-08-03: MBCI (part of Cornerstone) reported regional pricing pressure, noting increases up to 6% in a July/August notice context.
outlook: Expect flat-to-weak headline growth in 2026–27 with stronger dispersion between replacement-led, resilient roofing demand and rate-sensitive new build; operators that combine premium performance positioning with stable domestic steel sourcing should hold margin better than commodity competitors.
themes: Re-roofing-led demand resilience
Energy-efficient and climate-resilient roof performance
Domestic steel supply-chain positioning and Buy America effects
Input-cost inflation management
Regionalized distribution and contractor channel strategy
one_sentence: The industry is mature and concentrated, with modest near-term top-line growth but strong pricing sensitivity to steel inputs, installation channel shifts, and resilience-focused retrofit demand.

title: Ship Building in the US
one_liner: U.S. shipbuilding is a defense-led manufacturing industry where federal naval procurement now dominates near-term growth, with naval budgets rising sharply in 2025-26.
overview: The U.S. shipbuilding industry designs and builds naval vessels, submarines, and support ships, and also earns stable revenue from heavy maintenance and modernization services. In 2025-2026, policy and budget signals shifted toward higher, more front-loaded naval spending, while industrial-base reform and production stabilization became central themes. Commercial shipbuilding remains more constrained by cost and limited global competitiveness, even with Jones Act-protected domestic demand.
how_it_makes_money: Long-cycle procurement contracts for naval vessels (new builds, substitutions, and production programs such as Virginia-class and Columbia-class submarines)
Shipyard modernization, sustainment, and repair programs for active fleets
Capitalized service and long-lead material contracts for future builds across Navy and Coast Guard programs
Domestic commercial work protected by Jones Act demand, including offshore and inland waterway-related vessels

major_inputs: Highly skilled marine engineering and fabrication labor
Dock capacity, advanced tooling, and compliance/QA systems
Long lead-time procurement (nuclear, combat, and propulsion subsystems)
cost_pressure_factors: Persistent wage and skilled labor pressure in major shipyards
Material volatility (notably steel and specialty alloys)
Concurrent design/program change requirements that can raise integration and rework costs
Infrastructure backlog requiring near-term capital upgrades

current_dynamics: FY2026 DOD planning moved from a single-pot view to a split structure with 20.8B discretionary and 26.5B mandatory in SCN, totaling 47.4B.
The FY2026 budget message (2025-06-26) emphasized 19 new Navy ships, with two Virginia-class and one Columbia-class procurement focus.
Senate FY2026 defense appropriations (2026-02-03) boosted Navy shipbuilding appropriations to 27.2B, including major submarine-related add-ons.
The FY27 Shipbuilding Plan (2026-05-11) introduces a longer execution roadmap under the Golden Fleet concept with production sequencing and industrial-base performance targets.
whats_growing: 2025-06-26 to 2026-02-03: Navy shipbuilding budget emphasis increased sharply, especially in SCN and submarine-related line items.
2026-05-11: FY27 plan formalized a longer five-year build and sustainment profile and infrastructure modernization path.
2026-06-24: FY27-31 tables indicate sustained multi-year build volume (e.g., 75 planned ships in the planning horizon).
whats_shrinking: Commercial export competitiveness remains low and episodic relative to domestic-mandated demand.
Purely private commercial replacement demand is still secondary to defense demand in value terms.
Operational flexibility remains constrained by long-cycle design and qualification processes that limit rapid shifts in production mix.
recent_developments: 2025-06-26: FY2026 defense budget briefing announced a national defense request focused on 19 new Navy ships and specific submarine investments.
2025-06-26: Same defense budget message stated the DOD plan includes two Virginia-class submarines and one Columbia-class submarine and added $2.5B for nuclear shipyard productivity enhancements.
2026-02-03: Senate appropriations leadership approved the FY2026 defense bill with shipbuilding increased to $27.2B in the bill and $1.9B for a second Virginia-class submarine.
2026-05-11: Department of the Navy released the FY2027 Shipbuilding Plan, stating a $65.8B generational shipbuilding investment framework.
2026-06-24: FY27-31 plan tables showed FY2027 funding intensity of 65.8B and a total 75-ship planning profile across FY27-FY31.
outlook: Near-term outlook is positive if congressional support for FY2027 and follow-on authority remains intact, with growth concentrated in submarines and strategic surface combatants. The strongest uncertainty remains policy continuity, schedule discipline, and ability to absorb mandatory-plus-discretionary funding efficiently without production bottlenecks.
themes: Military demand-led expansion
Submarine industrial base modernization
Defense-driven capital intensity and long-cycle production
Industrial base resilience (workforce, facilities, and supplier stabilization)
one_sentence: The sector remains anchored by long-cycle military programs, especially submarines, and a stronger 2026-2027 budget posture that increases shipbuilding outlays while still leaving commercial exports and broad private demand comparatively muted.

title: Shipping Container Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US shipping-container manufacturing remains small in absolute capacity versus imports, with domestic makers serving niche and specialized demand while the industry’s demand cycle is driven by US trade flows and freight economics.
overview: US shipping-container manufacturing in 2022 was described as a low-concentration, mature segment tied to broad trade patterns and high steel costs. By 2026, the market context is still characterized by strong dependence on international containers for a large share of domestic cargo movement, while import penetration and transport-rate moves continue to reshape margins and order mix. Demand remains linked to e-commerce and industrial shipment demand, but high global inventories and normalized route choices after post-pandemic volatility create a more moderate environment.

key_stats.market_size: $790 million (US industry revenue in 2022)
key_stats.growth: 2022: +5.2% y/y; 2025: US retail e-commerce adjusted to $316.1 billion in Q4 2025 (+1.7% q/q)
key_stats.top_port: Port of Los Angeles 5,726,784 loaded TEUs in 2023

baseline_2022.growth: 5.2% increase in 2022
baseline_2022.note: Industry remained mature and highly import-competitive; steel historically a dominant input cost.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers generate revenue from new container sales (dry, reefer, and specialty designs), refurbishment and conversion, and domestic lead-time/specialty fabrication services. Margin is sensitive to steel input pricing, with value migration increasingly favoring custom features and shorter lead-time domestic sourcing when import lead times or quality concerns outweigh import price advantage.

cost_structure.primary_cost_driver: Steel has historically accounted for roughly 60% of manufacturing cost in container builds.
cost_structure.secondary_costs: Wages, fabrication overhead, transport/repositioning of empty equipment, and quality assurance/repair costs.
cost_structure.profitability_pressure: High import competition and volatile steel procurement keep pricing discipline tight, while short-cycle freight and logistics congestion can create intermittent operating leverage.

major_players: US and global carriers that indirectly shape demand through leasing/repositioning systems (for example, 2M, 5Y/large alliance members in trade lanes)
current_dynamics: Demand is anchored to trade balances and logistics chain behavior rather than standalone freight construction cycles. In 2026 monthly trade data, import and export values remain volatile: January 2026 showed stronger exports with lower imports and a narrower deficit, while March 2026 showed broad goods imports re-accelerating. Containerized shipping rates fell through 2025, improving near-term cost-to-ship for importers but pressuring shipping-linked equipment value recovery. Port-level activity data still shows high concentration in large gateways, with modest redistribution by coast rather than full structural re-routing.
whats_growing: 2026-05-05: US goods and services exports rose to $320.9 billion in March 2026 (vs $314.7 billion in February).
2026-03-10: Q4 2025 adjusted e-commerce sales reached $316.1 billion, maintaining a 16.6% share of adjusted total retail sales.
whats_shrinking: 2025-2023: Loaded TEUs in the top 25 US container ports were 40.6 million, down 11% from 2022.
2025-12: FMC reported 31% year-over-year decline in global containerized spot rates from Dec 2024 to Dec 2025.
2026-03: US 2025Q? March-to-date steel imports showed YTD through Feb 2026 3.0 million metric tons, down from 4.8 million metric tons through Feb 2025.
recent_developments: 2026-03-12: US international trade (Jan 2026 release) - goods and services deficit improved to $54.5bn; exports were $302.1bn and imports $356.6bn.
2026-05-05: March 2026 trade release - goods/services deficit rose to $60.3bn with exports $320.9bn and imports $381.2bn.
2026-03-10: Census 4Q 2025 e-commerce data - adjusted e-commerce was $316.1bn, 16.6% of total retail sales.
2026-01-14: BTS 2026 Port Performance Annual Report cited 2024 port import/export cargo value above $2.1tn and 41% share of US import/export activity for ports.
2025-09-22: Stoughton Trailers announced a return to US intermodal container manufacturing with a new 53-foot intermodal container.
outlook: In 2026, the most likely path is moderate, uneven growth in container demand: stable underlying goods movement with less post-pandemic demand shock, while domestic manufacturing remains constrained by scale and price competition. The industry’s upside is tied to faster US sourcing for specific industrial programs, resilient e-commerce-related freight demand, and potential shifts in trade-policy or tariff-driven sourcing behavior.
themes: US production capacity remains limited versus import-heavy demand
Trade-volume and freight-cycle shifts drive short- to mid-cycle orders
Material inflation (especially steel) remains the central profitability variable
Port concentration means a few gateway ports influence order mix and lead-times

title: Shooting Ranges
one_liner: The U.S. shooting range industry is a small, fragmented recreational-consumer services market where growth comes from repeat visits, memberships, and training demand rather than broad national consolidation.
overview: Shooting ranges in the United States generate revenue from lane rentals, memberships, classes, and on-site retail of firearms-related products. The industry is highly discretionary and sensitive to household income and macro conditions, but also cycles with firearm-policy sentiment. Recent operators increasingly hedge demand swings through recurring memberships and skill programs, while investing in safer, more controlled experiences (including smart-target and software workflows).

key_stats.market_size: USD 1.67 billion (projected 2025 IBIS-style baseline trajectory from prior 2019 level)
key_stats.growth: around +1.4% CAGR in the latest projected period; growth trend described as moderate/low-single-digit in the short term

baseline_2022.growth: about 1.4% annualized trend direction in the post-2019 normalization window

how_it_makes_money: Facility access: hourly lane/booth rentals and memberships (frequent users and recurring passes)
Services: lessons, coaching, competitions, certification, and membership programs
On-site sales: ammunition, reloading supplies, safety gear, targets, accessories
Ancillary demand: concessions, pro shop sales, and event/league hosting
cost_structure: High fixed costs for real estate/leases, noise control, ballistic containment, ventilation, and insurance
Heavy compliance and reporting overhead tied to ATF/FBI-linked processes and firearm-transfer workflows
Labor and safety staffing costs, especially for range officers, training staff, and customer management
Consumable and utility costs for ammunition handling, target systems, and environmental controls; periodic capex for technology and refurbishment
major_players: No single national operator is described as holding a large enough market share (fragmented structure)
NSSF membership network and the broader local/club and private range ecosystem
FFL-linked store-and-range operators that combine retail traffic with range usage and training
Range equipment/operations technology suppliers supporting indoor systems and digital range control
current_dynamics: A demand cycle tied to firearms sentiment remains active but less extreme than earlier spikes, with operators focusing on retention-led programming and service mix improvements. Compliance modernization (ATF digital filing, NICS process management) increases administrative load but also reduces friction for larger structured operators; smaller players face higher fixed overhead relative to turnover.
whats_growing: Indoor and weather-independent range formats where feasible
Recurring revenue from memberships, classes, and skill ladders for new shooters
Digital/tech enhancements: smart-target systems, digital booking, and operational software
Training-linked demand from law-enforcement/public safety and competition circuits
whats_shrinking: Walk-in-only casual traffic in some urban/suburban markets during periods of competing leisure spending
Pure transaction/reliance on one-off visits without retention mechanics
Margin resilience for operators with older infrastructure and low productivity per lane
recent_developments: 2024-08 to 2024-12: NSSF Range Survey data collection window for the 2025 report period (indoor/outdoor/combo range categories).
2025-03-05: NSSF published 2025 Range Survey materials and report index.
2025: NSSF’s 2025 firearm and ammunition impact report noted 3.9 million new U.S. gun owners in 2024.
2025: FBI NICS annual report reported 8,740,825 firearm checks processed in FY2025 with 99,174 checks on Nov 28, 2025 (Black Friday peak).
2026-01-15: ATF firearms Q&A page update confirms Form 1/Form 4/SOT workflows and November 1, 2025 eForms submission pathways; updated operational guidance remains in effect.
outlook: The most likely 2026 trajectory is stable, low-single-digit growth with winners being operators that add training depth, automate compliance and booking, and shift toward membership ecosystems. Competitive pressure and slower discretionary spend suggest weak price power without operational differentiation, but sector entry barriers from know-how and safety standards still protect credible operators.
themes: Policy-linked demand volatility
Fragmented local operator structure
Compliance-heavy operating model
Shift from transaction sales to recurring participation
Technology-enabled safety and customer analytics
one_sentence: Demand remains steady but slower than in prior fire-sale cycles, with operators relying on service mix upgrades and compliance readiness to protect margins.
